messages.subject: PyStan debian package
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

PyStan almost has a Debian package. Using the package would eliminate the
lengthy Stan compilation step. My hope is to get the package done and included
in the Debian repository before the Ubuntu LTS release in the spring. This may
or may not be a realistic goal.

If anyone knows a Debian packager/developer I would appreciate an off-list email
with any tips on getting through the administrative steps. I know there's
a bunch of GPG/PGP key signing steps that need to happen.

Best,

Allen

messages.subject: Interface for just NUTS / HMC?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all, I have a problem where I have a target likelihood whose calculation isn't easy to write in a stan model (just trust me), but I can write down approximate gradients which are much easier to compute than the formal gradient calculation and virtually free after the painful likelihood calculation. I'd like to use Stan's implementation of NUTS and HMC adaptation rather than rolling my own (fewer points of failure etc). I don't see it in the documentation, but is there a hook whereby I can pass log-posterior and gradient values and let your implementation of NUTS do the step-size calculations? I see that the LaplacesDemon package has an all-R NUTS that I can probably modify if this isn't doable in Stan.

Thanks,
C Ryan King
University of Chicago

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Interface for just NUTS / HMC?
messages.body_plain:
I'm afraid there's no way to do this through our R interface.

If you wanted to write it into C++ and add a special distribution
you could use it in Stan.  But it's a lot of fussy C++ coding work
that involves understanding our derivatives.

- Bob

On 12/1/13, 11:51 AM, Ryan King wrote:
> Hi all, I have a problem where I have a target likelihood whose calculation isn't easy to write in a stan model (just
> trust me),

We're actually interested in cases like this to guide our
future development, but we understand not everyone is willing
to share model details.

> but I can write down approximate gradients which are much easier to compute than the formal gradient

You have to be careful that the gradients are good enough for
HMC.  Bad gradients won't change correctness, but they can seriously
affect speed.

> calculation and virtually free after the painful likelihood calculation. I'd like to use Stan's implementation of NUTS
> and HMC adaptation rather than rolling my own (fewer points of failure etc). I don't see it in the documentation, but is
> there a hook whereby I can pass log-posterior and gradient values and let your implementation of NUTS do the step-size
> calculations?

No.  The only way to do that is in our C++ interface, which
requires understanding the way our gradients get calculated
at a much deeper level than the Stan modeling language.

It's something we should think about adding.  It could make
some models more efficient than using auto-diff.

Most of the people with hairy log probability functions seem
to use plug-and-play samplers that are gradient free, like
DREAM or emcee.

> I see that the LaplacesDemon package has an all-R NUTS that I can probably modify if this isn't doable in
> Stan.

I'm not trying to spread FUD, but I'd be very careful to
check that you're getting the right answers from another
implementation of NUTS --- there are several subtleties in
the algorithm that affect detailed balance and hence correctness
that we would have messed up had we not had an extensive unit test
suite and developers who understand NUTS and its boundary
conditions.

A good way to test is with simulated data if you can calculate
quantiles and test both those and the posterior means.

- Bob

Thanks, and apologies: I see now that I asked a similar question last spring where I similarly failed to put a parameter in the parameter block. Hopefully that'll stick now!

However, moving both "vector[N] scale" and "vector[N] shape" to the parameter block continues to yield the initialization failure, this time with error messages indicating that something relating to my calls to lognormal() yields something negative when it should be positive, as in:

Error in function stan::prob::lognormal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random variable[0]  is -1.6254974062520904:0, but must be >= 0!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

Any suggestions on what I might still be doing improperly?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

>         shapePopMean ~ uniform(0,2);
>         scalePopSD ~ uniform(0,1);
>         shapePopSD ~ uniform(0,1);
>         scale ~ lognormal(scalePopMean,scalePopSD);

>                 thisScale[i] <- scale[unit[i]];

messages.body_plain:
Ben Goodrich於 2013年11月26日星期二UTC+8上午11時21分47秒寫道：

> On Monday, November 25, 2013 9:20:02 PM UTC-5, KK Sasa wrote:
> > My question is whether I can do the same thing in Stan as in MATLAB when the singular Sigma matrix is parameterized (fixed singular in estimation)?
> >
> > However, I found that the p. 273 in Stan manual reads
> >
> > vector eigenvalues_sym(matrix A)
> >      The vector of eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix A in descending order
> > matrix eigenvectors_sym(matrix A)
> >      The matrix with the eigenvectors of symmetric matrix A
> >
> > The eigenvalues are sorted by default, so does eigenvectors?
> > In addition, I found the R function 'eigen' also sorts the eigenvalues in decreasing order, too.
>
> Yes, this method works for any matrix M such that M * M' = A. In this case, M is equal to the matrix of eigenvectors post-multiplied by a diagonal matrix with square roots of eigenvalues, so you have to manually intervene to make sure the last eigenvalue(s) are not slightly negative when they are exactly zero theoretically. You can do it inside Stan that way. The ordering doesn't matter if you are just multiplying by iid standard normals.
>
> Ben
>

Thank you very much. Your feedback is extremely helpful for me!

Here comes a new question.
If I use the Eigenvector decomposition and want to truncate correlated samples (e.g., y > 0), is it possible to do this in Stan?
I know Stan offer the normal() T[], but it cannot perform when sigma is not positive definite.
So, this is why I resort to Eigenvector decomposition.

>
> Ben

I have to do a nested simulation step conditional on the current parameters using specialized external code (something like ABC) to compute summary statistics whose distribution I am interested in. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan Initial Value Set Error
messages.body_plain:
I've spent a little more time exploring this issue, and I'm starting to wonder whether it's there's a bug in STAN instead of an issue with my own ignorance. I ran a simple experiment in which I set initial values for a model using a simple normal distribution, or a simple exponential distribution.

In both cases, I ran the model without overtly setting the initial values of the chain. I then took the STAN generated initial values, using the "get_inits" function, and reran the model with those initial values that were previously used.

The normal distribution model runs fine this way. However, the exponential model reverts the initial values to the lower bounds of lambda, and only samples from that. In other words, the exponential model works just fine when allowing STAN to decide the initial values, but when you declare the initial values, even using previous ones that STAN decided on itself, it reverts to only sampling the declared lower bound of the lambda as the parameter value.

Since the model I'm actually trying to run (not these examples) relies heavily on exponential distributions, this is a big problem for me. I was wondering if any of the Devs (or someone else) could comment on whether this is in fact a bug, or if I'm completely missing something?

I've attached the models, and the R script that I used to test this.

Thanks again!
Ryan

What exactly do you mean by "reverts"?

If you mean the chain ends up at the lower bounds, you may have a
problem getting estimates from the initial values, but not a difference
based on how you set the initial values.

Specifically, your script has (with labels added)
#run a exponential distribution fit without specific initial values
# fit 1
exp_fit1 <- stan(file = 'model_ex_simple.txt', data = norm_dat,
                  iter = 100, chains = 2)
used_exp_inits1 <- get_inits(exp_fit1)
la_exp1 <- extract(exp_fit1)

#rerun the exponential distribution fit with the previously used initial values
# fit 2
exp_fit2 <- stan(file = 'model_ex_simple.txt', data = norm_dat,
                 iter = 100, chains = 2, init = used_exp_inits1)

used_exp_inits2 <- get_inits(exp_fit2)
la_exp2 <- extract(exp_fit2)

are you saying the chains from fit 1 and fit 2 are different?

Your problem sounds similar to mine (see the "tuning troubles" thread
from last month).  For some initial values the chain simply stayed on
the initial values for every step. It sounds as if you got some
movement, but it moved to a point at which it stuck (like my initial
values).

I suggest setting the seed argument to assure you (and others) can
reproduce your results.  Actually, I'm not sure if the seed argument to
stan will affect the initial value creation (previous discussion on this
list said it would not affect the values drawn from a user-defined
initialization function, but you are not using such a function).  To be
sure, you could call set.seed at the start of the script (as well as
using the seed argument to the stan function).

Ross

with the model, the data, or with Stan itself.

By the way, you don't need the upper=positive_infinity()
constraint --- no constraint is the default.  It's OK
to leave it --- there's just a run-time conditional evaluation
that reduces it to the lower-bound-only transform if there is a +infinity
upper bound.

> If you mean the chain ends up at the lower bounds, you may have a
> problem getting estimates from the initial values, but not a difference
> based on how you set the initial values.
>
> Specifically, your script has (with labels added)
> #run a exponential distribution fit without specific initial values
> # fit 1
> exp_fit1 <- stan(file = 'model_ex_simple.txt', data = norm_dat,
>                    iter = 100, chains = 2)
> used_exp_inits1 <- get_inits(exp_fit1)
> la_exp1 <- extract(exp_fit1)
>
> #rerun the exponential distribution fit with the previously used initial values
> # fit 2
> exp_fit2 <- stan(file = 'model_ex_simple.txt', data = norm_dat,
>                   iter = 100, chains = 2, init = used_exp_inits1)
>
> used_exp_inits2 <- get_inits(exp_fit2)
> la_exp2 <- extract(exp_fit2)
>
> are you saying the chains from fit 1 and fit 2 are different?

Unless you specify a seed in the call to Stan, you can expect
results to vary across calls.

> Your problem sounds similar to mine (see the "tuning troubles" thread
> from last month).  For some initial values the chain simply stayed on
> the initial values for every step. It sounds as if you got some
> movement, but it moved to a point at which it stuck (like my initial
> values).
>
> I suggest setting the seed argument to assure you (and others) can
> reproduce your results.  Actually, I'm not sure if the seed argument to
> stan will affect the initial value creation (previous discussion on this
> list said it would not affect the values drawn from a user-defined
> initialization function, but you are not using such a function).

The seed passed to Stan determines all randomization within calls to stan().

I'm pretty sure that includes initialization if you don't specify initial
values.  Our intent is to make the results exactly reproducible.  I opened
an issue to clarify the RStan doc on this point:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/31

> To be
> sure, you could call set.seed at the start of the script (as well as
> using the seed argument to the stan function).

set.seed() will determine the randomization within R.

If you use a specified seed in the function stan(), set.seed() won't have
any effect on the sampling within the call to stan().

If you do not specify a seed for the call to stan(), then R generates
the seed and passes it to Stan.  (See the doc for stan() in the RStan doc.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] RStan Initial Value Set Error
messages.body_plain:
On 12/3/13, 9:11 PM, Ryan Brackney wrote:
> Thanks for the notes, Bob and Ross. To clarify, in the exponential, set init case, the chain starts at the lowerbound,
> and stays there, in other words, the chains for the first and second run are very different.
>

>   The /only /difference between the runs is that Stan decided on the inits in the first run, and in the second run those

> very same inits are instead declared ahead of time. The data and model are the same in both cases, which is what makes
> me think this is an issue with Stan.

I want to tease apart two issues here.

1.  Reproducible inits

  Whether the behavior is reproducible using inits.  You
should get the same behavior if you specify the same seeds for
the call.  Can you try reproducing the problem using fixed
random seeds?

2.  Sampler getting stuck

Whether it's a bug in Stan for samples not to move is another
issue.  That's usually a model problem, but can indicate
a problem in Stan.  Diagnosing these kinds of problems with models
is one of the reasons we recommend using a diffuse set of initial
values.

Samples for parameters can get pinned at boundaries if the boundary
were removed and the probability mass is beyond the boundary.
For instance, if I do this:

   parameters {
     real<lower=10> y;
   }
   model {
     y ~ normal(0,1);
   }

you would expect to see the samples converge to y=10 in warmup
and then not move (or move very very little).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Parallel chains now supported (sort of)
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I'm resurrecting this thread to ask whether people have an opinion on the use of an mc.preschedule=FALSE flag in the mclapply function.

>From the help there:

if set to TRUE then the computation is first divided to (at most) as many jobs are there are cores and then the jobs are started, each job possibly covering more than one value. If set to FALSE then one job is forked for each value of X. The former is better for short computations or large number of values in X, the latter is better for jobs that have high variance of completion time and not too many values of X compared to mc.cores.

It seems to me that the latter is going to be the situation corresponding best to Stan. Has anyone compared these strategies?

Thanks

Tom

On Friday, October 12, 2012 6:14:45 AM UTC+2, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> Good news everyone (particularly people who are willing to help us test)! Jiqiang wrote a function that will be included in rstan 1.0.3 that facilitates running chains in parallel. In particular, you can do something like
>

> stopifnot(require(rstan))
>
> schools_dat <- list(J = 8,
>                     y = c(28,  8, -3,  7, -1,  1, 18, 12),
>                     sigma = c(15, 10, 16, 11,  9, 11, 10, 18))
>
> eight_schools <- stan(file = "http://wiki.stan.googlecode.com/git/rstangettingstarted/8schools.stan",
>                       data = schools_dat, iter = 1, chains = 1) # just get it to compile the model

>
> library(parallel) # or some other parallelizing package

>
> chains <- 8
>
> posterior <- mclapply(1:chains, mc.cores = chains, FUN = function(chain) { # or another parallelizing function
>                stan(fit = eight_schools, data = schools_dat, chains = 1, verbose = FALSE, refresh = -1, chain_id=chain)

>
>              })
>
> posterior <- sflist2stanfit(posterior) # see below for function definition
> print(posterior)
> plot(posterior)

>
> where the necessary new function sflist2stanfit() is defined at the end of this post and is also attached.
>
> Some things to note. In the example above, I first ran the eight schools model for one iteration of one chain just to get the code to compile. Then I passed that eight_schools object to the fit argument of stan() in each of the eight chains (with the defaults for warmup, iter, etc.). This route avoids having to recompile the code eight times and will work for mclapply() in the parallel package, which executes the function locally on a multicore machine. Note that mclapply() does not do anything in parallel on Windows, so you need to use an alternative parallelizing library / function in that case.
>
> This route will probably not work if you are using the snow package or a similar package to execute the chains on a remote server because the remote server will not know what to do with the code compiled on your laptop. In that case, you would need to specify file or model_code rather than fit, so that the remote server would compile the code for each chain. Also, if file is a filepath on your laptop, the remote server will not be able to access it, so you would need to upload your .stan file to a readable directory on the remote server and specify file accordingly. Similarly, the data somehow need to be available on the remote server and the remote server obviously needs to have rstan installed and loaded. Note that stanfit objects can be quite large in size, so you could be pulling GB of uncompressed data from the remote server to your laptop at the end.
>
> If you have access to some sort of computer lab with a bunch of physical PCs that have rstan but are not networked, you could execute stan() with chains = 1 on each PC, save the  resulting stanfit object to a USB stick with something like save(chain_3, file = "chain_3.RData", compress = "xz"), use the load() command to load each .RData object onto a common machine, put them into a list, and use sflist2stanfit() to consolidate them into a stanfit object that can be analyzed by the tools in the rstan package. Note that each chain needs to be given a different object name to avoid them overwriting each other when you load() them onto the common machine.
>
> For the high-performance (including parallel) capabilities that are available in R or R packages, execute help(package = parallel) in R or see
>
> http://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html
>
> Ben (but mostly Jiqiang)
>
> P.S. The new function below can be pasted in now but is now defined in the rstan tree at the end of
>
> https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/rstan/rstan/R/stanfit-class.R
>
> sflist2stanfit <- function(sflist) {
>   # merge a list of stanfit objects into one
>   # Args:
>   #   sflist, a list of stanfit objects, each element of which
>   #   should have equal length of `iter`, `warmup`, and `thin`.
>   # Returns:
>   #   A new stanfit objects have all the chains in each element of sf_list.
>   #   The date would be where the new object is created.
>   # Note:
>   #   * method get_seed would not work well for this merged
>   #     stanfit object. But all the information is still there.
>   #   * When print function is called, the sampler is obtained
>   #     only from the first chain.
>   #
>   sf_len <- length(sflist)
>   if (sf_len < 2) stop("'sflist' should have more than 1 elements")
>   if (!is.list(sflist) ||
>       any(sapply(sflist, function(x) !is(x, "stanfit")))) {
>     stop("'sflist' must be a list of 'stanfit' objects")
>   }
>   if (any(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@mode != 0))) {
>     stop("each 'stanfit' object in 'sflist' must contain samples")
>   }
>   for (i in 2:sf_len) {
>     if (!identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$pars_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi) ||
>         !identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$dims_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi))
>       stop("parameters in element ", i, " (stanfit object) is different from in element 1")
>     if (sflist[[i]]@sim$n_save[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1] ||
>         sflist[[i]]@sim$warmup2[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1])
>       stop("all 'stanfit' objects should have equal length of iterations and warmup")
>   }
>   n_chains = sum(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$chains))
>   sim = list(samples = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$samples)),
>              chains = n_chains,
>              iter = sflist[[1]]@sim$iter,
>              thin = sflist[[1]]@sim$thin,
>              warmup = sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup,
>              n_save = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1], n_chains),
>              warmup2 = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1], n_chains),
>              thin = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$thin[1], n_chains),
>              permutation = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$permutation)),
>              pars_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi,
>              dims_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi,
>              fnames_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$fnames_oi,
>              n_flatnames = sflist[[1]]@sim$n_flatnames)
>   nfit <- new("stanfit",
>               model_name = sflist[[1]]@model_name,
>               model_pars = sflist[[1]]@model_pars,
>               par_dims  = sflist[[1]]@par_dims,
>               mode = 0L,
>               sim = sim,
>               inits = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@inits)),
>               stan_args = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@stan_args)),
>               stanmodel = sflist[[1]]@stanmodel,
>               date = date(),
>               .MISC = new.env())
>   invisible(nfit)
> }
>

messages.body_plain:
Sounds like an empirical question that may also vary by hardware.
So the best thing to do would be to try it on whatever setup you're
going to use.  We'd love to hear the results.

You probably don't want to fork more processes than you have cores,
because then the OS has to do the swapping of processes over cores.
This probably won't be too bad unless you wind up also having to swap
large chunks of memory.

I'm not an R programmer, but the standard solution to this is some
kind of execution queue.  You push all the processes that need to be run
onto a queue.  Then, for each core you want to use, you pull a process
off the queue.  If a core's process finishes, it pulls the next job.
Scheduling processes across core is, in general, a complicated business,
especially when the process resource usage and execution priority varies.

Hyperthreading on Intel machines makes tuning confusing.  A CPU with
hyperthreading reports twice as many cores as there are physical cores.
My own experience is to cap the number of processes at the actual number
of cores, not the number of virtual cores, but your mileage may vary.

- Bob

>     and will work for _mclapply()_ in the parallel package, which executes the function locally on a multicore machine.
>     Note that _mclapply()_ does not do anything in parallel on Windows, so you need to use an alternative parallelizing

>     library / function in that case.
>
>     This route will probably not work if you are using the snow package or a similar package to execute the chains on a

>     *remote server* because the remote server will not know what to do with the code compiled on your laptop. In that
>     case, you would need to specify _file_ or _model_code_ rather than _fit_, so that the remote server would compile
>     the code for each chain. Also, if _file_ is a filepath on your laptop, the remote server will not be able to access

>     it, so you would need to upload your .stan file to a readable directory on the remote server and specify

>     _file_ accordingly. Similarly, the data somehow need to be available on the remote server and the remote server

>     obviously needs to have rstan installed and loaded. Note that stanfit objects can be quite large in size, so you
>     could be pulling GB of uncompressed data from the remote server to your laptop at the end.
>
>     If you have access to some sort of computer lab with a bunch of physical PCs that have rstan but are not networked,

>     you could execute _stan()_ with _chains = 1_ on each PC, save the  resulting stanfit object to a USB stick with
>     something like _save(chain_3, file = "chain_3.RData", compress = "xz")_, use the _load()_ command to load each
>     .RData object onto a common machine, put them into a list, and use _sflist2stanfit()_ to consolidate them into a

>     stanfit object that can be analyzed by the tools in the rstan package. Note that each chain needs to be given a

>     different object name to avoid them overwriting each other when you _load()_ them onto the common machine.

>
>     For the high-performance (including parallel) capabilities that are available in R or R packages,

>     _execute help(package = parallel)_ in R or see

>
>     http://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html
>     <http://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html>
>
>     Ben (but mostly Jiqiang)
>
>     P.S. The new function below can be pasted in now but is now defined in the rstan tree at the end of
>
>     https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/rstan/rstan/R/stanfit-class.R
>     <https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/rstan/rstan/R/stanfit-class.R>
>
>     |
>
>     sflist2stanfit <- function(sflist) {
>        # merge a list of stanfit objects into one
>        # Args:
>        #   sflist, a list of stanfit objects, each element of which
>        #   should have equal length of `iter`, `warmup`, and `thin`.
>        # Returns:
>        #   A new stanfit objects have all the chains in each element of sf_list.
>        #   The date would be where the new object is created.
>        # Note:
>        #   * method get_seed would not work well for this merged
>        #     stanfit object. But all the information is still there.
>        #   * When print function is called, the sampler is obtained
>        #     only from the first chain.
>        #
>        sf_len <- length(sflist)
>        if (sf_len < 2) stop("'sflist' should have more than 1 elements")
>        if (!is.list(sflist) ||
>            any(sapply(sflist, function(x) !is(x, "stanfit")))) {
>          stop("'sflist' must be a list of 'stanfit' objects")
>        }
>        if (any(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@mode != 0))) {
>          stop("each 'stanfit' object in 'sflist' must contain samples")
>        }
>        for (i in 2:sf_len) {
>          if (!identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$pars_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi) ||
>              !identical(sflist[[i]]@sim$dims_oi, sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi))
>            stop("parameters in element ", i, " (stanfit object) is different from in element 1")
>          if (sflist[[i]]@sim$n_save[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1] ||
>              sflist[[i]]@sim$warmup2[1] != sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1])
>            stop("all 'stanfit' objects should have equal length of iterations and warmup")
>        }
>        n_chains = sum(sapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$chains))
>        sim = list(samples = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$samples)),
>                   chains = n_chains,
>                   iter = sflist[[1]]@sim$iter,
>                   thin = sflist[[1]]@sim$thin,
>                   warmup = sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup,
>                   n_save = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$n_save[1], n_chains),
>                   warmup2 = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$warmup2[1], n_chains),
>                   thin = rep(sflist[[1]]@sim$thin[1], n_chains),
>                   permutation = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@sim$permutation)),
>                   pars_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$pars_oi,
>                   dims_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$dims_oi,
>                   fnames_oi = sflist[[1]]@sim$fnames_oi,
>                   n_flatnames = sflist[[1]]@sim$n_flatnames)
>        nfit <- new("stanfit",
>                    model_name = sflist[[1]]@model_name,
>                    model_pars = sflist[[1]]@model_pars,
>                    par_dims  = sflist[[1]]@par_dims,
>                    mode = 0L,
>                    sim = sim,
>                    inits = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@inits)),
>                    stan_args = do.call(c, lapply(sflist, function(x) x@stan_args)),

messages.subject: Re: near positive definite function
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, December 3, 2013 9:10:42 PM UTC-5, KK Sasa wrote:
> Will Stan offer a  function like 'nearPD' function in R?
> Can it  run efficiently if I code it in Stan by myself?

I don't think it is a good idea to have such a function. If the covariance matrix is fixed, then you can do some sort of a transformation of the small eigenvalues before passing it to Stan (or you can do it in transformed data if you want). If the covariance matrix is a parameter, then declaring it to be a cov_matrix or a corr_matrix or using an appropriate construction algorithm will guarantee that it is positive definite. We do have a problem in Stan where the tolerance for rejecting a matrix that is barely positive definite is too strict, but that will just result in some proposals being rejected, which is generally not a big deal.

Mike is doing something similar with a softabs transformation of the eigenvalues of the Hessian in the RMHMC branch, but that is a bit of a different animal (because the Hessian is actually indefinite at some points in the posterior distribution) and I doubt any of that would get exposed into the modeling language.

Ben

                                             +std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity()));

If someone can create an example where Stan produces different values given
the same inits and same seed for the two declarations (1) and (2), I'll create
an issue and track it down.

- Bob

messages.subject: GAM-like treatment of possibly-non-linear effects?
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

In my field, it is occasionally the case that we want to evaluate the degree to which
some variable, Y, might be influenced by another variable, X, where X is measured across a range of continuous values, and we are not sure whether to assume that the effect of X on Y forms a linear relationship or some sort of non-linear relationship. Before I became a Bayesian, I found generalized additive modelling (GAM) very useful in such cases, because it permitted me to evaluate whether there was a relationship between X and Y without being sure of the precise form of that relationship because GAM uses data-driven methods to find functions that best fit the data (linear or otherwise). Now that I'm doing things a Bayesian way, I'm stuck on what to do with this scenario; does stan have any features/tools for this sort of inference problem?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] increment_log_prob
messages.body_plain:
The transformation chapter of the manual explains when
you need a Jacobian adjustment and when you don't.

The short answer is that you only need a Jacobian adjustment
if you use a transformed variable on the left-hand side of
a sampling statement.  The reparameterization you're talking
about won't need one, because it's the raw (untransformed)
parameters that show up with the normal(0,1).

- Bob

frequent, so easier to search for.  The mailing list is for
all of Stan, so it's not because there's more mailing list comments

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: HMM_precipitation_amount
messages.body_plain:
What you need to implement for HMMs depends on your
inferential goals.  Which HMM architecture and set of
distributions you want to use depend on the application
model.  HMMs are a rather vaguely defined class of limited-memory
time-series models.

I don't know anything about precipitation, either in
chemistry or meteorology, so you'd need to say more about
what you're trying to do.  Is there a reference model someone
defined in a book or paper that you're trying to implement
in Stan?

Also, HMMs are a difficult entry point into Bayesian inference.
Without a lot of supervised data, they tend to have highly
multi-modal posteriors, and even with supervised data have issues
with index identifiability.  That, and to make them efficient enough
requires a lot of index fiddling in the Viterbi and/or forward-backward
algorithms.

- Bob

Size shouldn't matter --- it's a program after all.

how to use Stan and the language reference be the definitive guide

figuring most users wouldn't want to dive into the reference manual.

We could've put them in separate docs following the way R has

have one.  At some point it might get so huge we'll have to change

manuals.

messages.subject: Dirichlet process mixture of product multinomial distributions‏
messages.subject_clean: Dirichlet process mixture of product multinomial distributions‏
messages.body_plain:
Hello all

I am starting to work on an implementation of the nonparametric Bayesian model for high dimensional multivariate categorical data described in

David B. Dunson & Chuanhua Xing (2009) Nonparametric Bayes Modeling of Multivariate Categorical Data, Journal of the American Statistical Association, 104:487, 1042-1051, DOI: 10.1198/jasa.2009.tm08439
http://dx.doi.org/10.1198/jasa.2009.tm08439

Abstract:
Modeling of multivariate unordered categorical (nominal) data is a challenging problem, particularly in high dimensions and cases in which one wishes to avoid strong assumptions about the dependence structure. Commonly used approaches rely on the incorporation of latent Gaussian random variables or parametric latent class models. The goal of this article is to develop a nonparametric Bayes approach, which defines a prior with full support on the space of distributions for multiple unordered categorical variables. This support condition ensures that we are not restricting the dependence structure a priori. We show this can be accomplished through a Dirichlet process mixture of product multinomial distributions, which is also a convenient form for posterior computation. Methods for nonparametric testing of violations of independence are proposed, and the methods are applied to model positional dependence within transcription factor binding motifs.

I would like to know if there are any similar examples that could help guide me, and also whether to expect any particular problems with this kind of model using Stan.

Thanks
JK

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Dirichlet process mixture of product multinomial distributions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Dirichlet process mixture of product multinomial distributions
messages.body_plain:
There are no mechanisms for categorical sampling in Stan, but
this may not be an issue for you if the categorical part is just data,
which we can handle.

We also don't implement Dirichlet processes or any other Bayesian
non-parametric method that potentially relies on varying numbers
of parameters (such as Bayesian additive regression trees, aka BART).
Our samplers assume a fixed parameter space and although we'd like
to be able to do more, we don't have any plans to expand this part
of Stan any time soon.

Sometimes you can approximate a Dirichlet process with a simple
Dirichlet of high enough dimension.  Don't know if that'll work in
this problem or not.

And any mixture model is going to run into label-switching problems,
which you need to be aware of when looking at things like the
R-hat convergence diagnostics, which no longer work.  As far as I
know, it's an open research problem to measure convergence in these
settings.

Another huge problem is that these mixture models can be very multi-modal,
which is also something Stan's not good at sampling through (and no system
is good at sampling through if the combinatorics are bad enough, as they are
in say, latent Dirichlet allocation).

- Bob

messages.subject: prior for intercept
messages.body_plain:
I'm estimating a logistic model and treat the parameters mostly  as
beta[i] ~ normal(0, sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
Where the beta are grouped into bunches by sdclass.

The intercept is beta[1]; it doesn't seem reasonable to group it with
anything else, since the prior that it's around 0 is less plausible.
But if I do this sdclass[1] is being estimated with only one parameter.
It certainly can't be estimated well, but is this at all reasonable?

Wrinkle: I'm using the Matt trick; the real specification looks like (in
shorthand)
beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
beta_raw[2..J] ~ normal(0, 1)
beta[i] <- beta_raw[i]*sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5)  // sigma beta has ~ 4 elements

Can anyone comment on the wisdom of this (I suspect it is not wise!) and
suggest a better alternative?

I'm using this all in a model that is having problems, though I suspect
the main source of the problem is elsewhere, perhaps the fact that there
are 2 levels of clustering.  But this seems worth cleaning up.

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior for intercept
messages.body_plain:
Why not just pull the intercept out of the beta term and
give it whatever prior you think is reasonable?

If there's some other reason to keep everything in the same
vector, you could write:

   beta_raw[1] ~ ...whatever...
   for (j in 2:J)
     beta[j] <- beta_raw[j-1] * sigma_beta[sdclass[j-1]];

declaring sdclass and beta_raw to be of size J-1 rather than size J.

- Bob

On 12/7/13, 12:34 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> One thing is, it's completely kosher in Stan to just add another prior for beta[1] or sdclass[1] on top of everything else.
>
> On Dec 7, 2013, at 3:01 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>
>> I'm estimating a logistic model and treat the parameters mostly  as
>> beta[i] ~ normal(0, sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
>> Where the beta are grouped into bunches by sdclass.
>>
>> The intercept is beta[1]; it doesn't seem reasonable to group it with anything else, since the prior that it's around 0 is less plausible.  But if I do this sdclass[1] is being estimated with only one parameter.  It certainly can't be estimated well, but is this at all reasonable?
>>
>> Wrinkle: I'm using the Matt trick; the real specification looks like (in shorthand)
>> beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
>> beta_raw[2..J] ~ normal(0, 1)
>> beta[i] <- beta_raw[i]*sigma_beta[sdclass[i]]
>> sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5)  // sigma beta has ~ 4 elements
>>
>> Can anyone comment on the wisdom of this (I suspect it is not wise!) and suggest a better alternative?

Your suspicion is right.

The primary problem with the above is that there's no way to define a
parameter beta_raw in Stan that has support (-5,5) in dimension 1 and (-inf,inf)
elsewhere.

It'd be easier to declare beta_raw to be of size J-1,
sdlcass to not include the intercept, and then take:

   alpha ~ ...whatever prior you want for intercept...

   beta_raw ~ normal(0,1);

Then there's one of two options.  Closest to what you did
is put everything back together into a beta vector:

   beta[1] <- alpha;
   for (j in 2:J)
     beta[j] <- beta_raw[j-1] * sigma_beta[sdclass[j-1]];

The alternative is to just use the intercept directly in the
regression.  The second option seems clearer because it doesn't
have the ugly off-by-one indexing and makes the role of the separate
prior clearer.

Stan supports the (vector + scalar) operation, which
adds the scalar to each dimension of the vector.  So you can
still use matrix arithmetic in the linear predictor part of
the regression.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior for intercept
messages.body_plain:
What I'm saying is that unless you constrain beta_raw in
its declaration, the model's ill formed.

Conventions vary.  That's what R requires you to do, but
if you look at books, they use different conventions.

On 12/7/13, 5:00 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On Sat, 2013-12-07 at 13:45 -0500, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> Why not just pull the intercept out of the beta term and
>> give it whatever prior you think is reasonable?
>>
>> If there's some other reason to keep everything in the same
>> vector, you could write:
>>
>>     beta_raw[1] ~ ...whatever...
>>     for (j in 2:J)
>>       beta[j] <- beta_raw[j-1] * sigma_beta[sdclass[j-1]];
>>
>> declaring sdclass and beta_raw to be of size J-1 rather than size J.
>>
> It seemed more like conventional notation to make beta[1] the intercept.

Conventions vary.  Andrew and Jennifer's book compare several for
several different kinds of models.

> But I have already given it a special distribution, as I indicated for
> the "real" specification:
>   beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
>   beta_raw[2..J] ~ normal(0, 1)
>
> Are you saying that rather than estimate sigma for beta[1] to just
> specify a prior and be done with it?

Yes.

> E.g., now I have
> beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> sigma_beta[1] ~ cauchy(0, 5)
> beta[1] <- beta_raw[1] * sigma_beta[1]
>
> whereas I could just have
> beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> beta[1] <- beta_raw[1]  // if I keep my current handling of the
> intercept
>

IMPORTANT:  For robustness, Stan models need to have non-zero probability
for all variables satisfying declared constraints (i.e., the type
declarations define the intended support).  Any parameter values that satisfy
declared constraints but have 0 probability will get rejected, and if you init
there you'll never move and if the proper estimate is close, sampling will
be very inefficient.

So you can fix your model by constraining all beta_raw to fall
between -5 and 5, or by removing the uniform distribution on beta_raw
and giving it a prior with support on all of (-inf, inf).

> With some of the earlier models I fit I found that pre-specifying the
> scale parameter often worked poorly.

See Andrew's blog for discussion of informative priors.  You should
set them based on what you know about their possible values from
what you're trying to model.

You can use whatever prior you want for beta_raw[1].  The compound
uniform-Cauchy is an unusual choice.    You could just use a cauchy(0,5)
if you want something that will allow extreme values given enough data.
The tighter the prior, the more stable the computations will be.

> BTW I upped the target acceptance rate to 90% (after seeing the comments
> here and on dev that hierarchical models often need higher acceptance
> rates) and the estimates are behaving pretty well.

How does 0.8 work?  That's going to be our new default based on some
theoretical work Michael's doing.

> sigma_beta[1] had a
> median of 1.2 but a mean of 2.1.  beta[1] had mean and median of -1.4
> (sd = 0.8).  sigma_beta[1] had a much lower n_eff than most of the
> parameters.

Nor surprising --- sigma_beta[1] is the latent parameter in the
compound prior you set up.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
This question doesn't deal with Stan itself, so feel free to delete the thread if it doesn't fit the purpose of the Stan mailing list.

I have been working on a few spatial models, and models with measurement error on the dependent variable; I'd like to find a way of doing model comparison.

First, I am wondering how WAIC (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf) deals with data imputation and measurement error. Can the llpd and effective number parameters be calculated when the dependent variable is a random node itself?

Secondly, WAIC, like other metrics, seems to be derived under assumptions of independent errors. Some people have found that measures like AIC and BIC perform reasonably in model comparison in spite of violating these assumptions (using simulated data). Would it be insane to include a WAIC comparison in a paper comparing spatial models?

> This question doesn't deal with Stan itself, so feel free to delete the thread if it doesn't fit the purpose of the Stan mailing list.

Oh, we love these kinds of questions.

> I have been working on a few spatial models, and models with measurement error on the dependent variable; I'd like to find a way of doing model comparison.
>
> First, I am wondering how WAIC (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf) deals with data imputation and measurement error. Can the llpd and effective number parameters be calculated when the dependent variable is a random node itself?
>
> Secondly, WAIC, like other metrics, seems to be derived under assumptions of independent errors. Some people have found that measures like AIC and BIC perform reasonably in model comparison in spite of violating these assumptions (using simulated data). Would it be insane to include a WAIC comparison in a paper comparing spatial models?

Actually AIC is an approximation to WAIC, which is an approximation to the KL divergence between the predictive posterior predictive distribution and the true data distribution (assuming one exists).  It's really not as assumption of independent errors for WAIC, but rather an assumption that each datum is really two independent data (as in cross validation).

The nice thing about WAIC is that it's coordinate independent and correctly incorporates any measurement error in the model.  Data imputation is a different beast given that it rarely comes from a consistent model so that there's no way to validate it in a mathematically consistent way.

What is the question?  You just need to specify the seed to the call to stan().
If you want to reproduce R's behavior, you need to set the R seed (and make sure
any global variables in your scripts are the same before starting).

> 2. In section 23.3 of the manual "See Section 23.3.1 for a full explanation." is missing. As I need to know and
> understand more on Increment log probability for poisson_log(n,lambda).

I found two references to 23.3.1, which doesn't appear under
that number because the subsections aren't numbered.  I need
to change those references to names --- 23.3.1 is just the
first subsection of section 23.3.   I added a to-do item to
our manual update issue:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/325

> 3. Saving coda files for later use.

RStan doesn't read or write Coda files.

Stan's sampler does produce a stanfit object, from which samples
can be extracted.  The samples can also be converted to
a data frame or matrix.  The stanfit object can also be saved (without the
executable model) using the save() function in R and read
back in later with load().

If you're trying to compare Stan to BUGS or JAGS, note that the
effective sample size calcs are more conservative in Stan and that
you should only worry about number of effective samples per second.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Dirichlet process mixture of product multinomial distributions
messages.body_plain:
Looks like I have implemented the same model in a commercial setting. Collapsed Gibbs is very easy with this model, but getting it to converge to a good mode is harder. One way is to start with a small number of samples, then gradually put more samples in while the chain is running. This is a bit analogous to tempering: Initially, with only few data, the chain is able to switch modes easily.

Hyperparameter optimization or sampling (the DP parameter and the prior parameters of the multinomials, i.e., \beta in  Dir(\beta)) is important for good performance, especially with sparse data.

Yes, this should be doable with Stan if one marginalizes over the categorical variables. Look at the LDA example in the Stan manual. The code will look a bit ugly, for you have to increase the log-likelihood manually (there is no sampling statement of the type ~ sum(…)). Probably the best approach is to use the truncated stick breaking approach, as someone already suggested. (The alternative is a finite Dirichlet.)

Let us know if you succeed with Stan. I'm also interested on trying these models in Stan.

On Sunday, December 8, 2013 9:09:43 PM UTC+2, sophie wrote:
> Hi Joe,
>
> I am pretty familiar with this model because my thesis is based on this to handle missing data for many categorical variables (http://jeb.sagepub.com/content/38/5/499.full?keytype=ref&siteid=spjeb&ijkey=jYj38jOWx2Qns <http://www.google.com/url?q=http%3A%2F%2Fjeb.sagepub.com%2Fcontent%2F38%2F5%2F499.full%3Fkeytype%3Dref%26siteid%3Dspjeb%26ijkey%3DjYj38jOWx2Qns&sa=D&sntz=1&usg=AFQjCNEvu29xl4u0YlHjoxC0cZwfh2FeDA>). I have not implemented it into Stan due to the slow updating of  the number of latent classes. But I believe it is doable using the truncated stick-breaking representation of DP. Dunson and Xing lay out the steps using slice sampling in the paper, which can also be done using the approximate blocked Gibbs or exact blocked Gibbs. I can provide the references if you need.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data
messages.body_plain:
10^3 categorical outcomes is going to be a problem with
a lot of predictors if the predictors are sparse.

Stan scales with the number of subexpressions in the
evaluation of the log probability, so if the predictors
are dense and you have to evaluate (10^5 * 10^3) = 10^8
multiplications per data point, it's going to be very very slow
pretty much no matter what you do.    And Stan will blow out
memory if you try to do that, because we require on the order
of 24 bytes per subexpression storage.

You might want to try something like Vowpal Wabbit, which
can stream the data.  It can also help if the data's sparse
among a large potential set of predictors (things
like all 5-character sequences in Unicode) because it allows
a lower-dimensional representation.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimizing stan code
messages.body_plain:
On 12/9/13, 6:19 AM, Leon-Alph wrote:

> I'm trying to convert my OpenBugs model in Stan. Among two ways of writing my model, I'm wondering wich one is the best.

You can always try both.  But there are some general guidelines
in the chapter of the manuals on arrays vs. vectors/matrices.
And more below.

> Here is an example:
>
> _code1:_

> ...
> for(i in 1:N)
>     model {
>           Z1[i] ~ normal(a*X[i] + b*Y[i] , tau)
>           Z2[i] ~normal(a*Y[i] + b *X[i] , tau)
>     }
>

> _or code2:_

> ...
> for(i in 1:N)
>     model {
>            for( j in 1:2) {
>                 Z[i,j] ~ normal(a*X[i,j] + b*Y[i,j] , tau)
>             }
>       }

 > Is it the same code, for the value "tau"?

I'm not sure what the type of X, Y, and Z1 are here, and
it looks like they're being used differently in (1) and (2).
Also, the "for" has to go inside the model.

Loops are cheap in Stan, but calls to probability functions
are not.  So vectorizing the sampling statement is your
best bet.  Rewriting your model 2 (so that the order of rows
and columns of Z is reversed and it uses an efficient array
of vectors representation):

   vector[I] Z[2];
   vector[I] X[2];
   vector[I] Y[2];

   for (j in 1:2)

     Z[j] ~ normal(a * X[j] + b * Y[j], tau);

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm assuming the poster meant a 10^3 = 1000-dimensional multi-logit.
Then if there are 10^5 predictors and they're dense, you're
looking at 10^8 multiplications per data point!

10^3 outcomes show up all the time if you're trying to do something
like predict which tag a user will attach to a post.  You get 10^5 or
so if you're trying to attach ICD-10 codes to a patient's medical
record.  And lots of predictors from the natural language plus
database content.

Yes, we've fit models with 10^6 predictors and with 10^6 data
points, but IRT is very sparse.  Binary outputs with three parameters
per data point (discriminativeness of item, difficulty of item,
ability of student, with outcome being correctness of answer).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior for intercept
messages.body_plain:
I got good results with an acceptance rate of 0.8 and some tweaks to the
priors.  I just realized they were not exactly what I intended, and that
I still have conflicts between the declared support on the
distributions..

Over 3/4 of the parameters had effective sample sizes = number of
iterations.  That seems a little too good to be true.

As for the changes, I omitted the estimation of a scale parameter for
the intercept.  My effort to get the support of the prior to match the
corresponding declaration went too far.

            declaration  prior
old:
intercept       N         Y
other           N         N

new:
intercept       Y         Y
other           Y         N

"other" means non-intercept beta parameters.
N = no bounds
Y = bounded

The old problem was that the intercept had a bounded prior but an
unbounded declaration; the new problem is that the other terms have
unbounded priors but bounded declarations!

Doing this right would require either giving the intercept and other
beta different parameter names so that I can remove the bound on the
other parameters, or accepting the bounds throughout.

On the one hand, it would be outlandish if any effects were bigger than
5; on the other hand, putting a bound on a parameter that is then
multiplied by an arbitrary positive number seems silly.

I wonder if the bounds on all parameters contributed to the speed of the
solution (the iterations ran about 3x faster, even ignoring the increase
in n_eff).

Ross

Code for now (excerpts for beta):
parameters {
    vector<lower=-5,upper=5>[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
    real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
}
transformed parameters {
    vector[J] beta;
    beta[1] <- beta_raw[1];                                                                                                                                                                                        for(ir in 2:J) {
    for(ir in 2:J) {
       beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
    }
}
model {
    sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
    beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5); // redundant give bounds
    for (j in 2:J) {
      beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);  // inconsistent with bounds
    }
....

On Sat, 2013-12-07 at 17:29 -0500, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What I'm saying is that unless you constrain beta_raw in
> its declaration, the model's ill formed.
>
> Conventions vary.  That's what R requires you to do, but
> if you look at books, they use different conventions.
>
>
> On 12/7/13, 5:00 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> > On Sat, 2013-12-07 at 13:45 -0500, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> Why not just pull the intercept out of the beta term and
> >> give it whatever prior you think is reasonable?
> >>
> >> If there's some other reason to keep everything in the same
> >> vector, you could write:
> >>
> >>     beta_raw[1] ~ ...whatever...
> >>     for (j in 2:J)
> >>       beta[j] <- beta_raw[j-1] * sigma_beta[sdclass[j-1]];
> >>
> >> declaring sdclass and beta_raw to be of size J-1 rather than size J.
> >>
> > It seemed more like conventional notation to make beta[1] the intercept.
>
> Conventions vary.  Andrew and Jennifer's book compare several for
> several different kinds of models.
>
> > But I have already given it a special distribution, as I indicated for
> > the "real" specification:
> >   beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> >   beta_raw[2..J] ~ normal(0, 1)
> >
> > Are you saying that rather than estimate sigma for beta[1] to just
> > specify a prior and be done with it?
>
> Yes.
>
> > E.g., now I have
> > beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> > sigma_beta[1] ~ cauchy(0, 5)
> > beta[1] <- beta_raw[1] * sigma_beta[1]
> >
> > whereas I could just have
> > beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5)
> > beta[1] <- beta_raw[1]  // if I keep my current handling of the
> > intercept
> >
>
>
> IMPORTANT:  For robustness, Stan models need to have non-zero probability
> for all variables satisfying declared constraints (i.e., the type
> declarations define the intended support).  Any parameter values that satisfy
> declared constraints but have 0 probability will get rejected, and if you init
> there you'll never move and if the proper estimate is close, sampling will
> be very inefficient.
>
> So you can fix your model by constraining all beta_raw to fall
> between -5 and 5, or by removing the uniform distribution on beta_raw
> and giving it a prior with support on all of (-inf, inf).
>
> > With some of the earlier models I fit I found that pre-specifying the
> > scale parameter often worked poorly.
>
> See Andrew's blog for discussion of informative priors.  You should
> set them based on what you know about their possible values from
> what you're trying to model.
>
> You can use whatever prior you want for beta_raw[1].  The compound
> uniform-Cauchy is an unusual choice.    You could just use a cauchy(0,5)
> if you want something that will allow extreme values given enough data.
> The tighter the prior, the more stable the computations will be.
>
> > BTW I upped the target acceptance rate to 90% (after seeing the comments
> > here and on dev that hierarchical models often need higher acceptance
> > rates) and the estimates are behaving pretty well.
>
> How does 0.8 work?  That's going to be our new default based on some
> theoretical work Michael's doing.
>
> > sigma_beta[1] had a
> > median of 1.2 but a mean of 2.1.  beta[1] had mean and median of -1.4
> > (sd = 0.8).  sigma_beta[1] had a much lower n_eff than most of the
> > parameters.
>
> Nor surprising --- sigma_beta[1] is the latent parameter in the
> compound prior you set up.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Sorry for the ambiguity. I am interested on a LASSO-type variable selection model. I am actually interested on a model:

Y = b_0 + GBX + Zu + e

with Y and nx1 matrix, X and nxk predictor's matrix, B a vector of coefficients and G a vector indicator variables which formally are the probability of the predictor to be associated with the outcome. The indicator variables generates the simplest form of the peak and slab prior.
The model was presented on Hanni P. Kärkkäinen and Mikko J. Sillanpää "Back to Basics for Bayesian Model Building in Genomic Selection" (http://www.genetics.org/content/191/3/969.abstract). Z diagonal matrix (when the Y observations are iid) and u ~ N(0,A*sigma_u) with A a symmetric dense matrix with A_{ij} being a distance measure between the y_{i} and y_{j} observation. In my application Y are observations for individuals and the matrix A measures the relatedness between individuals (e.g., 0.5 between siblings or 0.125 between cousins) and it is important on this models.

The authors presented a Generalised Expextation Maximisation algorithm to fit the model and obtain MAP estimates making use of conjugate priors through  but the MAP estimates underestimate the uncertainty of the B and G parameters and leads to overoptimistic results, i.e., too many false positives. I know the same model using MCMC leads to appropriate estimates.

In particular I am interested on extending the above model with a second level regression on the indicator variables, like
G ~ t_0 + TH (this would in practice be a probit or logistic model to link this linear predictor to a 0 to 1 variable)
with H a kxp matrix of predictor covariates and T the corresponding coefficients linking the predictor's covariates to the predictor's indicator variables. The idea is to allow the G indicator variables to borrow information from other predictors with similar covariates.

On a real data the dimensions would be:
n = 10^3 - 10^4
k = 10^4 - 10^6
p = 10^2

The X matrix would have predictors with values between 0 and 2 that are normalized to have mean = 0 and variance = 1.

So, more detailed questions:
1- Do you think STAN will be able to work on this model? Do you have any examples of code for this?
2- If the answer to 1 is yes, Any suggestions on what to do or not to do to implement this model?
3- On the extended model I am interested on I think I should be able to sample the T coefficients and the predictor variables G would become determined, so that could reduce the number of parameters. Is that thinking right ?

Thanks a lot in advance for your help,

PS: A similar model to Y = b_0 + GBX + Zu + e was presented by Xiang Zhou et al (http://www.plosgenetics.org/article/info%3Adoi%2F10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1003264).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Start sampling from well equilibrated values from previous run
messages.body_plain:
Per usual I have to advocate caution in these matters.  The problem is that as you add more data the neighborhood
of high posterior mass shrinks, so "equilibrated" values for small data may in fact be far away from equilibrium when
you add more data.

That said, my guess here is that adaptation is amplifying any changes as it tries to relearn the local curvature.

One option is to turn adaptation off entirely (sample adapt engaged=0) and set the step size to a previously learned value
(sample algorithm=hmc stepsize=0.001).  We do not yet have the capability of setting the metric explicitly.  The issue here
is that the optimal step size will likely shrink with more data so you'd want to allow adaptation.

Another option is to allow the step size to adapt but not the metric (sample algorithm=hmc metric=unit_e).  If your
parameters have varying scales this will lead to much less efficient sampling but smoother adaptation.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Failure to initialise after specifying upper bound
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Failure to initialise after specifying upper bound
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tom,

The issue has to do with initial values for constrained variables (and it touches on underflow). The manual covers both these things in full detail in:
* Chapter 20.2. "Initialization." See the section on "Random Initial Values."
* Chapter 49. "Transformations of Variables"

I'll try to add some concrete examples, but I would suggest re-reading those sections.

>From Tom's model:

Without the upper bound:

We'll just take a look at one of the variables, mu_p. It was originally declared as
    real<lower=0> mu_p;

with a prior of:
    mu_p ~ lognormal(log(2.0), 1);  // or lognormal(0.7, 1)

The defaults of Stan will initialize the *unconstrained* variable uniformly from -2 to 2. This puts the constrained variable, the mu_p, on a range of 0.13=exp(-2) to 7.39=exp(2), with the unconstrained value of 0 being mapped to a constrained value of 1=exp(0).

[In theory, since lognormal has support over where the parameter is constrained, this should work out just fine. In practice, due to restrictions on floating point arithmetic, some of these calculations will underflow and it isn't fine. At some value of mu_p way outside the prior mass, the calculation will underflow and the evaluation of lognormal_log(mu_p, 0.7, 1) will return -Inf. It's hard to add -Inf to other numbers without the result being -Inf or NaN.]

So, without the upper constraint on mu_p, there's a chance this will get initialized properly if the unconstrained value is sampled from -2 to 0 (I'm eyeballing it). In the model, p is also given the same constraint and there are 25k of those.

In some sense, it's amazing that the model initializes to something that it can calculate by randomly choosing starting values from -2 to 2 on the unconstrained scale.

With the upper bound

Let's change the parameter and see where the initialization takes us.
   real<lower=0,upper=10> mu_p;

Going into the manual, Chapter 49.4, "Lower and Upper Bounded Scalar," we see that the transformation is:
   X = a + (b - a) * logit^-1(Y),
where a is the lower bound, b is the upper bound, and Y is the unconstrained value.

So (-2, 0, 2) on the unconstrained scale corresponds to (1.2, 5, 8.9) on the constrained scale. That looks high.

This variable alone won't cause a problem, but having 25k other variables and other calculations pushes the calculation to -Inf.

Simple Example: uniform

Here's a simple example. The difference with uniform is that there isn't support everywhere, so it's easier to make it fail. This model works fine.

parameters {
  real theta;
}
model {
  theta ~ uniform(-1, 1);
}

Let's change theta to have a lower bound of 0 and an upper bound of 10.
  real<lower=0,upper=10> theta;

Stan can't find an appropriate starting value.

Possible Fixes

Here are a couple of possible fixes.
Provide initial values. Help your model out a bit. Give it starting values that has some probability mass.
Think about your model.
Perhaps reconsider the constraints on your parameters.
Rethink priors. The prior on mu_p is pretty narrow. Should it be if you're really saying mu_p could be between 0 and 10?

That's it for now. Hopefully that's enough to get your model working.

Daniel

> I got good results with an acceptance rate of 0.8 and some tweaks to the

> distributions..
>
> Over 3/4 of the parameters had effective sample sizes = number of
> iterations.  That seems a little too good to be true.

NUTS is very effective if the posterior's normal.

The effective sample sizes are estimated as shown in the manual,
using a conservative variance estimate based on the same chain
splitting and within/across calculations as for R-hat.

> As for the changes, I omitted the estimation of a scale parameter for
> the intercept.  My effort to get the support of the prior to match the
> corresponding declaration went too far.
>
>              declaration  prior
> old:
> intercept       N         Y
> other           N         N
>
> new:
> intercept       Y         Y
> other           Y         N
>
> "other" means non-intercept beta parameters.
> N = no bounds
> Y = bounded
>
> The old problem was that the intercept had a bounded prior but an
> unbounded declaration; the new problem is that the other terms have
> unbounded priors but bounded declarations!
>
> Doing this right would require either giving the intercept and other
> beta different parameter names so that I can remove the bound on the
> other parameters, or accepting the bounds throughout.

Exactly --- that's what I was trying to say in my previous reply
in the paragraph marked "IMPORTANT".

> On the one hand, it would be outlandish if any effects were bigger than
> 5; on the other hand, putting a bound on a parameter that is then
> multiplied by an arbitrary positive number seems silly.

Not silly if you want to help identify it.  Better yet to
skip the multiplication and just use the "arbitrary" positive number.
That's what I was suggesting for reparameterization by pulling
the intercept out from the slopes.

> I wonder if the bounds on all parameters contributed to the speed of the
> solution (the iterations ran about 3x faster, even ignoring the increase
> in n_eff).

Yes --- tightening priors will help --- it has the effect of tightening
the prior on the unconstrained space where sampling is done.
The chapter near the end of the manual provides details, but you'll need
to ask Michael for intuitions about the geometric aspects of the problem.

- Bob

There is a section (section 19.2 in the manual for Stan v2.0.1) discussing vectorization
in the "Optimizing Stan Code" chapter of the manual.  There is a discussion of
arrays vs. vectors in the chapter on containers (chapter 8 in v2.0.1).

One note about your #method 3:  Given that the mean is fixed at 0,
you'd want to declare that as a transformed data parameter rather than
a local variable.  Transformed data is not auto-diffed, so is much
more efficient than using a local variable, which will be an auto-diff
variable if declared in the model block.  See figure 24.3 in v2.0.1.

Sorry the doc's so long!

- Bob

Hello,

I wanted to inquire about the status of initial parameter specification with pystan.

I'm checking because I have found that I get an "INDEX OPERATOR" error (below) when I specify initial parameters.  Many of the parameters in my model (including the flagged raw_t1.) are 2 dimensional, with the first dimension tagging the object ID and the second dimension equaling 5 (the number of type options for the data).  The error only happens when I specify initial parameters and try to fit the model with more than 1 object, i.e. the parameter shape specified to be [>1,5] (one object, or [1,5], works fine).  Fitting the model with more than 1 object works fine with random initial parameters.

Note that I don't think this problem is due to incorrect dimensions in the initial parameter specification.  If I introduce a problem of that type, I get a different error ("mismatch in number dimensions declared and found in context").

Any suggestions for how to debug or fix this problem are welcome, and my thanks to the PyStan team!

Best,

~Nathan

messages.body_plain:
On 12/10/13, 5:46 AM, Inti Pedroso wrote:
> Hi,

> Sorry for the ambiguity. I am interested on a LASSO model. I am actually interested on a model:

>
> Y = b_0 + GBX + Zu + e

> with Y and nx1 matrix, X and nxk predictor's matrix, B a vector of coefficientsand G a vector indicator variables which

> formally are the probability of the predictor to be associated with the outcome. The indicator variables generates the
> simplest form of the peak and slab prior.

Andrew's got issues with these priors:

http://andrewgelman.com/2012/09/07/prior-distributions-for-regression-coefficients/

If the spike really is a delta function, Stan has problems
because it intrinsically involves sampling from a discrete
distribution, which Stan doesn't do.  So you can't explicitly
model a discrete unknown indicator in Stan.

Without a true delta-function spike, there will be zero
probability mass associated with coeff=0.  Is that OK?

> The model was presented on Hanni P. K�rkk�inen and Mikko J. Sillanp�� "Back to Basics for Bayesian Model Building in

> Genomic Selection" (http://www.genetics.org/content/191/3/969.abstract). Z diagonal matrix (when the Y observations are
> iid) and u ~ N(0,A*sigma_u) with A a symmetric dense matrix with A_{ij} being a distance measure between the y_{i} and
> y_{j} observation. In my application Y are observations for individuals and the matrix A measures the relatedness
> between individuals (e.g., 0.5 between siblings or 0.125 between cousins) and it is important on this models.

Right --- that's typical of linkage analyses and shouldn't itself
be an issue.

> The authors presented a Generalised Expextation Maximisation algorithm to fit the model and obtain MAP estimates making
> use of conjugate priors through  but the MAP estimates underestimate the uncertainty of the B and G parameters and leads
> to overoptimistic results, i.e., too many false positives. I know the same model using MCMC leads to appropriate estimates.
>
> In particular I am interested on extending the above model with a second level regression on the indicator variables, like
> G ~ t_0 + TH (this would in practice be a probit or logistic model to link this linear predictor to a 0 to 1 variable)

I'd stick to logistic for efficiency.

> with H a kxp matrix of predictor covariates and T the corresponding coefficients linking the predictor's covariates to
> the predictor's indicator variables. The idea is to allow the G indicator variables to borrow information from other
> predictors with similar covariates.
>
> On a real data the dimensions would be:
> n = 10^3 - 10^4
> k = 10^4 - 10^6
> p = 10^2

I think it's going to be close with 10^4 to 10^6 predictors.
That's k * n multiply-adds required for the basic regression for
each log prob evaluation --- at the low end, that's 10M and
at the high end of your ranges, it's 10G.  Assuming you pack
this into matrix multiplies, the lower end will fit in memory,
but the higher end almost certainly not.

What's p?  Is that the dimensionalty of the second level regression?

> The X matrix would have predictors with values between 0 and 2 that are normalized to have mean = 0 and variance = 1.
>
> So, more detailed questions:
> 1- Do you think STAN will be able to work on this model? Do you have any examples of code for this?

We have lots of hierarchical regression models, but not this specific one.
There are all the ARM models from Jennifer and Andrew's book.  There

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure exactly what you mean by starting smoothly.

Unless you explicitly turn adaptation off, Stan's going
to start from your initial values and adapt both a diagonal mass
matrix (roughly inverse scales of the various parameters) and
a step size.  Step size gets adapted based on a target acceptance
probability and the mass matrix is estimated from warmup samples
in increasingly large blocks (always using only the last half or
so of the warmup iterations for the next estimate in order to
forget bad starting points).

The next release of Stan (2.1.0) will make the warmup more
flexible in terms of windows, but it's not clear that if you dramatically
up the data size that the same step sizes and mass matrix will be applicable.
I'm sure Michael has a better handle on this than I do.

- Bob

On Tue, Dec 10, 2013 at 4:42 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> Hi Tom,
>
> The issue has to do with initial values for constrained variables (and it touches on underflow). The manual covers both these things in full detail in:
> * Chapter 20.2. "Initialization." See the section on "Random Initial Values."
> * Chapter 49. "Transformations of Variables"
>
> I'll try to add some concrete examples, but I would suggest re-reading those sections.
>
>
> From Tom's model:
>
> Without the upper bound:
>
> We'll just take a look at one of the variables, mu_p. It was originally declared as
>     real<lower=0> mu_p;
>
> with a prior of:
>     mu_p ~ lognormal(log(2.0), 1);  // or lognormal(0.7, 1)
>
> The defaults of Stan will initialize the *unconstrained* variable uniformly from -2 to 2. This puts the constrained variable, the mu_p, on a range of 0.13=exp(-2) to 7.39=exp(2), with the unconstrained value of 0 being mapped to a constrained value of 1=exp(0).
>
> [In theory, since lognormal has support over where the parameter is constrained, this should work out just fine. In practice, due to restrictions on floating point arithmetic, some of these calculations will underflow and it isn't fine. At some value of mu_p way outside the prior mass, the calculation will underflow and the evaluation of lognormal_log(mu_p, 0.7, 1) will return -Inf. It's hard to add -Inf to other numbers without the result being -Inf or NaN.]
>
> So, without the upper constraint on mu_p, there's a chance this will get initialized properly if the unconstrained value is sampled from -2 to 0 (I'm eyeballing it). In the model, p is also given the same constraint and there are 25k of those.
>
> In some sense, it's amazing that the model initializes to something that it can calculate by randomly choosing starting values from -2 to 2 on the unconstrained scale.
>
> With the upper bound
>
> Let's change the parameter and see where the initialization takes us.
>    real<lower=0,upper=10> mu_p;
>
> Going into the manual, Chapter 49.4, "Lower and Upper Bounded Scalar," we see that the transformation is:
>    X = a + (b - a) * logit^-1(Y),
> where a is the lower bound, b is the upper bound, and Y is the unconstrained value.
>
> So (-2, 0, 2) on the unconstrained scale corresponds to (1.2, 5, 8.9) on the constrained scale. That looks high.
>
> This variable alone won't cause a problem, but having 25k other variables and other calculations pushes the calculation to -Inf.
>
>
> Simple Example: uniform
>
> Here's a simple example. The difference with uniform is that there isn't support everywhere, so it's easier to make it fail. This model works fine.
>
> parameters {
>   real theta;
> }
> model {
>   theta ~ uniform(-1, 1);
> }
>
> Let's change theta to have a lower bound of 0 and an upper bound of 10.
>   real<lower=0,upper=10> theta;
>
> Stan can't find an appropriate starting value.
>
>
>
> Possible Fixes
>
> Here are a couple of possible fixes.
> Provide initial values. Help your model out a bit. Give it starting values that has some probability mass.
> Think about your model.
> Perhaps reconsider the constraints on your parameters.
> Rethink priors. The prior on mu_p is pretty narrow. Should it be if you're really saying mu_p could be between 0 and 10?
>
>
> That's it for now. Hopefully that's enough to get your model working.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>

The spike in the original spike and slab is not a true delta function, although its role is certainly that of a delta, that is, to represent coefficients that are practically zero.

Spike and slab could well be a realistic prior in some applications. Genetics ((maybe too) broadly speaking) is an obvious example. Even if it is not realistic, it may be practical, if models with such a prior can be estimated. Results from models with a huge number of potential predictors are kind of work hypotheses anyway. They point to possible effects that should be further tested and quantified.

(I have played with doubly hierarchical Cauchy priors in Stan months ago, and was surprised of their power to choose variables form simulated data with a large number of predictors, around 1–10x number of samples. None of the priors was probably not the true spike and slab, though. The Cauchy geometry is hard for Stan, or HMC or almost any sampler, so these might be difficult to get scaled to large data. R's spikeSlabGAM has a different, dedicated sampler, maybe Gibbs, and it is usable at least for ~10000 observations and ~1000 predictors.)

messages.body_plain:
Christian,

Just to verify, you run the below code first then run again with adaptation off?

If adaptation is off and you're seeing huge variations in iteration timing then you're likely dealing with a very nasty posterior (a consequence of concentration of measure with increasing dimension that I had mentioned before).  This is very common in hierarchical models where there are tails with very high curvature that cause HMC to become numerically unstable and get stuck (same thing happens with other sampling algorithms and it's all a consequence of the geometry of the underlying distribution).

That said, there is a lot you can improve in your model.  Firstly, use poisson_log() intend of poisson(exp( ) ).  Secondly, you need to use a non-centered parameterization for the eta[i], a la

hat_eta[i] ~ multi_normal(0, 1) // Actually faster to define hat_eta as a matrix and use vectorization with the univariate normal(0, 1) here
eta[i] <- Sigma * hat_eta[i] + mu

This will go a long way to improving the geometry of your posterior and dramatically speed up sampling (in big hierarchical models it's not uncommon to get speed ups of a few orders of magnitude).
