messages.subject: [stan-users] I hate the slab
messages.body_plain:
This is getting off-topic, but . . . let me say that the "spike" may be reasonable in various settings where there are many small effects that are indistinguishable from 0.  My problem is more with the "slab."  Real, nonzero effects still tend to be concentrated not toooo far from 0.  I like lasso because it does some partial pooling.  The slab doesn't do any pooling at all.
A

P.S.  If you really want to work with Cauchy models in Stan, perhaps it would make sense to hard-code a reparameterization so that the distribution has a more reasonable tails in the transformed space.

On Dec 11, 2013, at 1:17 PM, Janne Sinkkonen wrote:

> The spike in the original spike and slab is not a true delta function, although its role is certainly that of a delta, that is, to represent coefficients that are practically zero.
>
> Spike and slab could well be a realistic prior in some applications. Genetics ((maybe too) broadly speaking) is an obvious example. Even if it is not realistic, it may be practical, if models with such a prior can be estimated. Results from models with a huge number of potential predictors are kind of work hypotheses anyway. They point to possible effects that should be further tested and quantified.
>
> (I have played with doubly hierarchical Cauchy priors in Stan months ago, and was surprised of their power to choose variables form simulated data with a large number of predictors, around 1–10x number of samples. None of the priors was probably not the true spike and slab, though. The Cauchy geometry is hard for Stan, or HMC or almost any sampler, so these might be difficult to get scaled to large data. R's spikeSlabGAM has a different, dedicated sampler, maybe Gibbs, and it is usable at least for ~10000 observations and ~1000 predictors.)
>

messages.body_plain:
The model and the way its coded are two issues.  You get the
same number of effective samples per iteration with vectorized
vs. unvectorized code, because you'll get exactly the same samples.
Stan's behavior is fully determined by the log probability function
and the random number generation seed.

The vectorized code will take less time per iteration.

The model dictates how the statements have to be grouped,
then just vectorize as much as you can given the model for
efficiency.

Reparameterization in hierarchical regressions is also often
very useful --- see the chapter in the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan with large data
messages.body_plain:
Unfortunately I don't remember details related to the speed of spikeSlabGAM. I had 8000 samples and the number of predictors varied in hundreds, and it was not inconveniently slow, at most tens of minutes (or a couple of hours?) per run.

spikeSlabGAM has a hierarchy that pools related parameters, i.e., those that are of a particular spline, variable, interaction or random effect. So the prior is somewhat modified from the original spike and slab, but probably not the way Andrew suggests.

I have no affiliation with either the spike or the slab… but an ultra-concave prior does seem useful sometimes.

There is also a machine learning paper in which a sampler with spike-and-slab priors outperformed L1 with CV, under a fixed CPU budget: http://arxiv.org/pdf/1106.1157.pdf

On Wednesday, December 11, 2013 6:56:40 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> On 12/11/13, 7:17 AM, Janne Sinkkonen wrote:
> > ...R's spikeSlabGAM has a different, dedicated sampler, maybe Gibbs,
> > and it is usable at least for ~10000 observations and ~1000 predictors.)
>
> Those sizes should be possible in Stan --- it's only
> 10M multiplications and a 1K-dimensional gradient.  It's the
> 100-times or 1000-times bigger problem that will blow out memory.
>
> How fast is spikeSlabGAM?  Stan's not going to fit a problem this
> size instantly.

messages.subject: Pystan parallelization status
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a question about the status of parallelization in Pystan v.2.0.1.2.  The n_jobs parameter of pystan.stan says, in the docstring, "Sample in parallel."  My expectation is that this means multiple cores will be used to sample from multiple chains in parallel, and the other (more complicated) possibility would seem to be that it parallelizes some of the sampling steps within individual chains. But in my tests it's not clear to me that either is working.

What I find is that, regardless of the value of n_jobs, only 1 core on my CPU seems to be utilized and the chains seem to sample in serial.  Additionally, the sampling time reported by Pystan seems to be the same either way, so I don't think there is any speedup.  I do see that model.py imports and uses multiprocessing, and I can confirm that this python module is installed on my system.

Below I have pasted example input and output using the 8 schools model and data from the Pystan Getting Started page.

~Nathan

> >
> > Y = b_0 + GBX + Zu + e
>
> > with Y and nx1 matrix, X and nxk predictor's matrix, B a vector of coefficientsand G a vector indicator variables which
> > formally are the probability of the predictor to be associated with the outcome. The indicator variables generates the
> > simplest form of the peak and slab prior.
>
> Andrew's got issues with these priors:
>
> http://andrewgelman.com/2012/09/07/prior-distributions-for-regression-coefficients/
>
> If the spike really is a delta function, Stan has problems
> because it intrinsically involves sampling from a discrete
> distribution, which Stan doesn't do.  So you can't explicitly
> model a discrete unknown indicator in Stan.
>
> Without a true delta-function spike, there will be zero
> probability mass associated with coeff=0.  Is that OK?
>

messages.subject: comment on stan manual
messages.body_plain:
I'd love to see an example of linear regression with multiple predictors, y=Xb+error, in vector-matrix form.  That is, an example where the predictors come in as a matrix and the coefficients are estimated as a vector, but just regular linear regression.  I'm trying to write such a model, and the difficulty is that the first example with vector notation for b is in section 12.5, but then there's also a bunch of other things going on with softmax etc., so it's hard for me to figure out exactly what I need to do.

So I'll try to figure it out and write it up as a section in the Stan manual, I think it would go right in section 12.1, it doesn't really need a new section since it's not a new model.

So, since I am doing it, just a quick question:  is there a way of doing such a model so that the likelihood can be written in a single line (without a loop)?

Also, this is just personal taste, but in that example in Section 12.5, is it really the best advice to give different lower bounds on K, N, and D in the data statements?  I understand what you're doing:  you need at least 2 outcomes, at least 0 data points, and at least 1 beta, but to me, as a user, I find all this a bit intimidating.  A simple int K,N,D; would do the job just fine for me (or, if they have to be on separate lines:  int K; int N; int D;).  I understand the value of supplying info in the declaration, but I worry that a user will get tangled in these details and, if anything, I could see someone being _more_ likely to mess up because of screwing up somehow in the bounds in the declarations (for example, giving a lower bound of 2 on D).  So in this (and similar) examples, I'd vote for not putting any bounds on the discrete parameters, with a note saying that there is a tradeoff:  giving a correct bound is a debugging device and provides some information about the model, but the cost is that the declarations look more complicated and there is a chance of getting it wrong.

A

messages.subject: Re: WAIC in the context of spatial models, data imputation/censoring, and/or measurement error
messages.subject_clean: WAIC in the context of spatial models, data imputation/censoring, and/or measurement error
messages.body_plain:
Cody> "First, I am wondering how WAIC (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf) deals with data imputation and measurement error. Can the llpd and effective number parameters be calculated when the dependent variable is a random node itself?"

I assume that you have multivariate dependent variable y_ij, where i=1,...,n and j=1,...p.  I think it is easiest first to think how CV would work as WAIC is approximation of CV. There's two options.

The first options is the pure M-open approach (see http://dx.doi.org/10.1214/12-SS102 for discussion of M-open etc.) where you compute the llpd only for the observed outputs. For example, if p=2 the collection of lppd_i's contain mix of terms p_post(-i)(y_i1), p_post(-i)(y_i2), p_post(-i)(y_i1,y_i2) depending which observations y_ij are missing. As same observations are missing for all models, obtained lppd_CV is ok for model comparison.

The second option is to use mix of M-open and M-completed/closed approaches. For example, if p=2 the collection of lppd_i's contain the terms p_post(-i)(y_i1,y_i2), where in case of missing data we integrate over the missing data distribution using the imputation model (which may be problematic if the imputation algorithm is not consistent as Mike warned).

In the case of measurement error, I assume that you have all observations and it's just that your model is slightly more complicated.

WAIC can be used in these cases, too. The first option is simpler to implement.

Cody> "Secondly, WAIC, like other metrics, seems to be derived under assumptions of independent errors. Some people have found that measures like AIC and BIC perform reasonably in model comparison in spite of violating these assumptions (using simulated data). Would it be insane to include a WAIC comparison in a paper comparing spatial models?"

If WAIC is derived from cross-validation it does not need the assumption of independent errors. The prediction task consists of a collection of independent marginal predictions (1a). It depends on your decision problem, whether this the correct prediction task or should you care more about the joint predictions (1b). Although WAIC and CV are asymptotically equal, they assume slightly different prediction tasks: WAIC) interested in the predictions only at the observed covariate values (2a), CV) interested in the predictions also at the not yet observed covariate values (2b). If your answer is 1a+2a, then WAIC is sane choice although it seems that it can break sometimes when using very flexible models (like Gaussian process or Markov random field spatial models). See the slides http://www.lce.hut.fi/~ave/slides_trondheim.pdf (we are writing a paper about this and further developments).

Mike> "Actually AIC is an approximation to WAIC, which is an approximation to the KL divergence between the predictive posterior predictive distribution and the true data distribution (assuming one exists).  It's really not as assumption of independent errors for WAIC, but rather an assumption that each datum is really two independent data (as in cross validation)."

cross-validation assumes exhangeability, not independence

To summarise: if your choice is between WAIC or some other *IC, use WAIC. If you can use CV, it is a more robust choice.

You're even more literal than me!

Are you trying to follow the instructions in:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/wiki/RStan-Getting-Started

If not, I'd say try that first, then help us make them better
where they're not clear.

There is a section:

   Special Steps for Xcode 5.0.1 + R 3.0.2 + Mac OS X 10.9 (Mavericks)

which says:

   you need to create a file

     ~/.R/Makevars

   with content

     CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++

     CXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"

I just modified it to read:

   You need to create or edit the file

     ~/.R/Makevars

   so that its content is exactly

     CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++

     CXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"

I hope that helps.

If other things are unclear in the install instructions, please let
us know and we can try to reword them.

- Bob

messages.subject: custom model: truncated data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to try out STAN to do  parameter estimation for a model.
Lets start simple.

I have a parameter vector v, which I would like to determine.

My log-likelihood is

ln L = D1*v + D2*v + ... + Dn*v - n * (v * A)

I have n vectors, D1 to Dn, of the same length as v. Di * v is a vector multiplication (element-wise multiplication, then sum). A is another vector. (For explanation, this is a binomial likelihood for truncated data, A is the response, and D correspond to the probabilities over the vector, which is a discretisation of a parameter space).

How do I implement this simple model in STAN?

Is there *any* example code for C++ available?

Later on, I would like to do something slightly more advanced, in the likelihood and priors.
Still, it will not exceed using addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and
the exponential function, so it should be autodiff-able.

Kind regards,
                      Johannes

PS: my email is johannes.buchner.acad [ät] gmx.com <http://gmx.com> . But Google Groups requires a Google account as far as I can see :(

On 12/12/13, 2:25 PM, gel...@stat.columbia.edu wrote:
> The difficulty isn't just the cutting-and-pasting, it's also that a new
> file needs to be created, and that it is being put in a weird place.  For
> example, if there were a file to save, and I clicked on it in the Mac, I'd
> have no way to navigate to ~/.R/

My understanding is that given the way R does builds from source,
there's no way to get around this configuration step.  Something needs
to put that text in that file.

You can copy it into the right place from the terminal using "cp" or
move it there using "mv".  You can create the file in R and save it
into that directory (maybe easiest for an R user?  Do you know how to
do that in R?).  Or we could provide a file and you could save it.
But then you need to know how to save in your browser on your operating
system.

The "~/" is a unix shorthand for your home directory.   For me, it's
a synonym for "/Users/carp".  In Safari (the Mac built-in web browser),
you select menu option "File >> Save as...", and it pops up a little
dialog box and under the heading "FAVORITES", I see "carp", which is
my home directory.  Now the problem.  Because R chose to use ".R" (as
is popular for config), it doesn't get listed by default when you click
on your home directory.  But, if you type "~" into the "Export as" box,
it will pop up another dialog box that will let you type the full
path to the file in, here "~/.R/", and hit return, it will go to .R and
list the contents.    Then you can add Makevars.

It's hard to know where to stop our instructions in terms of how to
interact with browsers and operating systems.  We assumed people knew
how to create and store files, but it looks like we assumed too much
given the tricky nature of this file.

I'm worried about just piling in instructions.  Then people don't read
them.  You'll note that the last comment from Shravan on your blog
was asking for simpler instructions --- that's because he knew how to
do all the little things we were trying to explain.

We drew the line at telling users how to make a file and
put it in a directory, but perhaps we should keep on going down and give
people a bit more tutorial on using Safari and the Mac OS?  The
issue is that then the instructions get huge.  Or maybe we have a
"help on this step" button that pulls out more information?

- Bob

Hi, Bob.  I don't think that we need to tell users how to save a file into a directory.  After all, I was able to do it, it just wasn't so easy.   But I think the following instructions would be easier (see below).  Perhaps Jiqiang can take a look and make sure the command is bulletproof.
A

---

>From the R console:

> if (!file.exists ("~/.R/Makevars")) cat ('CXX=g++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256 -stdlib=libstdc++\nCXXFLAGS="-mtune=native  -O3 -Wall -pedantic -Wconversion"\n', file="~/.R/Makevars")

---

On Dec 12, 2013, at 9:33 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>

> On 12/12/13, 2:25 PM, gel...@stat.columbia.edu wrote:
>> The difficulty isn't just the cutting-and-pasting, it's also that a new
>> file needs to be created, and that it is being put in a weird place.  For
>> example, if there were a file to save, and I clicked on it in the Mac, I'd
>> have no way to navigate to ~/.R/
>
> My understanding is that given the way R does builds from source,
> there's no way to get around this configuration step.  Something needs
> to put that text in that file.
>
> You can copy it into the right place from the terminal using "cp" or
> move it there using "mv".  You can create the file in R and save it
> into that directory (maybe easiest for an R user?  Do you know how to
> do that in R?).  Or we could provide a file and you could save it.
> But then you need to know how to save in your browser on your operating
> system.
>
> The "~/" is a unix shorthand for your home directory.   For me, it's
> a synonym for "/Users/carp".  In Safari (the Mac built-in web browser),
> you select menu option "File >> Save as...", and it pops up a little
> dialog box and under the heading "FAVORITES", I see "carp", which is
> my home directory.  Now the problem.  Because R chose to use ".R" (as
> is popular for config), it doesn't get listed by default when you click
> on your home directory.  But, if you type "~" into the "Export as" box,
> it will pop up another dialog box that will let you type the full
> path to the file in, here "~/.R/", and hit return, it will go to .R and
> list the contents.    Then you can add Makevars.
>
> It's hard to know where to stop our instructions in terms of how to
> interact with browsers and operating systems.  We assumed people knew
> how to create and store files, but it looks like we assumed too much
> given the tricky nature of this file.
>
> I'm worried about just piling in instructions.  Then people don't read
> them.  You'll note that the last comment from Shravan on your blog
> was asking for simpler instructions --- that's because he knew how to
> do all the little things we were trying to explain.
>
> We drew the line at telling users how to make a file and
> put it in a directory, but perhaps we should keep on going down and give
> people a bit more tutorial on using Safari and the Mac OS?  The
> issue is that then the instructions get huge.  Or maybe we have a
> "help on this step" button that pulls out more information?
>
> - Bob
>
>
>>
>> Ideally we could have some code to cut and paste directly into the R
>> console that would write the file.  Would that be possible?  Other parts
>> of the Stan instructions involving cutting and pasting into the R console,
>> and that seems to work well.
>>
>> A
>>
>>>
>>>
>>> On 12/12/13, 1:19 PM, gel...@stat.columbia.edu wrote:
>>>> OK, now it works.  I had been missing one character when I cut and
>>>> pasted
>>>> the strings into that file using vi.
>>>>
>>>> Maybe we can have new instructions that don't require the user to cut
>>>> and
>>>> past into a file etc???
>>>
>>> Any suggestion on how we do this?  Someone else did

>>>
>>> Would it be easier to just link a file to download and replace the
>>> existing one with?
>>>
>>> (All of these problems seem to stem R's global config that
>>> lives outside of wherever the package downloads.)
>>>
>>> - Bob

messages.subject: speeding up a space-time model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi again Stan team,

I've been running a spatio-temporal model using Stan. The model is written as a predictive process where we sample at knots throughout the domain. The smooth spatial process (the vegetation) is then linked to count data (pollen) through a dirichlet multinomial process. I would like to run the model for a large spatial domain, but things are quite slow (2 days and still on first iteration). Currently I am subdiving the domain so I can get results, but this is not ideal. The attached data is for one of these sub-domains that has about ~3000 parameters (6 different spatial processes with about 50 knots each, times the number of times which is about 10). There are some matrices that are quite large (16000000 entries), that get built and multiplied, but I didn't think this was huge.

Sampler seems to do well, but it takes a (very) long time. I'm looking for ways to speed this up, but am not quite sure where the bottle-neck is. When I try to profile, the model seems to spend a lot of time in the agrad namespace - is this the auto-diff computing the gradient? I can write down my gradient by hand, and suspect that using this will make things faster, but I see a previous post on the users list (see: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/gradient/stan-users/RqT5SZFn9Ks/XzmpEJvDnGQJ) which seems to suggest that it's more complicated than writing down the gradient and modifying the C++ code. I'm not quite sure what Bob means when he refers to log Jacobian determinant adjustments...

Any thoughts on adjustments I could make to speed things up, or ideas about where the bottle-neck is?

Cheers,
Andria

>
> My log-likelihood is
>
> ln L = D1*v + D2*v + ... + Dn*v - n * (v * A)

> I have n vectors, D1 to Dn, of the same length as v. Di * v is a vector multiplication (element-wise multiplication,

You can just code this directly in Stan.

>
> Is there *any* example code for C++ available?

The unit tests in src/test are the simplest examples of how the
C++ functions work.

There's also a doc on the Wiki on GitHub on writing
user functions.

And there's  doc on the Wiki (may not be up to date) on what the
target of compling a model is.  From there, you'd need to work through
what the main does.

It's a bit complex because of the I/O and constraints and the
transforms/Jacobians for constrained params.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speeding up a space-time model?
messages.body_plain:
What you likely need is the multi_gp distribution that I implemented a few months back.  It's been pending someone having the time to write some more unit tests.  You can follow the pull request here: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/350

Of more immediate practical note here are a few tips:
- inverse() is *very* inefficient in Stan right now.  It's also generally a bad idea to explicitly compute the inverse of a matrix unless you absolutely have to.  I expect that if you can rewrite your model without inverse it would probably be faster.
- As strange as it sounds, it's almost always faster to create a large vector full of entries and then call sum(vec) than looping to sum the entries on the fly.
- C_t doesn't depend on k at all, so it would be much faster to construct it (and C_t_inv if you really need it) outside of the loop over k.  That way it's only done once.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: new web site
messages.body_plain:
I played around using pandoc to convert LaTeX -> HTML.  The only things giving it problems were the use of \vspace in the \date macro and the use of the \Verb macro (which it didn't recognized as starting a verbatim area). Editing those out produced a reasonable result, although it didn't translate all the macros; what I noticed was that \sf, font sizes, and the custom macros like \fitem, \farg didn't translate.  The branch https://github.com/jrnold/stan/tree/feature/pandoc-manual has the results of my hacking.

If you want to support LaTeX->PDF & HTML output, then my best guess is that the easiest way to do that would be to rewrite the reference in pandoc's markdown and then use pandoc to convert it into LaTeX to PDF and HTML, using specialized templates and snippets of LaTeX or css for each conversion. It may still work with the original in LaTeX if the problem LaTeX is removed, but might require a little heavier postprocessing to get HTML output.
I'm not saying its worth the time to do that, but as far as I am aware, that would be the easiest way to do.

On Wednesday, December 11, 2013 11:43:00 PM UTC-8, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I'd love to see an example of linear regression with multiple predictors, y=Xb+error, in vector-matrix form.  That is, an example where the predictors come in as a matrix and the coefficients are estimated as a vector, but just regular linear regression.  I'm trying to write such a model, and the difficulty is that the first example with vector notation for b is in section 12.5, but then there's also a bunch of other things going on with softmax etc., so it's hard for me to figure out exactly what I need to do.
>
> So I'll try to figure it out and write it up as a section in the Stan manual, I think it would go right in section 12.1, it doesn't really need a new section since it's not a new model.
>
> So, since I am doing it, just a quick question:  is there a way of doing such a model so that the likelihood can be written in a single line (without a loop)?
>
> Also, this is just personal taste, but in that example in Section 12.5, is it really the best advice to give different lower bounds on K, N, and D in the data statements?  I understand what you're doing:  you need at least 2 outcomes, at least 0 data points, and at least 1 beta, but to me, as a user, I find all this a bit intimidating.  A simple int K,N,D; would do the job just fine for me (or, if they have to be on separate lines:  int K; int N; int D;).  I understand the value of supplying info in the declaration, but I worry that a user will get tangled in these details and, if anything, I could see someone being _more_ likely to mess up because of screwing up somehow in the bounds in the declarations (for example, giving a lower bound of 2 on D).  So in this (and similar) examples, I'd vote for not putting any bounds on the discrete parameters, with a note saying that there is a tradeoff:  giving a correct bound is a debugging device and provides some information about the model, but the cost is that the declarations look more complicated and there is a chance of getting it wrong.
>
> A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] comment on stan manual
messages.body_plain:
On 12/14/13, 2:43 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> So, since I am doing it, just a quick question:  is there a way of doing such a model so that the likelihood can be
> written in a single line (without a loop)?

The yet-to-be-written FAQ should be pointing you to page 166/167
of the 2.0.1 manual.  I think that has what you're looking for.

It probably makes sense to duplicate the model back in the
regression section because this is the obvious way to write
the model for users with even a basic comfort level with matrix
multiplication.

> ... So in this (and similar) examples, I'd vote for not putting any bounds on the
> discrete parameters,

This is just data --- there are no discrete parameters in Stan.
I'm not just being pedantic here.  Data constraints are optional
and may (a) help with debugging, (b) help clarify the model, and/or (c)
confuse everyone (user and reader).  Parameter constraints are also
optional, but if you don't include them, chances are sampling will be
either inefficient or not work at all.

> with a note saying that there is a tradeoff:  giving a correct bound is a debugging device and
> provides some information about the model, but the cost is that the declarations look more complicated and there is a
> chance of getting it wrong.

Let's present this discussion in the manual and leave it
up to the users.  It's more likely in my experience that users
will provide too lax a bound (or no bound at all as is your
preference).  If they get tangled in the bound and make it too
strict, they'll find that out when they try to read in data.

I can present the model first your way and then with stricter
constraints.

The real issue's where to put all of these things, since we can't
expect users to read the whole manual.

- Bob

> Of more immediate practical note here are a few tips:
> - inverse() is *very* inefficient in Stan right now.  It's also generally a bad idea to explicitly compute the inverse of a matrix unless you absolutely have to.  I expect that if you can rewrite your model without inverse it would probably be faster.
> - As strange as it sounds, it's almost always faster to create a large vector full of entries and then call sum(vec) than looping to sum the entries on the fly.
> - C_t doesn't depend on k at all, so it would be much faster to construct it (and C_t_inv if you really need it) outside of the loop over k.  That way it's only done once.

foo.sm <http://foo.sm> <- stan_model("foo.stan", ...)

foo.sf <- sampling(foo.sm <http://foo.sm>, data=...)

would be better than:

but I've not tried - and I'd like to look at warnings.

the command line.  RStan rewrites the command.hpp to
use R I/O and data structures rather than what the command

it could be done in the code:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/453

The same sort of thing will need to be done for RStan (and
presumably PyStan).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] silent stan?
messages.body_plain:
As you've observed on the R mailing lists, the easy questions
get more attention.

Like all of our minor bug fixes, it requires a few minutes
to create the issue, a few minutes to code, probably an hour
to write tests for (which should've been there in the first
place), then a few more minutes to get it code reviewed, then
as long as it takes to get it through Jenkins integration testing
without failure.   But then it takes longer if we can't get
it reviewed, if someone has comments on the way it's written
and it needs to be rewritten, if another fix comes in in parallel
and they need to be merged, etc..

Overall, I'd be surprised if we could fix an issue like this
using our current process in less than several person hours
and less than forty CPU, hours (about how long our tests
take to run --- we do four cores in parallel, so that's only
ten hours wall time).

The reason we're being so Draconian on all the testing is
that we don't want "little fixes" like this one to break
anything else that matters.

I think the real danger is that we spend all of our time
effectively straightening our desks and marching in tune with
our process on issues like this one and less time on the
issues that really matter.

messages.body_plain:
It's easy.
Let's say that the model is in a "foo.stan" file:

A)
rt <- stanc("foo.stan", model_name = "foo")
foo.sm <http://foo.sm> <- stan_model(stanc_ret = rt)

B)
foo.sm <http://foo.sm> <- stan_model("foo.stan", model_name = "foo")

If your model is a string, such as

foo.string <- "
data { ... }
parameters { ... }
model { ... }
"

then:

A)
rt <- stanc(model_code = foo.string, model_name = "foo")
foo.sm <http://foo.sm> <- stan_model(stanc_ret = rt)

B)
foo.sm <http://foo.sm> <- stan_model(model_code = foo.string, model_name = "foo")

Sergio

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Varying intercepts, varying slopes model
messages.body_plain:
On 12/15/13, 5:47 PM, Shravan Vasishth wrote:
> I just fit a varying intercepts, varying slopes model analogous to this model in lmer:
>
> lmer(y ~ x + (1+x|fac1) + (1|fac2),data)
>
> My question is: do I compute the estimate for the correlation parameter (the correlation between the varying intercepts
> and varying slopes) by looking at the variance covariance matrix estimated for random effects, and computing the
> estimate of rho from there? In JAGS, I could have defined a prior on rho and explicitly specified that that has to be
> estimated.

These days we like to do what you did and use a scaled correlation matrix
as a hierarchical prior.  Using the LKJ(2) prior you're using, there's a slight
regularization toward the identity correlation.

You can then just read the correlation out of
the entries in the correlation matrix in the posterior.  The usual
estimate would be the posterior mean (which is itself a correlation
matrix because the class of correlation matrices is closed under averaging).

You could also have translated the JAGS model directly including
the Wishart priors and read out rho in the same way as you did there.

If you have some other kind of covariance prior, you can just calculate
correlation in the usual way (divide by scales of the parameters).

The best overview I know of the available priors in Stan is this paper
from Goodrich et al. which we've discussed here before:

It would be easier to see how these models align if you
used the same variable names.    The rho in your JAGS model
is used as follows:

 >          sigma.a ~ dunif(0,10)
 >          sigma.b ~ dunif(0,10)

 >          rho ~ dunif(-1,1)

 >          R[1,1] <- pow(sigma.a,2)
 >          R[2,2] <- pow(sigma.b,2)
 >          R[1,2] <- rho*sigma.a*sigma.b
 >          R[2,1] <- R[1,2]

 >          Omega.u  ~ dwish( R, 2 )

 >          Sigma.u <- inverse(Omega.u)

 >          # Intercept and slope for each person, including random effects
 >          for( i in 1:I )
 >          {
 >             u[i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(zero,Omega.u)
 >          }

I don't understand why you have so many levels.  I would've
expected R to be a constant because there's only a single Omega.u.

The usual correlation to expect would be for the hierarchical
prior for u:

   Sigma.u[1,2] / ( sqrt(Sigma.u[1,1]) * sqrt(Sigma.u[2,2]) )

Stan:

 >     parameters {
 >       ...

 >       corr_matrix[2] Omega;     // correlation matrix for random intercepts and slopes

 >     transformed parameters {
 >       cov_matrix[2] Sigma;  // constructing the variance/cov matrix for random effects

 >         for (c in 1:2) {
 >           Sigma[r,c] <- sigma_u[r] * sigma_u[c] * Omega[r,c];
 >         }
 >       }
 >     model {

 >       for (i in 1:I)
 >         u[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_prior, Sigma);  // loop for subj random effects

And the Sigma.u in JAGS is (I'm pretty sure) the same Sigma
as in your Stan model (though with a different prior).

 > And related to that,
> when I do not specify a prior for the correlation,

If you have a correlation parameter, you need to constrain it to (-1,1),
which provides a proper uniform prior.  A correlation matrix without
a prior also gets an implicit proper uniform distribution over all correlation
matrices.

> is it legitimate to compute correlation from the estimated variance
> components for varying intercept and slope? If I know these two quantities and the value in the off-diagonal, I can
> compute the correlation even though it is never mentioned in the model. I hope my question is making sense.

I'm not sure what you mean here.

- Bob

I meant that if you could write an appropriate C++,
we could add it to Stan itself (appropriate means that
it has templates for all the double-type parameters and
that it has error checking and unit tests;  lots of examples
in the Stan code itself).

It looks like Genz's MATLAB function implementation is under
new BSD.  His R package is GPL-ed, which is too restrictive
to go into the core of Stan (we're maintaining new BSD for Stan).

There's not a good way of writing Stan extensions without
modifying the Stan code.  There are some hints on how to do
that here:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Contributing-New-Functions-to-Stan

A mechanism for user-defined extensions along the lines of
that used by Eigen is on our short-term to-do list.  And when
we do that, we'll doc it more thoroughly.

There's also this paper:

  http://www.jstatsoft.org/v52/i10/paper

- Bob

Thanks!

> My question really is: if I want to look at the posterior distribution
> of the correlation parameter in Stan, should I just construct the
> variance covariance matrix cell-wise as I did in the corresponding JAGS
> model?

If you define priors for the std devs, you can_
a) construct a covariance matrix, then compute the correlation(s);
b) construct diagonal matrix, D=diag(sigma), and define a correlation
matrix.
In the first case, you'll use:

for (i in 1:I) u[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_prior, Sigma);

In the second one, since
Sigma = D * Omega * D = D(LL')D = (DL)(DL)'
where L is the Cholesky factor, you can use:

matrix[2,2] L;
matrix[2,2] DL;
L <- cholesky_factor(Omega);
DL <- D * L;
for (i in 1:I) u[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, DL);

which is more effcient (example attached: vasishth2.stan).

> And related to that, when I do not specify a prior for the
> correlation, is it legitimate to compute correlation from the estimated
> variance components for varying intercept and slope?

Omega without a prior is just implicitly Omega ~ lkj_corr(1), i.e. a
uniform (joint) prior. Correlations are there and you don't need to
compute them.

> If I know these two
> quantities and the value in the off-diagonal, I can compute the
> correlation even though it is never mentioned in the model.

Of course (toy example attached: corr.R).

> I hope my
> question is making sense.

I hope my answers make sense!

On Mon, Dec 16, 2013 at 3:13 PM, Sergio Polini <srgp...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Il 16/12/2013 08:28, Shravan Vasishth ha scritto:
>
> > You can download all data and code from a course on data analysis that
> > I'm teaching right now:

> > data: http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/data/gibsonwu2012data.txt
> >
> > And here is all the relevant
> > code: http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth/lmmexamplecode.txt
>
> Thanks!
>
>
> > My question really is: if I want to look at the posterior distribution
> > of the correlation parameter in Stan, should I just construct the
> > variance covariance matrix cell-wise as I did in the corresponding JAGS
> > model?
>
> If you define priors for the std devs, you can_
> a) construct a covariance matrix, then compute the correlation(s);
> b) construct diagonal matrix, D=diag(sigma), and define a correlation matrix.
> In the first case, you'll use:
>
>
> for (i in 1:I) u[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_prior, Sigma);
>
> In the second one, since
> Sigma = D * Omega * D = D(LL')D = (DL)(DL)'
> where L is the Cholesky factor, you can use:
>
> matrix[2,2] L;
> matrix[2,2] DL;
> L <- cholesky_factor(Omega);
> DL <- D * L;
> for (i in 1:I) u[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, DL);
>
> which is more effcient (example attached: vasishth2.stan).
>
>
> > And related to that, when I do not specify a prior for the
> > correlation, is it legitimate to compute correlation from the estimated
> > variance components for varying intercept and slope?
>
> Omega without a prior is just implicitly Omega ~ lkj_corr(1), i.e. a uniform (joint) prior. Correlations are there and you don't need to compute them.
>
>
> > If I know these two
> > quantities and the value in the off-diagonal, I can compute the
> > correlation even though it is never mentioned in the model.
>
> Of course (toy example attached: corr.R).
>
>
> > I hope my
> > question is making sense.
>
> I hope my answers make sense!
>
> Sergio (just a learner)

> --

On 12/16/13, 5:51 AM, Shravan Vasishth wrote:
...

> On Mon, Dec 16, 2013 at 9:04 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
...

>      > And related to that,
>
>         when I do not specify a prior for the correlation,
>
>
>     If you have a correlation parameter, you need to constrain it to (-1,1),
>     which provides a proper uniform prior.  A correlation matrix without
>     a prior also gets an implicit proper uniform distribution over all correlation
>     matrices.

Which, as Sergio points out, is the same as an lkj_correlation(1) prior,
because in lkj_correlation(nu), nu - 1 is a power, so when it's 1, everything's
constant.  Just like the beta or Dirichlet in that regard.  When nu > 1, the
probability mass concentrates around the unit correlation matrix.  You can work
out explicitly what it does for a 2 x 2 correlation matrix by evaluating the determinant,
which only has one variable (symmetric, diagonal constrained to 1).

- Bob

> Hi, Shravan. Others can give you better advice than I can, but my quick guess is that you do not want to be parameterizing the covariance matrix piece by piece in this way.  I think it will be much better to just give a prior to the covariance matrix and let it go at that.  Also, I think you might be able to speed your code with some vectorization.
> A
>
> On Dec 16, 2013, at 8:29 PM, Shravan Vasishth <vasishth...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Thanks to Sergio and Bob, I fit a slightly more complicated model (psycholinguistic models can be quite a bit more complex than this). This one has three contrasts (plus an intercept) and then varying intercepts by subject, and varying slopes, i.e., six correlations and four variance components are estimated for the subject, and of course the variance for the residuals.
> >
> > The data are from: http://openscience.uni-leipzig.de/index.php/mr2/article/view/11
> >
> > I link the data here <https://www.dropbox.com/s/pwuz1g7rtwy17p1/KWDYZ_test.rda>.
> >
> > The code is given below. One surprising thing is that Stan runs amazingly slow (MacBook Air OS X 10.6).  I thought Stan was supposed to be fast. Am I doing something wrong? (Bob, I tried to indent the comments, it was OK on my editor, but it got messed up once I copied it into this google groups message window; sorry about that).
> >
> > ## data source:
> > ## http://read.psych.uni-potsdam.de/pmr2/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=10:kliegt-type&catid=11:publications&Itemid=13
> >
> > library(lme4)
> > # Various transformations stored in the following data frame
> > load("KWDYZ_test.rda")
> >
> > summary(m2 <- lmer(rt ~ 1 + c1 + c2 + c3 + (1 + c1 + c2 + c3 | id),
> >                     data=dat))
> >
> > library(car)
> > qqPlot(residuals(m2))
> >
> > #getME(m2, name="theta")
> > #confint(m2, method="boot")  # Takes a long time
> >
> > ## Stan analysis:
> > dat2 <- list(mu_prior=c(0,0,0,0),
> >                      id=sort(as.integer(factor(dat$id))),
> >                      rt = dat$rt,
> >                      c1 = dat$c1,
> >                      c2 = dat$c2,
> >                      c3 = dat$c3,
> >                      N = nrow(dat),
> >                      I = length(unique(dat$id)))
> >
> >
> > klieglvaryingintslopes_code<- 'data {
> > int<lower=1> N;
> > real rt[N];                         //outcome
> > real c1[N];                         //predictor
> > real c2[N];                         //predictor
> > real c3[N];                         //predictor
> > int<lower=1> I;                     //number of subjects
> > int<lower=1, upper=I> id[N];        //subject id
> > vector[4] mu_prior;                 //vector of zeros passed in from R
> > }
> > parameters {
> > vector[4] beta;                     // intercept and slope
> > vector[4] u[I];                     // random intercept and slopes
> > real<lower=0> sigma_e;              // residual sd
> > vector<lower=0>[4] sigma_u;         // subj sd
> > corr_matrix[4] Omega;               // correlation matrix for random intercepts and slopes
> > }
> > transformed parameters {
> > cov_matrix[4] Sigma;  // constructing the variance/cov matrix for random effects
> > for (r in 1:4) {
> > for (c in 1:4) {
> > Sigma[r,c] <- sigma_u[r] * sigma_u[c] * Omega[r,c];
> > }
> > }
> > }
> > model {
> > real mu[N];                         // mu for likelihood
> > for (i in 1:I) u[i] ~ multi_normal(mu_prior, Sigma);
> > // loop for subj random effects
> > for (n in 1:N) {
> > mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*c1[n] + beta[3]*c2[n] + beta[4]*c3[n] +  u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n] + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];
> > }
> > rt ~ normal(mu,sigma_e);           // likelihood
> > beta ~ normal(0,100);
> > sigma_e ~ cauchy(0,2);
> > sigma_u ~ cauchy(0,2);
> > Omega ~ lkj_corr(4.0);
> > }
> > generated quantities {
> > real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho12;
> > real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho13;
> > real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho14;
> > real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho23;
> > real<lower=-1,upper=1> rho24;

On 12/16/13, 12:49 PM, Christian Roy wrote:
> I believe that the lkj_correlation  refer to the Lewandowski et al. paper in the Journal of Multivariate Analysis
>
> Generating random correlation matrices based on vines and extended onion method
>
> http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047259X09000876
>
> Good luck

That paper's pretty difficult.  I think Ben's the only
one who fully understands it other than the authors!

The density is quite simple, though:

   lkj_corr(Sigma|nu)  propto  det(Sigma)^(nu - 1)

where det(Sigma) is the determinant of Sigma.

It works like the Beta distribution in that if nu > 1, there's
a mode at the identity matrix, but if nu < 1, there's a trough
at the identity, whereas at nu = 1, it's flat.

But that's just repeating what our manual says.

The way to get intuitions about how it works is to draw
random samples and visualize them as in Ben's paper.

- Bob

It's all relative to other options.  MCMC is quite a bit
slower than optimization-based fits.

Does the model (or its analogue with different priors) run faster in JAGS?

 > Am I doing something wrong?

The model looks OK, but you have very fat priors (e.g., normal(0,100)).
Do you really expect coefficients in that range?

Also, are you sure you need 1000 iterations?  How fast does it
converge and how many effective samples do you need?  When you
compare MCMC algorithms, the only thing that matters is effective
samples per second, not the time per iteration.  See the section
in the manual on MCMC analysis if you're not familiar with effective
sample size estimation.

The other thing to do is look at the traceplots.  Are any of
the chains getting stuck?  Are you exploring unrealistic values?
These can sometimes be controlled by tightening the constraints and/or
priors.

The last thing to do is to reparameterize using a non-centered
parameterization --- see the manual section around the funnel
for both the technique and the motivation.  This can make a big
difference in hierarchical models, but it requires more work on
the user's part.

Dear List,

I returned today to a model I estimated some time back in Stan 1.3.0, thinking I would check the results in Stan 2.0.1 before going on to do some additional analysis. To my surprise, I was immediately greeted with following error when estimating the model in 2.0.1:

~Jason

Il 16/12/2013 19:53, Shravan Vasishth ha scritto:
> Thanks Chris, I'll try to figure out what's in that article. Andrew, I
> did look at the appendix in BDA. I think that a little bit more
> explanation would help people like me who don't know much.

Well, let me try. "Someone" (!) will surely correct my mistakes.

Defining priors for variances looks easy (it's not that easy, but let's
go on).
Defining priors for 2x2 covariance matrices is easy too (see above): two
variances and one correlation, just a number in [-1,1].
But defining priors for KxK, K>2, covariance matrices is difficult
because of constraints among the correlation parameters. So you have to
define a prior for a large (K>2) covariance matrix "en bloc".

One often use the inverse-Wishart distribution, but its parameters are
difficult to interpret and a single parameter controls the precision of
all elements of the covariance matrix [1].
BTW: reading
http://andrewgelman.com/2012/08/29/more-on-scaled-inverse-wishart-and-prior-independence/
is mandatory!

This is why Barnard, McCulloch and Meng [2] recommend a separation
strategy, i.e.:

Sigma = D R D

where D is a diagonal matrix of std devs and R a correlation matrix.
This is pretty useful if you are willing to express prior beliefs about
the standard deviations, but less willing about the correlation matrix
(as in your models, I'd say).

But modeling a correlation matrix is a tough task. So, O'Malley and
Zaslavsky have suggested a scaled inverse-Wishart:

Sigma = diag(xi) Q diag(xi), Q ~ Inv-Wishart(...)

For example, you could set degrees-of-freedom = K+1 and get marginal
uniform distribution for the correlations, then "correct" the
constrained variances by a vector xi of scale parameters.
See Gelman & Hill, pp. 286-287.

A few years ago Lewandowski, Kurowicka and Joe [3] have found efficient
algorithms to generate random correlation matrices whose distribution
depends on a single "eta" parameter; if eta = 1 then their distribution
is jointly uniform.
So the original separation strategy is now feasible and very efficient
in Stan.
You could notice that the joint uniformity results in marginal priors
for individual correlations which are not uniform and the more favors
values close to zero over values close to +/-1 the more K is large, but
it could make sense because the positive definite constraint is more
restrictive as the correlations move away from zero [2].

HTH

Sergio

--------------------------
[1] A. James Oï¿½Malley & Alan M. Zaslavsky, "Domain-Level Covariance
Analysis for Multilevel Survey Data With Structured Nonresponse",
Journal of the American Statistical Association, 103:484, 1405-1418,
http://dx.doi.org/10.1198/016214508000000724
[2] John Barnard, Robert McCulloch and Xiao-Li Meng, "Modeling
Covariance Matrices in Terms of Standars Deviations and Correlations,
with Application to Shrinkage", Statistica Sinica 10(2000), 1281-1311,
http://www3.stat.sinica.edu.tw/statistica/oldpdf/A10n416.pdf
[3] You know:
http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0047259X09000876

Are you using the same initialization?  If you can verify
it works in 1.3 but fails in 2.0.1 with the same initialization
value, I'll file an issue and look into it more deeply.

That error arises when the sampler can't move from
the initial parameter values.  Usually this happens
because of an error such as providing out-of-support
inputs to a distribution (e.g.,  1.2 ~ beta(1,1)) or
because of NaN values introduced as arguments, such as
dividing 0 by 0.  It can also arise due to overflow
or underflow issues.

One issue with your model is:

     pos_raw[n-3,K] ~ normal(0, 4);

This only supplies a prior for a single entry in the pos_raw
matrix.  If you want all of pos_raw to get this prior, you need
to write:

   for (n in 1:(n-3))
     pos_raw[n] ~ normal(0,4);

or more efficiently given that n >> K and that
pos_raw is a matrix (stored in column-major order), use:

   for (k in 1:K)
     col(pos_raw,k) ~ normal(0,4);

Otherwise, you get an implicit uniform prior on the declared
support, which is (-10,10).

To deal with arithmetic stability for the Poisson, we
have a poisson_log() distribution, which takes its parameter
on the log scale and lets you replace:

  y ~ poisson(exp(beta - D));

with

  y ~ poisson_log(beta - D);

- Bob

>

>     This only supplies a prior for a single entry in the pos_raw
>     matrix.  If you want all of pos_raw to get this prior, you need

>     or more efficiently given that n >> K and that

>
>         for (k in 1:K)
>           col(pos_raw,k) ~ normal(0,4);

>

messages.subject: lmer vs Stan comparison
messages.body_plain:
Here is a comparison of lmer vs Stan output on a mildly complicated dataset from a psychology expt. (Kliegl et al 2011). The data are attached.

Data and paper, along with lots of challenging datasets for Stan, are available from:

http://openscience.uni-leipzig.de/index.php/mr2

I should say that datasets from psychology and psycholinguistic can be much more complicated than this example. So this was only a modest test of Stan.

The basic result is that I was able to recover in Stan the parameter estimates (fixed effects) that were primarily of interest, compared to the lmer output. The sds of the variance components all come out pretty much the same in Stan vs lmer. The correlations estimated in Stan are much smaller than lmer, but this seems to be normal: bayesian models seem to be more conservative when it comes to estimating correlations between random effects (I know Andrew does not like this term, and also not fixed effects, but they are convenient).

Traceplots are attached. They look generally fine to me.

One very important fact about lmer vs Stan is that lmer took 23 seconds to return an answer, but Stan took 18,814 seconds (about 5 hours), running 500 iterations and 2 chains.

One caveat is that I do have to try to figure out how to speed up Stan so that we get the best performance out of it that is possible. But could Stan developers provide some fully worked examples of a mildly challenging dataset like this What's the absolute best that Stan can do with professional intervention, compared to lmer?

If the present analysis can be sped up a lot more, I have another dataset in the Stan-queue with 150 subjects and three contrasts, plus another random factor (items) that I will test Stan vs lmer on.

klieglvaryingintslopes_codefast <- 'data {
int<lower=1> N;

real c3[N];                         //predictor

corr_matrix[4] Omega;               // correlation matrix for random intercepts and slopes
}
transformed parameters {
    matrix[4,4] D;
    D <- diag_matrix(sigma_u);
}
model {
matrix[4,4] L;
matrix[4,4] DL;
real mu[N];                         // mu for likelihood

//priors:
beta ~ normal(0,50);
sigma_e ~ cauchy(0,2);
sigma_u ~ cauchy(0,2);
Omega ~ lkj_corr(4.0);

L <- cholesky_decompose(Omega);
DL <- D * L;
for (i in 1:I)                             // loop for subj random effects
    u[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, DL);

for (n in 1:N) {
mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*c1[n] + beta[3]*c2[n] + beta[4]*c3[n] +  u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n] + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];
}
rt ~ normal(mu,sigma_e);           // likelihood
}
generated quantities {
    cov_matrix[4] Sigma;
    Sigma <- D * Omega * D;
}
'

messages.body_plain:
Hi, one of our items in the queue (as Bob would say) is an implementation of the marginal mode approach of blmer/bglmer using conditional optimization and Laplace approximations in Stan.  This is waiting on our implementation of 2nd derivatives.  Until that, I expect that for moderate sized problems with small well-behaved models, blmer etc are likely to outperform Stan in speed.  In the current environment, I'd expect Stan to outperform blmer etc in the following scenarios:
- Models such as ordered logit which simply do not exist in lmer etc
- Models with many nonnested variance components and varying intercepts and slopes (thus, multiple hierarchical cov matrices to estimate); these can stump lmer etc
- Very sparse data where the Laplace approximation of glmer doesn't work well
- Models with extra structure (for example, Yair used Stan for a model with time-series correlations)
- Huge data sets (Bob has said that he thinks that Stan will scale better than lmer etc as data sets become huge).
But in your basic ARM-type hierarchical models, it might well be that blmer/bglmer is the best bet for now.  A year or so ago, Vince and I had some thoughts about improving blmer in various ways, but at this point I think we're best off waiting for the 2nd derivatives to come in Stan and then we can try programming the optimization and approximations directly.
A

Il 16/12/2013 20:29, Shravan Vasishth ha scritto:
> The code is given below. One surprising thing is that Stan runs
> amazingly slow (MacBook Air OS X 10.6).

You could try parallel sampling. Instead of:

fit <- stan(model_code = klieglvaryingintslopes_code,
             data = dat2,
             iter = 1000, chains = 4)

try:

library(parallel)
# translate to C++ and compile
sm <- stan_model(model_code = klieglvaryingintslopes_code)
# execute chains in parallel
sflist <- mclapply(1:4, mc.cores = detectCores(),
             function(i) sampling(sm, data = dat2,
               chains = 1, chain_id = i, iter = 1000,
               seed = <an integer>))
# merge
fit <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)

You can save a lot of time even if you just have a dual-core processor.
NB: Setting the seed is "best practice" (i.e. mandatory). Please, read
help(sflist2stanfit).

Sergio

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] lmer vs Stan comparison
messages.body_plain:
We're not (yet at least) trying to compete with (bg)lmer on speed!
bglmer is Vince Dorie's project (with Andrew) to extend lmer with
priors:

   http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/blme/blme.pdf )

But before talking about speed, let's be clear that

   * your models in Stan and lmer are not doing the same thing;  your
     hierarchical priors can't be expressed in lmer or in bglmer.

   * the fitting performed is different;  lmer uses maximum marginal
     likelihood, which finds the mode after integrating out the hierarchical
     variance parameters;  this mode is not the same as the Bayesian estimate
     you get from Stan based on the posterior mean (though they're often very
     close if there's enough data and the posterior's roughly symmetric).

   * lmer approximates posterior covariance using a Laplace approximation
     at the mode, whereas Stan uses MCMC for full Bayesian inference.

We are working in Stan on three approaches to optimization-based
inference:

   * (stochastic) variational inference

   * maximum marginal likelihood (like lmer)

   * (MC) expectation propagation

Hopefully these approximate methods will be as fast as lmer, especially
on larger-scale problems (lmer uses matrix solving, which is ideal for
small to medium size problems, but doesn't scale to large problems --- it's
why you see so much stochastic-gradient descent in the "machine learning" world).

Now onto specifics of your models and fits.

When you ran, what were the effective sample sizes and R-hat
values?   You don't need many effective samples
to get reasonable posterior mean estimates (error drops with sqrt(N_eff)).
You need even less precision when doing initial model exploration.

I'll append some comments on the model below.  The bottom line is
that I don't think it can be sped up significantly at this point.
Two improvements we have scheduled will probably give you around
a 10 times speedup for this model:

   * a Cholesky factor for correlation matrix data type and
     matching LKJ density, and

   * vectorizing the multivariate normal.

Even after that, which might give you a factor of 10 speedup, MCMC is
still not going to be competitive with optimization-based approaches.

Every field has the same problem --- the models we want to fit
go beyond the software we want to fit them with.  I don't see any indication
this trend will slow down.

Andrew's been using lmer and bglmer for years because he couldn't fit the
models he wanted to in BUGS/JAGS.  We tried to build Stan so it would at
least be possible to do the full Bayesian inference for these models and more
general multilevel ones that can't be expressed in lmer's modeling
language (many examples of which can be found in Andrew's research papers and
in his and Jennifer's book).

- Bob

On 12/17/13, 3:14 PM, Shravan Vasishth wrote:
...

> The model code:

I'll grin and bear the lack of indentation, but
I would very very strongly recommend pulling the model
out of the R code and into its own file.   I really don't like
this tendency to bundle the model and code together that
our examples in R are leading people to.  There's an emacs
mode for Stan, for one thing!

> klieglvaryingintslopes_codefast <- 'data {
> int<lower=1> N;
> real rt[N];                         //outcome
> real c1[N];                         //predictor
> real c2[N];                         //predictor
> real c3[N];                         //predictor
> int<lower=1> I;                     //number of subjects
> int<lower=1, upper=I> id[N];        //subject id
> vector[4] mu_prior;                 //vector of zeros passed in from R
> }
> parameters {
> vector[4] beta;                     // intercept and slope
> vector[4] u[I];                     // random intercept and slopes
> real<lower=0> sigma_e;              // residual sd
> vector<lower=0>[4] sigma_u;         // subj sd
> corr_matrix[4] Omega;               // correlation matrix for random intercepts and slopes
> }
> transformed parameters {
>      matrix[4,4] D;
>      D <- diag_matrix(sigma_u);
> }

This is very inefficient.  Multiplying out the scaling
directly rather than filling a matrix is much better.
You get all those multiplications by zero when you multiply
a diagonal matrix by a matrix.  Get rid of this and replace
the DL <- D * L below with a loop.  Fill in all the zero
values with the same temporary 0 for even more speed.

> model {
> matrix[4,4] L;
> matrix[4,4] DL;
> real mu[N];                         // mu for likelihood
>
> //priors:
> beta ~ normal(0,50);
> sigma_e ~ cauchy(0,2);
> sigma_u ~ cauchy(0,2);
> Omega ~ lkj_corr(4.0);
>
> L <- cholesky_decompose(Omega);
> DL <- D * L;

Replace this with a loop.

   for (m in 1:4)
     for (n in 1:m)
       DL[m,n] <- L[m,n] * sigma_u[m];

and fill in zeroes with a single value, which is
a hack that helps with auto-diff by reducing expression
stack size.

   {
     real zero;
     zero <- 0;
     for (m in 1:4)
       for (n in (m+1):4))
         DL[m,n] <- zero;
   }

This will get more efficient and cleaner to write
when we introduce a Cholesky factor for correlation matrix data type (mostly
coded -- just needs testing and should show up in 2.2).

Given the small size of your correlation matrix, I doubt this will make
a measurable difference in overall model speed.

> for (i in 1:I)                             // loop for subj random effects
>      u[i] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, DL);

This should get a lot faster after we vectorize
multi_normal so you can write this as:

   u ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu_prior, DL);

> for (n in 1:N) {
> mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*c1[n] + beta[3]*c2[n] + beta[4]*c3[n] +  u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n]
> + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];
> }
> rt ~ normal(mu,sigma_e);           // likelihood
> }
> generated quantities {
>      cov_matrix[4] Sigma;
>      Sigma <- D * Omega * D;

Sigma <- L * L';

There's a built-in function for multiplying a lower-triangular matrix
by its own transpose, but with generated quantities, it'll be about
as fast to write it this way.

- Bob

I've been mulling this same problem over as well and initially I was tending to put everything into one file, but soon that became large and unwieldy when a couple of models were there.  I am working on models which are related and evolving as my understanding improves.  The dataset is the same, but needs to be manipulated a little for some models - i.e. rescaled, or groups progressively added together.  I came to the conclusion a week or two ago that by breaking things down into the data preparation stage, a model and the post-processing stages that I got more clarity.  The pre-processing stage can be done in a couple of different ways and wrapped in a few different functions. The post -processing stage of summary output and graphics etc is pretty much the same for each - this can also be wrapped in a function or two for clarity - parameterised.

So this leaves me with the model code (say I call it H2) which changes slightly, so I put that in a file named like H2.Stan, and I have the driver code which is quite short in a file called H2.R - which means that when I print out things, it is quite short and I can see everything that I need to see on two or three pages - easier to show others.  I put the output into a folder named H2, since I sometimes I create a lot of files - but that is not confusing as I have parameterised the pre/post processing functions to prepend the model name "H2" in this case to all the files - e.g. H2_pairs.pdf, H2_absd_plot.pdf, H2_fit.txt etc...

Of course currently the code I am using is still in the transition from ugly and is not quite at the above stage of clarity but that is where I am aiming for ! :-)

Kind regards,
Seán

Daniel and I have come up with some conventions for projects we've been
working on together.  If you modify files rather than copying them, you lose
the ability to rerun the older models.  (Unless you've checked them into
some kind of version control system that'll let you restore them.)  At the
same time, you want to reuse some of the R infrastructure, data readers, etc.

On Tuesday, December 17, 2013 10:29:03 PM UTC+1, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Maybe we could construct some default system where the stan objects automatically get a name that is derived from the file name, or something like that.

My 2 cents.
I'm using the following naming convention:

- "foo": model_name
- "foo.stan": model source
- "foo.data.R": data file
- "foo.sm <http://foo.sm>": compiled model
- "foo.sm.RData": saved compiled model
- "foo.sf": final stanfit object
- "foo.sf.RData": eventual saved stanfit object

and a function:

mystan <- function(model, data=model, iter = 2000, seed = 12345, new=FALSE, ...) {
    stopifnot(require(parallel)) # should never happen!
    model.data <- paste(data, ".data.R", sep='')
    model.file <- paste(model, ".stan", sep='')
    model.sm <- paste(model, ".sm", sep='')
    model.saved <- paste(model.sm, ".RData", sep='')
    model.sf <- paste(model, ".sf", sep='')
    if (!file.exists(model.file))
        stop(paste(model.stan, "not found"))
    if (!file.exists(model.data))
        stop(paste(model.data, "not found"))
    if (new) { # you have a previous compiled model, but you've changed the source
        if (exists(model.sm))
            rm(list=model.sm, envir = .GlobalEnv)
        if (file.exists(model.saved))
            unlink(model.saved)
    }
    if (!exists(model.sm)) {
        if (file.exists(model.saved)) {
            # load the saved model and put its name in .GlobalEnv
            load(model.saved, envir = .GlobalEnv, verbose = FALSE)
        } else {
            rt <- stanc(model.file, model_name = model)
            sm <- stan_model(stanc_ret = rt)
            # create the compiled model variable name
            assign(model.sm, sm, envir = .GlobalEnv)
            save(list=model.sm, file = model.saved)
        }
    }
    sm <- get(model.sm) # sm <- the model to whom its variable name refers
    sflist <- mclapply(1:4, mc.cores = detectCores(),
                       function(i) sampling(sm, data = read_rdump(model.data),
                           chains = 1, chain_id = i,
                           iter = iter, seed = seed, ...))
    sf <- sflist2stanfit(sflist)
    # create the stanfit object variable name
    assign(model.sf, sf, .GlobalEnv)
}

An example session:

> library(rstan)
...
> source("mystan.R")
> N <- 100
> x <- rnorm(N,0,4)
> y <- 2 + 0.5 * x - 1.5 * x^2 + rnorm(N)
> stan_rdump(c("N", "x", "y"), file = "linreg.data.R")
> ls()

What about allowing a single file to include several different Stan models, for example using some sort of # tag?  This would allow me to modify a model via cut and paste instead of needing to keep track of multiple files.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] conventions for stan file naming
messages.body_plain:
I think Sean's message nicely outlines the problems we're
all having with our models and data munging evolving as we work
on a problem.  Daniel and I are feeling this now in some applied
work we're doing together.  Andrew --- what did you do with
BUGS/JAGS for this?  Do they have any recommendations, given that
they've been playing this game for roughly two decades?

I have a very strong preference for:

   * data in its own dump-format file

   * models in their own files

These formats are cross-interface (CmdStan, RStan, PyStan),
so anyone on the dev team could use them, not just the R
users.  This is the same reason I don't like muddling R and
LaTeX in Sweave or Python and web presentations in IPython
notebooks.

I'd also strongly prefer

   * one model per file

It's just fewer moving pieces to code, test, document,
and maintain inside of Stan.  I realize this goes against
R's one-function-to-rule-them-all mentality and is more
unix-like in giving you small pieces to cobble together.

I'd then like to see in separate files in the project:

   * scripts to fit the models

   * scripts to test the fit of models

   * scripts to plot

This is just good for reproducibility and sharing with others.
As much as possible, common functions should be factored out of
these pieces for ongoing work.

These are going to be platform-specific, though.   I don't want
to write a scripting language for Stan like the one for JAGS (and
maybe BUGS).

I realize tastes vary on this.  I don't personally like IDEs
for the same reason --- they tangle your otherwise portable code
with a tool for compilation and browsing.  It's also a chef-like
mentality of fewer gadgets and better knife skills.  I work
on all sorts of coding environments, and it's easier for me to
just do everything in the shell and in emacs.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
While JSON offers certain advantages for data exchange, it would also pose a significant barrier to entry for some potential users.  For example, I do most of my data manipulation and analysis in Stata. While the R-dump format is, uhm, different, it is brutally straight-forward.  Writing code to write my data into the R-dump format was pretty straight-forward and didn't require me to know anything about R.    Writing out my data in JSON, however, would be significantly more difficult and require me to learn about the intricacies of a moderately convoluted data format (at least relative to R-dump).

At the moment, I suspect most users to Stan are already users of Python or R, meaning they have easily available tools for producing a JSON file and probably the programming expertise to make it a non-issue.  If the hope is to grow the use of Stan towards a slightly more general audience, however, JSON might be sub-optimal.  Since the Stan syntax itself is pretty straight-forward for someone comfortable with the statistical concepts, just getting the data ready to go might actually be the biggest barrier for some.

An old-fashioned comma (or tab) delimited file with variable names in the top row (data.csv) may have disadvantages in this setting that I don't grasp, but I would offer it for consideration as (a) very easy to produce from almost any package, (b) not connected to any particular statistical package (the term "r-dump file" is infelicitous to the ear of someone who hasn't used R), and (c) easy to import into almost any package, even if it is subsequently munged into something else.  Since Stan output is comma-delimited, it also provides a nice symmetry.

Just something for your consideration.  I'm enjoying learning to use Stan and find it a powerful, useful package.  Thanks to all who are moving it forward!

Glenn Hoetker
WP Carey School of Business
Arizona State University

>
>
> On 3/7/13 3:54 AM, Dan Stowell wrote:
> > I agree, JSON should be a good choice for data interchange. (Gives one
> > ideas of stan models as web services...)
> >

messages.subject: Some comments on Stan usage, emacs, and code management
messages.subject_clean: Some comments on Stan usage, emacs, and code management
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to everyone who responded to the lmer vs Stan comparison. I wanted to briefly respond to a few things that were said there:

Bob wrote: "Andrew's been using lmer and bglmer for years because he couldn't fit the models he wanted to in BUGS/JAGS."

But then I don't understand why Andrew always keeps saying use Stan whenever I ask him a question!!! :)

Bob wrote:  "I'll grin and bear the lack of indentation, but
I would very very strongly recommend pulling the model
out of the R code and into its own file.   I really don't like
this tendency to bundle the model and code together that
our examples in R are leading people to.  There's an emacs
mode for Stan, for one thing! "

I developed RSI using emacs back in 2002 and had to quit using it. I am tied to RStudio for that reason, and I think there are others out there whose hands were ruined by emacs (I should have remapped the keys, but it's too late now).

Regarding bundling: Andrew told me that he does not release his code associated with his published work because he has lots of different files and he doesn't have time to put them together to release his code. (This is astonishing because he goes after people for not releasing their data/code!!!! See: http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ChanceEthics1.pdf, and see http://andrewgelman.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/03/chanceletters.pdf)

In order to help Andrew meet the standards he advocates for open data and open methods, it would help him to have a simple workflow that can actually result in a code+data release upon publication. A single file to work with will probably do the job (it will be messy, but it's better than nothing). In Gelman and Hill 2007, it was a real headache to figure out how the radon data got assembled ready for analysis. It needed some detective work and quite a bit of code rewriting.

There are lots of people out there like Andrew who would benefit from a single file world view, because then they can actually release their code.

best,

--
Shravan Vasishth
Professor für Psycholinguistik und Neurolinguistik
Department Linguistik
Universität Potsdam, D-14476 Potsdam

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
I haven't been using Stan as much as I could, but Jeroen's remark makes me think that you're overanalyzing this.  Many users won't ever use Stan directly.  If you want someone to use a stats tool, it should probably resemble Excel, the most widely used statistical analysis package in the known universe.   The data can live in a table, but the relationships that define pivot tables, functions, etc. are substantially more complicated, and it's those we're concerned about.

As long as your data structures are flat (like tables), a CSV file is great.  The instant your data structures diverge from a regular tabular structure, something like JSON has enormous advantages in terms of representing hierarchies, etc. in an easily parsed form, supported by a vast number of potential "producer" and "consumer" applications.  If Stan is going to take over the world it might as well support distributed operation, which is greatly facilitated by having this sort of widely supported data exchange format.

Here's one scenario to consider.  You have smallish samples (relative to the complexity of the model you want to fit) and a lot of semi-technical people with domain knowledge and common sense, but no real interest in programming.  They just want to know where to buy ads, what stuff to work on, etc.  They notice that Bayesian models tend to offer better predictive performance in such situations and would like to build and fit them without learning how to program.  They're willing to consider pictures of distributions, etc. and have a program generate pictures of marginals, posteriors, etc. for sanity checking, and they'd like to store the models that did / did not work somewhere "in the cloud" (i.e., somewhere they don't have to back up manually, like Dropbox or a database).  Some clever guy realizes that he can be a hero if he rigs up a web interface that guides people towards less-stupid model choices and draws some pictures for them to sign off on when each model is constructed.  Then the models get shipped off to Stan, which grinds through them as compute power permits, and the users get emails when their models converge, along with a reference to allow predictive fits on new data that looks like the old data.

Maybe users drag and drop colorful bits into a canvas object or some such (I'm already throwing up a little bit in the back of my mouth).  It would sure be nice to compactly represent those distributions and their relationships to each other, wouldn't it? Especially if you wanted to visualize certain marginal or posterior distributions.  But if everything is in a CSV-formatted table with a fixed number of columns, you have to somehow kludge in a place for any dependencies between variables.  With a loosely structured "object" (list of stuff) like JSON or YAML allows, you just pass everything & pull it back out on the other end.

Something like this: http://www.jsoneditoronline.org/  (See?  Not so complex!)

The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.

JSON became a de facto standard because it's just about the simplest thing that could possibly work, for the task.  People would just use CSV if it were easier, but for passing around data structures, it rapidly becomes apparent that it's actually harder with a flat tabular representation.  Strange but true.

Anyways, that's my piece for the day.  YMMV and I respect your opinion.  But I disagree with it, and I wanted to lay out my reasoning for why I disagreed.

Best,

--t

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
This isn't an either-or situation.  We can implement multiple
data formats and let users use whatever they like.  The only
thing holding us back is programming time.  So if someone wants
to volunteer to write a JSON interface, we can help you plug
it into Stan's C++ layer.  JSON's pretty easy, but unfortunately,
like R's dump format, doesn't have a built-in typing mechanism
for integer vs. real values.

The way Stan actually works is that it has a low-level
abstract base class representation for reading data that gets
called in the constructor of a class that reads data and then
is used to evaluate log probabilities and gradients and transforms.

Currently the abstract base class is implemented three different ways:

    - reading from R-style dump format streams/files (used in CmdStan)

    - reading from R data structures/environments (used in RStan)

    - reading from Python data structures (not sure the details, used in PyStan)

Writing something to read from a std::ostream for JSON is on
our to-do list, but not a high priority at the moment.  If someone wants
to take it on, we're happy to help!

Andrew's asked for something to read from CSV files, but given his
response (most of our data's non-rectangular), we've apparently been
succesfull in explaining why it's challenging.

We haven't thought much about bringing something like Stan down
to users who don't know stats --- the whole thing's based on writing
your own probability function!  Our target's more the people who understand
how to express the log probabilty function for their model, but don't want
to code a sampler/estimator for it.

We have thought about GUIs and cluster distribution to make exploring
models easier.  But nothing's come of it because we don't have
any GUI programmers and we only have half-formulated ideas on how to
make it work in limited domains like hierarchical GLMs.   Andrew and Ben
have gone down this path with their multiple imputation (mi) package in R,
so maybe they have some insight to offer.

We have thought about shipping models off to the cluster to grind
through --- in fact, we're doing that.  But model fitting is usually more
of an interactive process where you don't try twenty models at once, but
you try one, see how it works and what you learn from fitting it, and
then use that to guide the next model.  Just managing all the results
and model specifications is hard in this setting, which is why it would
be nice to automate it with a GUI or scripting language or something.

- Bob

The idea is to put a Gaussian Process prior on the variance like so:
 y_i =  a + bX_i + e_i with e_i ~ N(0, r(x) = e^g(x))  and g(x) ~ GP(mu0,k(x,x') ).
k(x,x') is the standard squareq-exponential covariance function.
