I think my problem stems from a misunderstanding of the way STAN works... or my code is simply not implementing what I think it is.
I would be happy if anyone could tell me whether something is fundamentally wrong with my STAN code.

Thanks!
Ben

messages.body_plain:
I've thought about writing the reader for JSON, but I've been stuck for a while because there aren't standard conventions in JSON.

Tim points out:

On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. <tim.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.

Thanks for the recap. I'm not sure how to deal with the intricacies of "curlies" and "brackets." Here's a quick example that I can figure out:

Stan model:
  data {
    int N;
    real x[N];
  }

An example piece of JSON data:
  {
    "N": 3,
    "x": [
      0.1,
      0.2,
      0.3
    ]
  }

For this example, I think it's straightforward, but what happens if x is reported as a list? Or as brackets in brackets? Like [ [0.1], [0.2], [0.3] ].

Here's a more complex example. Suppose the data block looks like:
  data {
    int I;
    int J;
    int K;
    real a[I];
    vector[I] b;
    matrix[I,J] c;
    real d[I,J,K];
  }

Questions:
1. Should the variables a and b be written out in JSON using the array notation? Or are these things fundamentally different and the user needs to understand how to shape the data when they write it out?
2. What is the standard way of writing out 2-dimensional matrices? For c, would that look something like (suppose I=2, J=2):
    {
       ...

> On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 1:13 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> > I've thought about writing the reader for JSON, but I've been stuck for a while because there aren't standard conventions in JSON.

I'd be interested to hear if the vignette covers all your concerns, or where it needs further specification.

That's great that you're trying to solve the JSON mapping problem for R, but for Stan, the requirements are different. You've taken the approach of limiting the JSON language down to a subset that maps unambiguously to R objects. That's probably the approach I'd take too. For the vignette, it would be nice if you specified some sort of grammar at some point in the document.

The question I have is: are JSON users well behaved?
- Do users only use arrays for numeric data? Or do they use objects as well?
- Is it easy for users to go back and forth in external tools?
- Should we support a very narrow format that ignores most of JSON and its language? The narrowest possible format would only allow object members that are assigned to a number or an array of numbers or nested arrays of numbers, but nothing else. No parsing of "null," "true," or "false."
- Should we support something a little broader than that? Do we allow collections to be swapped in for arrays? Or maybe we parse "null," "true," and "false"?

It wouldn't be hard to implement something that only allows members to be values and arrays of values, assuming the values are specified in row-major.

One additional question -- if anyone is using JSON for bigger data applications, how do you split data across JSON objects?

Daniel

to JSON then we still need to define a spec for how we handle vectors, matrices, etc.  In fact I have working JSON
parser coded up, I just got stuck on defining a specification as there was no obvious better choice.

As Bob notes, there are two issues here: internal storage and external storage.  We need to define a specification
for internal storage first, and then we can worry about having I/O from R, csv, and the like.

These will be addressed in the future, but there are more pressing issues and features unless there are developers
who volunteer.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
What got me thinking about this is a grant that I wrote a while ago that revolves around dynamic model averaging as a means to model structural changes in 20-30 years' worth of pre- and post-op survival probabilities in a disease where there have been a lot of structural changes.  Writing the grant got me thinking about how best to structure the backend (i.e. minimal intervention required from the users) but also make the assumptions/features considered by the model fit apparent to users.  In other words, both the model fitting and model checking need to be transparent (check!), and should be intuitive (more challenging).

Say you have a drug that didn't exist prior to 2001 and a segment of the population that responds, if not beautifully, at least a lot better when treated with it.  Now say you have a dozen such drugs punctuating the history of the disease, along with some of the most meticulous record keeping in medicine.  It would be very nice for clinicians NOT to try and extrapolate from disparate data sets what is/is not informative, since the data and its temporal relationship to various innovations is capable of telling you more, but rather use estimates from a collection of models where structural NAs are marginalized out.  Since the model predictions and marginal estimates could be very consequential, this has to be as transparent as possible to the target group of domain experts, and it ought to be possible to re-run the fit accordingly, subject to certain privacy protections on the original data (which is obviously valuable).

I ran this by the domain experts in question, who were generally thrilled about not trying to draw statistical conclusions from disparate, previously published point estimates.  And obviously since they're the experts (pulling the trigger, when it comes right down to it) they need complete transparency as well.

This sort of thing (albeit with, IMHO, less transparency) has worked fine for other diseases with single structural innovations.  It's a bit of a paradox that it doesn't exist for the disease and procedure in question, but hopefully the above paragraph illustrates some pitfalls and potential remedies available by making the process transparent to domain (not statistical) experts.  I knocked together a prototype frontend in a couple hours a long time ago, thanks in part to the enormous number of libraries available in R.  However, for a lightweight frontend that eats spreadsheets, it would be more scalable to have it in JavaScript, with the best collection of models, their weights, and the new data run through a comparatively trivial pipeline to give instantaneous estimates.  Even a computation of credible intervals should not be too much for client code to manage.  Full re-fits of the data, for many reasons (privacy, DoS worries) more or less have to be done somewhere else, but the user ought to have the option to pick a refitted model if necessary (e.g. another structural innovation) and push it back to the origin if it outperforms the existing ones.

As I was thinking about this, it dawned on me that simply shipping things around as JSON was probably the easiest way to represent these things, and if I'm going to write something like that for the grant, I might as well write it for Stan (minimal marginal effort).  So (contingent upon funding), I plan to do so.

(He said, aiming the gun barrel squarely at his head :-))

He that would live in peace and at ease,
Must not speak all he knows, nor judge all he sees.

Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack <http://archive.org/details/poorrichardsalma00franrich>

On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 12:30 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> This isn't an either-or situation.  We can implement multiple
> data formats and let users use whatever they like.  The only
> thing holding us back is programming time.  So if someone wants
> to volunteer to write a JSON interface, we can help you plug
> it into Stan's C++ layer.  JSON's pretty easy, but unfortunately,
> like R's dump format, doesn't have a built-in typing mechanism
> for integer vs. real values.
>
> The way Stan actually works is that it has a low-level
> abstract base class representation for reading data that gets
> called in the constructor of a class that reads data and then
> is used to evaluate log probabilities and gradients and transforms.
>
> Currently the abstract base class is implemented three different ways:
>
>    - reading from R-style dump format streams/files (used in CmdStan)
>
>    - reading from R data structures/environments (used in RStan)
>
>    - reading from Python data structures (not sure the details, used in PyStan)
>
> Writing something to read from a std::ostream for JSON is on
> our to-do list, but not a high priority at the moment.  If someone wants
> to take it on, we're happy to help!
>
> Andrew's asked for something to read from CSV files, but given his
> response (most of our data's non-rectangular), we've apparently been
> succesfull in explaining why it's challenging.
>
> We haven't thought much about bringing something like Stan down
> to users who don't know stats --- the whole thing's based on writing
> your own probability function!  Our target's more the people who understand
> how to express the log probabilty function for their model, but don't want
> to code a sampler/estimator for it.
>
> We have thought about GUIs and cluster distribution to make exploring
> models easier.  But nothing's come of it because we don't have
> any GUI programmers and we only have half-formulated ideas on how to
> make it work in limited domains like hierarchical GLMs.   Andrew and Ben
> have gone down this path with their multiple imputation (mi) package in R,
> so maybe they have some insight to offer.
>
> We have thought about shipping models off to the cluster to grind
> through --- in fact, we're doing that.  But model fitting is usually more
> of an interactive process where you don't try twenty models at once, but
> you try one, see how it works and what you learn from fitting it, and
> then use that to guide the next model.  Just managing all the results
> and model specifications is hard in this setting, which is why it would
> be nice to automate it with a GUI or scripting language or something.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On 12/18/13, 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. wrote:

> > I haven't been using Stan as much as I could, but Jeroen's remark makes me think that you're overanalyzing this.  Many
> > users won't ever use Stan directly.  If you want someone to use a stats tool, it should probably resemble Excel, the
> > most widely used statistical analysis package in the known universe.   The data can live in a table, but the
> > relationships that define pivot tables, functions, etc. are substantially more complicated, and it's those we're
> > concerned about.
> >
> > As long as your data structures are flat (like tables), a CSV file is great.  The instant your data structures diverge
> > from a regular tabular structure, something like JSON has enormous advantages in terms of representing hierarchies, etc.
> > in an easily parsed form, supported by a vast number of potential "producer" and "consumer" applications.  If Stan is
> > going to take over the world it might as well support distributed operation, which is greatly facilitated by having this
> > sort of widely supported data exchange format.
> >
> > Here's one scenario to consider.  You have smallish samples (relative to the complexity of the model you want to fit)
> > and a lot of semi-technical people with domain knowledge and common sense, but no real interest in programming.  They
> > just want to know where to buy ads, what stuff to work on, etc.  They notice that Bayesian models tend to offer better
> > predictive performance in such situations and would like to build and fit them without learning how to program.  They're
> > willing to consider pictures of distributions, etc. and have a program generate pictures of marginals, posteriors, etc.
> > for sanity checking, and they'd like to store the models that did / did not work somewhere "in the cloud" (i.e.,
> > somewhere they don't have to back up manually, like Dropbox or a database).  Some clever guy realizes that he can be a
> > hero if he rigs up a web interface that guides people towards less-stupid model choices and draws some pictures for them
> > to sign off on when each model is constructed.  Then the models get shipped off to Stan, which grinds through them as
> > compute power permits, and the users get emails when their models converge, along with a reference to allow predictive
> > fits on new data that looks like the old data.
> >
> > Maybe users drag and drop colorful bits into a canvas object or some such (I'm already throwing up a little bit in the
> > back of my mouth).  It would sure be nice to compactly represent those distributions and their relationships to each
> > other, wouldn't it? Especially if you wanted to visualize certain marginal or posterior distributions.  But if
> > everything is in a CSV-formatted table with a fixed number of columns, you have to somehow kludge in a place for any
> > dependencies between variables.  With a loosely structured "object" (list of stuff) like JSON or YAML allows, you just
> > pass everything & pull it back out on the other end.
> >
> > Something like this: http://www.jsoneditoronline.org/  (See?  Not so complex!)
> >
> > The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's
> > anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.
> >
> > JSON became a de facto standard because it's just about the simplest thing that could possibly work, for the task.
> >   People would just use CSV if it were easier, but for passing around data structures, it rapidly becomes apparent that
> > it's actually harder with a flat tabular representation.  Strange but true.
> >
> > Anyways, that's my piece for the day.  YMMV and I respect your opinion.  But I disagree with it, and I wanted to lay out
> > my reasoning for why I disagreed.
> >
> > Best,
> >
> > --t
> >
> > On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 9:44 AM, Glenn Hoetker <ghoe...@mainex1.asu.edu <mailto:ghoe...@mainex1.asu.edu>> wrote:
> >
> >     While JSON offers certain advantages for data exchange, it would also pose a significant barrier to entry for some
> >     potential users.  For example, I do most of my data manipulation and analysis in Stata. While the R-dump format is,
> >     uhm, different, it is brutally straight-forward.  Writing code to write my data into the R-dump format was pretty
> >     straight-forward and didn't require me to know anything about R.    Writing out my data in JSON, however, would be
> >     significantly more difficult and require me to learn about the intricacies of a moderately convoluted data format
> >     (at least relative to R-dump).
> >
> >     At the moment, I suspect most users to Stan are already users of Python or R, meaning they have easily available
> >     tools for producing a JSON file and probably the programming expertise to make it a non-issue.  If the hope is to
> >     grow the use of Stan towards a slightly more general audience, however, JSON might be sub-optimal.  Since the Stan
> >     syntax itself is pretty straight-forward for someone comfortable with the statistical concepts, just getting the
> >     data ready to go might actually be the biggest barrier for some.
> >
> >     An old-fashioned comma (or tab) delimited file with variable names in the top row (data.csv) may have disadvantages
> >     in this setting that I don't grasp, but I would offer it for consideration as (a) very easy to produce from almost
> >     any package, (b) not connected to any particular statistical package (the term "r-dump file" is infelicitous to the
> >     ear of someone who hasn't used R), and (c) easy to import into almost any package, even if it is subsequently munged
> >     into something else.  Since Stan output is comma-delimited, it also provides a nice symmetry.
> >
> >     Just something for your consideration.  I'm enjoying learning to use Stan and find it a powerful, useful package.
> >       Thanks to all who are moving it forward!
> >
> >     Glenn Hoetker
> >     WP Carey School of Business
> >     Arizona State University

Hi Allen,

Thanks for diagnosing this bug, and suggesting the sampling method, which seems to be working!

As a follow up, I'm still not clear on how the parallelization is achieved.  Using the sampling workaround, Pystan still prints out the status and completion times of each chain in sequence, leading me to believe that the sampling within each chain is being parallelized.  However, I have found that (regardless of the value of n_jobs used), Pystan seems to be leveraging a number of cores on my machine equal to the number of chains I specify (i.e. 1 core if I set chains=1, 3 if I set chains=3, etc.).  That would seem to instead suggest that chains are being run in parallel.

If I am correct that sampling within chains is parallelized, am I encountering a bug or mis-understanding how the parameters are specified?  Or are the chains run in parallel and I am mis-understanding the Pystan command line output?

Thanks in advance for any information!

P.S. for posterity, the TypeError was due to passing a float for the number of samples to the Pystan sampling method.  Allen has now merged a fix for this (https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/commit/d003682c8df4f4896c124201d940a92b9f508a09)

Hi Allen and Noah,

I have a question related to the logging error that you both mentioned, which I also encounter every time I run models.  What exactly does this error mean and what effect does it have?

The reason I ask is that I have found that Pystan does not pass along information about parsing errors that prevent stan code from compiling.  For example, if you fail to leave a semicolon at the end of a line, Rstan will tell you:

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Parser expecting: ";"

Whereas Pystan will not return this information, and only raises a ValueError.  I was planning to open an issue for this on GitHub, but perhaps this is the logging error being referred to and the development team is already well aware of the behavior.

Best,

~Nathan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
On 12/18/13, 5:17 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:

 > As Dan notes, the issue with JSON is that its flexibility comes at the cost of not being fully specified.

I don't really know anything about JSON.  Is it that JSON itself isn't fully
specified or just that the JSON spec doesn't tell us how to encode structured,
named, data types?  If it's the former, that's very worrying and would make me
far less keen to adopt JSON.  If it's the latter, then that's just like XML and
it's on us to come up with a spec.

 > If we turn
 > to JSON then we still need to define a spec for how we handle vectors, matrices, etc.  ...

Absolutely.  I think that's what Daniel's getting at.

 > As Bob notes, there are two issues here: internal storage and external storage.  We need to define a specification
 > for internal storage first, and then we can worry about having I/O from R, csv, and the like.

I'm not sure what you mean by internal vs. external here.  Do
you mean internal as in the model class's constructor storing
data as member objects and external as in a file format for I/O?
In that case, internal storage is a C++ issue and I think we should
do it with natural C++ data types, not by passing streams of bytes
around in some encoding.

Having said that, if we want to think about issues like cross-chain
communication from different processes, we'll need a spec for
sending data across processes.

I think there are also several I/O interfaces we're thinking
about without being very clear about it in this thread.

1.  Data input

This is already abstracted in a var_context object.  All we'd
need to add JSON data input is an implementation of var_context
that accepted JSON.  And of course, as Michael and Daniel mentioned,
a specification for how we code up structured objects in JSON.

We don't need to handle everyone's JSON --- we get to define our
own format here.  We could base that on an R version if it's
sensible.

2.  Inits input

This is also implemented in a var_context object.  So whatever
works for data input should also work for inits.

3.  Sample/optimization output

I know less about this one.  I know Michael wrote an mcmc_writer
abstraction at some point.  This would need to be implemented with
JSON.  We'll need another JSON spec for how to dump output.  The
output's a little more complicated because there is text, the ongoing
samples, adaptation, etc.

4.  Command, etc. "pacifier" output

The command also dumps out information as it goes, like how many iterations
have been completed.  We probably don't need to do this with any more
structure than a text stream.  Or do we?

- Bob

>
> These will be addressed in the future, but there are more pressing issues and features unless there are developers
> who volunteer.
>
> On Dec 18, 2013, at 4:13 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>
>> I've thought about writing the reader for JSON, but I've been stuck for a while because there aren't standard conventions in JSON.
>>
>> Tim points out:
>> On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. <tim.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.
>> Thanks for the recap. I'm not sure how to deal with the intricacies of "curlies" and "brackets." Here's a quick example that I can figure out:
>>
>> Stan model:
>>    data {
>>      int N;
>>      real x[N];
>>    }
>>
>> An example piece of JSON data:
>>    {
>>      "N": 3,
>>      "x": [
>>        0.1,
>>        0.2,
>>        0.3
>>      ]
>>    }
>>
>> For this example, I think it's straightforward, but what happens if x is reported as a list? Or as brackets in brackets? Like [ [0.1], [0.2], [0.3] ].
>>
>> Here's a more complex example. Suppose the data block looks like:
>>    data {
>>      int I;
>>      int J;
>>      int K;
>>      real a[I];
>>      vector[I] b;
>>      matrix[I,J] c;
>>      real d[I,J,K];
>>    }
>>
>> Questions:
>> 1. Should the variables a and b be written out in JSON using the array notation? Or are these things fundamentally different and the user needs to understand how to shape the data when they write it out?
>> 2. What is the standard way of writing out 2-dimensional matrices? For c, would that look something like (suppose I=2, J=2):
>>      {
>>         ...
>>          "c": [
>>             [1,2],
>>             [3,4]
>>          ]
>>      }
>>      Is that stored in row major or column major? (JSON only has the concept of an array) Or should these be made into objects themselves? Like this:
>>      {
>>         ...
>>          "c": [
>>             { "row1": [1,2]},
>>             { "row2": [3,4]}
>>          ]
>>      }
>> 3. How are multidimensional data structures stored in JSON? If the 2-d case was ambiguous, how do we deal with 3-d. That is, how do I write data for the variable d?
>> 4. Should vectors and matrices really be objects? If they shouldn't, should object notation be allowed?
>> 5. Can we get around these issues by only supporting a subset of JSON? If so, someone's got to write out the actual rules for what is and isn't allowed. If we go down that route, do we need to write our own JSON writers so someone can convert valid JSON into valid Stan JSON? (RStan has stan_rdump() which will output a Stan readable data file.)
>>
>>
>> The short is, I'm not an expert in JSON data structures. I don't know how data is typically stored when it's more than just a vector. If someone can clue me in on these things, it wouldn't be hard to implement a JSON parser.
>>
>>
>>
>> Daniel
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 3:30 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>> This isn't an either-or situation.  We can implement multiple
>> data formats and let users use whatever they like.  The only
>> thing holding us back is programming time.  So if someone wants
>> to volunteer to write a JSON interface, we can help you plug
>> it into Stan's C++ layer.  JSON's pretty easy, but unfortunately,
>> like R's dump format, doesn't have a built-in typing mechanism
>> for integer vs. real values.
>>
>> The way Stan actually works is that it has a low-level
>> abstract base class representation for reading data that gets
>> called in the constructor of a class that reads data and then
>> is used to evaluate log probabilities and gradients and transforms.
>>
>> Currently the abstract base class is implemented three different ways:
>>
>>     - reading from R-style dump format streams/files (used in CmdStan)
>>
>>     - reading from R data structures/environments (used in RStan)
>>
>>     - reading from Python data structures (not sure the details, used in PyStan)
>>
>> Writing something to read from a std::ostream for JSON is on
>> our to-do list, but not a high priority at the moment.  If someone wants
>> to take it on, we're happy to help!
>>
>> Andrew's asked for something to read from CSV files, but given his
>> response (most of our data's non-rectangular), we've apparently been
>> succesfull in explaining why it's challenging.
>>
>> We haven't thought much about bringing something like Stan down
>> to users who don't know stats --- the whole thing's based on writing
>> your own probability function!  Our target's more the people who understand
>> how to express the log probabilty function for their model, but don't want
>> to code a sampler/estimator for it.
>>
>> We have thought about GUIs and cluster distribution to make exploring
>> models easier.  But nothing's come of it because we don't have
>> any GUI programmers and we only have half-formulated ideas on how to
>> make it work in limited domains like hierarchical GLMs.   Andrew and Ben
>> have gone down this path with their multiple imputation (mi) package in R,
>> so maybe they have some insight to offer.
>>
>> We have thought about shipping models off to the cluster to grind
>> through --- in fact, we're doing that.  But model fitting is usually more
>> of an interactive process where you don't try twenty models at once, but
>> you try one, see how it works and what you learn from fitting it, and
>> then use that to guide the next model.  Just managing all the results
>> and model specifications is hard in this setting, which is why it would
>> be nice to automate it with a GUI or scripting language or something.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>> On 12/18/13, 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. wrote:
>> I haven't been using Stan as much as I could, but Jeroen's remark makes me think that you're overanalyzing this.  Many
>> users won't ever use Stan directly.  If you want someone to use a stats tool, it should probably resemble Excel, the
>> most widely used statistical analysis package in the known universe.   The data can live in a table, but the
>> relationships that define pivot tables, functions, etc. are substantially more complicated, and it's those we're
>> concerned about.
>>
>> As long as your data structures are flat (like tables), a CSV file is great.  The instant your data structures diverge
>> from a regular tabular structure, something like JSON has enormous advantages in terms of representing hierarchies, etc.
>> in an easily parsed form, supported by a vast number of potential "producer" and "consumer" applications.  If Stan is
>> going to take over the world it might as well support distributed operation, which is greatly facilitated by having this
>> sort of widely supported data exchange format.
>>
>> Here's one scenario to consider.  You have smallish samples (relative to the complexity of the model you want to fit)
>> and a lot of semi-technical people with domain knowledge and common sense, but no real interest in programming.  They
>> just want to know where to buy ads, what stuff to work on, etc.  They notice that Bayesian models tend to offer better
>> predictive performance in such situations and would like to build and fit them without learning how to program.  They're
>> willing to consider pictures of distributions, etc. and have a program generate pictures of marginals, posteriors, etc.
>> for sanity checking, and they'd like to store the models that did / did not work somewhere "in the cloud" (i.e.,
>> somewhere they don't have to back up manually, like Dropbox or a database).  Some clever guy realizes that he can be a
>> hero if he rigs up a web interface that guides people towards less-stupid model choices and draws some pictures for them
>> to sign off on when each model is constructed.  Then the models get shipped off to Stan, which grinds through them as
>> compute power permits, and the users get emails when their models converge, along with a reference to allow predictive
>> fits on new data that looks like the old data.
>>
>> Maybe users drag and drop colorful bits into a canvas object or some such (I'm already throwing up a little bit in the
>> back of my mouth).  It would sure be nice to compactly represent those distributions and their relationships to each
>> other, wouldn't it? Especially if you wanted to visualize certain marginal or posterior distributions.  But if
>> everything is in a CSV-formatted table with a fixed number of columns, you have to somehow kludge in a place for any
>> dependencies between variables.  With a loosely structured "object" (list of stuff) like JSON or YAML allows, you just
>> pass everything & pull it back out on the other end.
>>
>> Something like this: http://www.jsoneditoronline.org/  (See?  Not so complex!)
>>
>> The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's
>> anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.
>>
>> JSON became a de facto standard because it's just about the simplest thing that could possibly work, for the task.
>>    People would just use CSV if it were easier, but for passing around data structures, it rapidly becomes apparent that
>> it's actually harder with a flat tabular representation.  Strange but true.
>>
>> Anyways, that's my piece for the day.  YMMV and I respect your opinion.  But I disagree with it, and I wanted to lay out
>> my reasoning for why I disagreed.
>>
>> Best,
>>
>> --t
>>
>> On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 9:44 AM, Glenn Hoetker <ghoe...@mainex1.asu.edu <mailto:ghoe...@mainex1.asu.edu>> wrote:
>>
>>      While JSON offers certain advantages for data exchange, it would also pose a significant barrier to entry for some
>>      potential users.  For example, I do most of my data manipulation and analysis in Stata. While the R-dump format is,
>>      uhm, different, it is brutally straight-forward.  Writing code to write my data into the R-dump format was pretty

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
We need arbitrary K-dimensional arrays.  So that'd be last-index
major.  See the R dump format for how it's done now.

C++ array indexing and Stan's array indexing is row major
at run time.

Eigen's matrix indexing is column major by default and that's
what we went with.  It's all just a huge pain to translate back
and forth, but we've done it before.

What's the motivation for converting the models to a structured
notation?  To do that right, you'd need to get into our model
parser code.  From what I can tell, we only need to be able to
code up arbitrary n-dimensional arrays with names.

We can do the coercion to matrices or whatever on the inside.
At least that's what we did with the R dump format.  A 2D
array and matrix are represented the same way in the dump format,
then the reader pulls out the dimensions and values and converts
as necessary.  Similarly, we look for scientific notation or
decimals and treat anything that has them as floating point (real),
whereas if there aren't any of those, it's a valid int (which can
be converted to real).

- Bob

On 12/18/13, 6:02 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. wrote:
> FWIW, the backend for what I wrote in the grant is not, at the moment, Stan-based.  It's just a slow R library.  But it
> could sure as hell stand to be Stanified, so that is my motivation to work on this.  If it benefits others, that's nice
> too, but really I just want to decouple some aspects of model fitting from model checking and model usage.  That's all I
> care about in my application.
>
> I've never passed an array as anything other than column-major if I can help it.
>
> I hadn't really considered encapsulating the data properly, since in my application, on the client side, it comes in one
> at a time, and on the server side, it's not supposed to be pulling the data in as JSON.  But column-major solves two
> problems at once, especially if you hint it:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] JSON data/sample format & Python interface
messages.body_plain:
Re: JSON
--------------

No, JSON does not encode types.  That makes is VERY flexible, especially when combining
numerical and textual data.

JSON really just defines a format for arbitrarily nested key/value pairs.  If we wanted to use
JSON then we'd have to define a spec on top of that which defines

- required keys and their valid value formats
- optional keys and their valid value formats

There is a lot of flexibly in how we define this, which I would consider a plus.

Re: Stan I/O
----------------

My opinion is that we have three layers.

Internally Stan uses C++ types.

The immediate interface to those C++ types is JSON (or another format, but only one format)
with a well-defined spec for input data/inits and output samples/optimization/configuration.

To facilitate our users we would have parsers to and from JSON to a variety of formats such
as Rdump, csv, etc.  This would isolate the core of Stan from all of this I/O junk.  Also we would
have a JSON to stream translator for screen output (this would also facilitate the refactoring of
command.hpp).

A writer class would handle the translation from C++ to  JSON and then any additional formats.
A matching reader would do the same the other way.  The mcmc_writer (perhaps an optimizer_writer, etc)
and var_context would interface with these classes.

On Dec 18, 2013, at 6:10 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> On 12/18/13, 5:17 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> > As Dan notes, the issue with JSON is that its flexibility comes at the cost of not being fully specified.
>
> I don't really know anything about JSON.  Is it that JSON itself isn't fully
> specified or just that the JSON spec doesn't tell us how to encode structured,
> named, data types?  If it's the former, that's very worrying and would make me
> far less keen to adopt JSON.  If it's the latter, then that's just like XML and
> it's on us to come up with a spec.
>
> > If we turn
> > to JSON then we still need to define a spec for how we handle vectors, matrices, etc.  ...
>
> Absolutely.  I think that's what Daniel's getting at.
>
> > As Bob notes, there are two issues here: internal storage and external storage.  We need to define a specification
> > for internal storage first, and then we can worry about having I/O from R, csv, and the like.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by internal vs. external here.  Do
> you mean internal as in the model class's constructor storing
> data as member objects and external as in a file format for I/O?
> In that case, internal storage is a C++ issue and I think we should
> do it with natural C++ data types, not by passing streams of bytes
> around in some encoding.
>
> Having said that, if we want to think about issues like cross-chain
> communication from different processes, we'll need a spec for
> sending data across processes.
>
>
> I think there are also several I/O interfaces we're thinking
> about without being very clear about it in this thread.
>
> 1.  Data input
>
> This is already abstracted in a var_context object.  All we'd
> need to add JSON data input is an implementation of var_context
> that accepted JSON.  And of course, as Michael and Daniel mentioned,
> a specification for how we code up structured objects in JSON.
>
> We don't need to handle everyone's JSON --- we get to define our
> own format here.  We could base that on an R version if it's
> sensible.
>
> 2.  Inits input
>
> This is also implemented in a var_context object.  So whatever
> works for data input should also work for inits.
>
> 3.  Sample/optimization output
>
> I know less about this one.  I know Michael wrote an mcmc_writer
> abstraction at some point.  This would need to be implemented with
> JSON.  We'll need another JSON spec for how to dump output.  The
> output's a little more complicated because there is text, the ongoing
> samples, adaptation, etc.
>
> 4.  Command, etc. "pacifier" output
>
> The command also dumps out information as it goes, like how many iterations
> have been completed.  We probably don't need to do this with any more
> structure than a text stream.  Or do we?
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
>>
>> These will be addressed in the future, but there are more pressing issues and features unless there are developers
>> who volunteer.
>>
>> On Dec 18, 2013, at 4:13 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
>>
>>> I've thought about writing the reader for JSON, but I've been stuck for a while because there aren't standard conventions in JSON.
>>>
>>> Tim points out:
>>> On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. <tim.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.
>>> Thanks for the recap. I'm not sure how to deal with the intricacies of "curlies" and "brackets." Here's a quick example that I can figure out:
>>>
>>> Stan model:
>>>   data {
>>>     int N;
>>>     real x[N];
>>>   }
>>>
>>> An example piece of JSON data:
>>>   {
>>>     "N": 3,
>>>     "x": [
>>>       0.1,
>>>       0.2,
>>>       0.3
>>>     ]
>>>   }
>>>
>>> For this example, I think it's straightforward, but what happens if x is reported as a list? Or as brackets in brackets? Like [ [0.1], [0.2], [0.3] ].
>>>
>>> Here's a more complex example. Suppose the data block looks like:
>>>   data {
>>>     int I;
>>>     int J;
>>>     int K;
>>>     real a[I];
>>>     vector[I] b;
>>>     matrix[I,J] c;
>>>     real d[I,J,K];
>>>   }
>>>
>>> Questions:
>>> 1. Should the variables a and b be written out in JSON using the array notation? Or are these things fundamentally different and the user needs to understand how to shape the data when they write it out?
>>> 2. What is the standard way of writing out 2-dimensional matrices? For c, would that look something like (suppose I=2, J=2):
>>>     {
>>>        ...
>>>         "c": [
>>>            [1,2],
>>>            [3,4]
>>>         ]
>>>     }
>>>     Is that stored in row major or column major? (JSON only has the concept of an array) Or should these be made into objects themselves? Like this:
>>>     {
>>>        ...
>>>         "c": [
>>>            { "row1": [1,2]},
>>>            { "row2": [3,4]}
>>>         ]
>>>     }
>>> 3. How are multidimensional data structures stored in JSON? If the 2-d case was ambiguous, how do we deal with 3-d. That is, how do I write data for the variable d?
>>> 4. Should vectors and matrices really be objects? If they shouldn't, should object notation be allowed?
>>> 5. Can we get around these issues by only supporting a subset of JSON? If so, someone's got to write out the actual rules for what is and isn't allowed. If we go down that route, do we need to write our own JSON writers so someone can convert valid JSON into valid Stan JSON? (RStan has stan_rdump() which will output a Stan readable data file.)
>>>
>>>
>>> The short is, I'm not an expert in JSON data structures. I don't know how data is typically stored when it's more than just a vector. If someone can clue me in on these things, it wouldn't be hard to implement a JSON parser.
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> Daniel
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 3:30 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>> This isn't an either-or situation.  We can implement multiple
>>> data formats and let users use whatever they like.  The only
>>> thing holding us back is programming time.  So if someone wants
>>> to volunteer to write a JSON interface, we can help you plug
>>> it into Stan's C++ layer.  JSON's pretty easy, but unfortunately,
>>> like R's dump format, doesn't have a built-in typing mechanism
>>> for integer vs. real values.
>>>
>>> The way Stan actually works is that it has a low-level
>>> abstract base class representation for reading data that gets
>>> called in the constructor of a class that reads data and then
>>> is used to evaluate log probabilities and gradients and transforms.
>>>
>>> Currently the abstract base class is implemented three different ways:
>>>
>>>    - reading from R-style dump format streams/files (used in CmdStan)
>>>
>>>    - reading from R data structures/environments (used in RStan)
>>>
>>>    - reading from Python data structures (not sure the details, used in PyStan)
>>>
>>> Writing something to read from a std::ostream for JSON is on
>>> our to-do list, but not a high priority at the moment.  If someone wants
>>> to take it on, we're happy to help!
>>>
>>> Andrew's asked for something to read from CSV files, but given his
>>> response (most of our data's non-rectangular), we've apparently been
>>> succesfull in explaining why it's challenging.
>>>
>>> We haven't thought much about bringing something like Stan down
>>> to users who don't know stats --- the whole thing's based on writing
>>> your own probability function!  Our target's more the people who understand
>>> how to express the log probabilty function for their model, but don't want
>>> to code a sampler/estimator for it.
>>>
>>> We have thought about GUIs and cluster distribution to make exploring
>>> models easier.  But nothing's come of it because we don't have
>>> any GUI programmers and we only have half-formulated ideas on how to
>>> make it work in limited domains like hierarchical GLMs.   Andrew and Ben
>>> have gone down this path with their multiple imputation (mi) package in R,
>>> so maybe they have some insight to offer.
>>>
>>> We have thought about shipping models off to the cluster to grind
>>> through --- in fact, we're doing that.  But model fitting is usually more
>>> of an interactive process where you don't try twenty models at once, but
>>> you try one, see how it works and what you learn from fitting it, and
>>> then use that to guide the next model.  Just managing all the results
>>> and model specifications is hard in this setting, which is why it would
>>> be nice to automate it with a GUI or scripting language or something.
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>
>>> On 12/18/13, 1:38 PM, Tim Triche, Jr. wrote:
>>> I haven't been using Stan as much as I could, but Jeroen's remark makes me think that you're overanalyzing this.  Many
>>> users won't ever use Stan directly.  If you want someone to use a stats tool, it should probably resemble Excel, the
>>> most widely used statistical analysis package in the known universe.   The data can live in a table, but the
>>> relationships that define pivot tables, functions, etc. are substantially more complicated, and it's those we're
>>> concerned about.
>>>
>>> As long as your data structures are flat (like tables), a CSV file is great.  The instant your data structures diverge
>>> from a regular tabular structure, something like JSON has enormous advantages in terms of representing hierarchies, etc.
>>> in an easily parsed form, supported by a vast number of potential "producer" and "consumer" applications.  If Stan is
>>> going to take over the world it might as well support distributed operation, which is greatly facilitated by having this
>>> sort of widely supported data exchange format.
>>>
>>> Here's one scenario to consider.  You have smallish samples (relative to the complexity of the model you want to fit)
>>> and a lot of semi-technical people with domain knowledge and common sense, but no real interest in programming.  They
>>> just want to know where to buy ads, what stuff to work on, etc.  They notice that Bayesian models tend to offer better
>>> predictive performance in such situations and would like to build and fit them without learning how to program.  They're
>>> willing to consider pictures of distributions, etc. and have a program generate pictures of marginals, posteriors, etc.
>>> for sanity checking, and they'd like to store the models that did / did not work somewhere "in the cloud" (i.e.,
>>> somewhere they don't have to back up manually, like Dropbox or a database).  Some clever guy realizes that he can be a
>>> hero if he rigs up a web interface that guides people towards less-stupid model choices and draws some pictures for them
>>> to sign off on when each model is constructed.  Then the models get shipped off to Stan, which grinds through them as
>>> compute power permits, and the users get emails when their models converge, along with a reference to allow predictive
>>> fits on new data that looks like the old data.
>>>
>>> Maybe users drag and drop colorful bits into a canvas object or some such (I'm already throwing up a little bit in the
>>> back of my mouth).  It would sure be nice to compactly represent those distributions and their relationships to each
>>> other, wouldn't it? Especially if you wanted to visualize certain marginal or posterior distributions.  But if
>>> everything is in a CSV-formatted table with a fixed number of columns, you have to somehow kludge in a place for any
>>> dependencies between variables.  With a loosely structured "object" (list of stuff) like JSON or YAML allows, you just
>>> pass everything & pull it back out on the other end.
>>>
>>> Something like this: http://www.jsoneditoronline.org/  (See?  Not so complex!)
>>>
>>> The rules are simple: Lists in { curlies }, arrays in [ brackets ], separate different items with commas.  If there's
>>> anything more brutally simple, I haven't seen it.
>>>
>>> JSON became a de facto standard because it's just about the simplest thing that could possibly work, for the task.
>>>   People would just use CSV if it were easier, but for passing around data structures, it rapidly becomes apparent that
>>> it's actually harder with a flat tabular representation.  Strange but true.
>>>
>>> Anyways, that's my piece for the day.  YMMV and I respect your opinion.  But I disagree with it, and I wanted to lay out
>>> my reasoning for why I disagreed.
>>>
>>> Best,
>>>
>>> --t
>>>
>>> On Wed, Dec 18, 2013 at 9:44 AM, Glenn Hoetker <ghoe...@mainex1.asu.edu <mailto:ghoe...@mainex1.asu.edu>> wrote:
>>>
>>>     While JSON offers certain advantages for data exchange, it would also pose a significant barrier to entry for some
>>>     potential users.  For example, I do most of my data manipulation and analysis in Stata. While the R-dump format is,
>>>     uhm, different, it is brutally straight-forward.  Writing code to write my data into the R-dump format was pretty
>>>     straight-forward and didn't require me to know anything about R.    Writing out my data in JSON, however, would be
>>>     significantly more difficult and require me to learn about the intricacies of a moderately convoluted data format
>>>     (at least relative to R-dump).
>>>
>>>     At the moment, I suspect most users to Stan are already users of Python or R, meaning they have easily available
>>>     tools for producing a JSON file and probably the programming expertise to make it a non-issue.  If the hope is to
>>>     grow the use of Stan towards a slightly more general audience, however, JSON might be sub-optimal.  Since the Stan
>>>     syntax itself is pretty straight-forward for someone comfortable with the statistical concepts, just getting the
>>>     data ready to go might actually be the biggest barrier for some.
>>>
>>>     An old-fashioned comma (or tab) delimited file with variable names in the top row (data.csv) may have disadvantages
>>>     in this setting that I don't grasp, but I would offer it for consideration as (a) very easy to produce from almost
>>>     any package, (b) not connected to any particular statistical package (the term "r-dump file" is infelicitous to the
>>>     ear of someone who hasn't used R), and (c) easy to import into almost any package, even if it is subsequently munged
>>>     into something else.  Since Stan output is comma-delimited, it also provides a nice symmetry.
>>>
>>>     Just something for your consideration.  I'm enjoying learning to use Stan and find it a powerful, useful package.
>>>       Thanks to all who are moving it forward!
>>>
>>>     Glenn Hoetker
>>>     WP Carey School of Business
>>>     Arizona State University
>>>
>>>

messages.subject: RE: [stan-users] Re: GeoBUGS distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrance,

Marcus has been so kind to send me a pre-final version of the matrix_normal_prec distribution, and it works like a charm for small spatial matrices.  However, with more areas (e.g. 100+) STAN quickly becomes orders of magnitude slower than GeoBUGS.

Cheers,
Marcel

Date: Wed, 18 Dec 2013 14:17:41 -0800
From: tds...@gmail.com

To: stan-...@googlegroups.com
Subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: GeoBUGS distributions

Hi, While one could certainly directly update lp for the log_det and matrix variate kernel associated to a separable covariance matrix (e.g.  a covariance matrix formulated as a tensor product of lower order covariance matrices), a matrix variate normal (that would input precision matrices) would be very nice as it would presumably provide an easy-to-use implementation.  I didn't fit it in the manual for Stan 2.0.1.  Did this ever happen?

thank you, terrance.

On Friday, May 3, 2013 5:44:24 PM UTC-4, Marcus wrote:
> Hi Marcel,
>
> I've been working on something related to this and I realized that
> perhaps the easiest way to do what you need in Stan in a reasonably
> efficient way is to implement a matrix_normal(_prec) distribution.  I
> believe the distribution you're computing can formulated in terms of a
> matrix normal distribution, see
> http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_normal_distribution for details.
>
> If this is the case let me know and I should be able to get a fairly
> efficient version of that in Stan pretty quickly.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus
>
> On Thu, May 2, 2013 at 1:47 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > On Thursday, May 2, 2013 1:16:49 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> >>
> >> On Thursday, May 2, 2013 12:52:18 PM UTC-4, Marcel Jonker wrote:
> >>>
> >>>  If there is a way to estimate the model with the current version of
> >>> STAN, that would be great - even if it samples very slowly - because it's
> >>> somewhat urgent by now. The problematic matrix is the Kronecker product of a
> >>> 4x4 correlation matrix and a large adjacency matrix (loaded as data), so the
> >>> correlation matrix itself is pretty small. Only the precision matrix of the
> >>> mult_normal_prec is large. Perhaps that makes a difference?
> >>
> >>
> >> It wouldn't help much, in part because the correlation matrix is small and
> >> in part because even if you had the Cholesky factor, our matrix
> >> multiplication operations generally wouldn't exploit the fact that it is
> >> triangular.
> >>
> >> If you have something like
> >>
> >> Sigma^-1 = (D - a * W) %x% Lambda
> >>
> >> where Lambda is a correlation matrix and are going to multiply that from
> >> both sides by a vector y and D - a * W is sparse, then you can be more
> >> efficient without explicitly constructing the Kronecker product. Basically,
> >> make an array of 4-vectors that holds the product of Lambda post-multiplied
> >> by each 4-element segment of y. Scale those by the appropriate (if non-zero)
> >> element of D - a * W, sum up to get a single vector, premultiply that by
> >> transpose(y), multiply that sum by 0.5 and subtract it from lp__.
> >
> >
> > Attached is an R script that demonstrates this idea of circumventing the
> > Kronecker product, which could be adapted to Stan syntax fairly easily but
> > it would probably be worth the effort to avoid multiplying by elements of D
> > - a * W that are zero.
> >
> > Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for your reply and input on the relative performance.  The dimension of each GP trajectory would be about 300 for me, so I take note.  In my case, however, I'd like to additively chain together multiple covariance kernels, while also modeling the dependence among a set of units where each expresses a function (drawn from a GP).  So GeoBUGS isn't going to get it.  In theory, STAN has the flexibility to model something like this.

Re: speed, I know the best approach would be to project an N dimension GP to a lower dimension N_1 < N.  The resulting approximation would also numerically stabilize the covariance matrix.  This is what Aki implements in GPstuff in a variety of flavors.  Though STAN is a wonderful tool, I've never achieved reasonable chain mixing in STAN under a variety of research-calibre models due to scale differences across the parameter space.  a black box HMC with a sparse/diagonal mass matrix just doesn't seem to work for anything I've ever tried to implement.  So before I invest a lot of time to perform the projection to a lower dimension, myself (by directly updating lp_) in STAN, I'd like to have a quicker solution that I can test to see if I achieve good mixing.  My model is less hierarchical than is typical for my work, so I'm hoping this time I will achieve good mixing.

So Marcus, may I have a copy of your matrix_normal() distribution.  I also found a post about a multi_gp() distribution.  Is this available, as well?

Thank you, Terrance

morning, and (to answer my earlier question) the revised logging makes

sequence (because the logging switches to the next active chain after
the first one finishes).  In case anyone else shares my confusion,

messages.body_plain:
Working on cdfs, complementary cdfs, and their log versions
would be a great project for someone who wants to dive
deep into numerical processing.  The hard part is getting
derivatives w.r.t. the parameters and stable complementary cdfs.

There are intrinsic problems with floating point for representing
cdfs near 1 --- the closest you can get is about 1e-14.  That's
why you get both erf() and erfc() in numerical libs, and both log()
and log1m().

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 12/19/13, 4:58 PM, Linas Mockus wrote:
> rstan users:
>
> Is it possible implement the attached WinBUGS model on Rstan?

You could translate this one line-for-line into Stan.
Presumably x[i] == gamma won't come up, but if it did,
you'd wind up using both terms.

Conditionals are more efficient in Stan, and arguably easier
to understand:

for (i in 1:N) {

   if (x[i] > gamma)
     y[i] ~ normal(alpha1 * x[i] + beta1, sigma);
   else
     y[i] ~ normal(alpha2 * x[i] + beta2, sigma);
}

Note that I'm skipping the case where x[i] == gamma, because
presumably you didn't want both terms used in that case.

Note that Stan's normal() takes a standard deviation parameter,
not a precision parameter.

For most efficiency, you'd vectorize:

for (i in 1:N) {

   if (x[i] > gamma)
     mu[i] <- alpha1 * x[i] + beta1;
   else
     mu[i] <- alpha2 * x[i] + beta2;
}
y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

We've already translated all of the BUGS models if you
want more examples.  And there's an appendix in the manual comparing
BUGS and Stan's modeling.

We'd recommend at least weakly informative priors instead
of the gamma and normals you're using.  BUGS has changed their
examples away from those gammas.  Stan supports improper priors,
so you can also just drop them as long as the posterior is proper.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] step function in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Because this comes up a lot (people asking about fitting discontinuous models with Stan) I thought I'd expand on *why* it will be bad.

If the posterior is very discontinuous or has no gradient, then Stan (well, HMC/NUTS specifically) is going to be, at the very least, extremely inefficient.  To be clear, technically the Markov Chain that Stan simulates will eventually mix for most such models...it's just that none of us are likely to be alive when that finally happens.  You'd be better off actually using Random-Walk Metropolis (one reason we should have something like a good adaptive RWM implemented in Stan).  The inefficiency comes from at least two places:

- Unnecessary use of autodiff.  Considering this is probably 95% or more of the time spent sampling, that's big.
- Unnecessary evaluations of the log probability caused by unnecessarily long trajectories. If the gradient is useless, then your best bet is to just take a single step and accept or reject.

A model like this would be one where the parameters are, e.g., rounded to the nearest integer or piped through a step function, so that they have no gradient.

Now, maybe your posterior is *mostly* continuous but has a few discontinuities.  (E.G., a mixture model of a Gaussian and a uniform over a small region.)  Such a model can work OK with Stan (using HMC/NUTS), however, it may cause adaptation to break or result in inefficient sampling of some parts of the space.  (E.G., you may see a lot of parameter "sticking" in your trace plots.)

At any rate, Linus' model is somewhere between the extremes.  It's possible that Stan would work ok, but for all such models you can't expect the same level of performance and should approach the samples with a healthy amount of skepticism.  As the WinBUGS manual says "Beware: MCMC sampling can be dangerous!"  Stan is no exception to that, although we like to think that maybe its a little bit less so.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: GeoBUGS distributions
messages.body_plain:
I don't know GeoBUGS very well but I can pretty easily guess two of the major culprits:

- Stan has no support for sparse matrices and some of these are very sparse.  Alternatively, we don't support the specific spatial distributions which could be specified in a more restricted form without requiring the use of sparse matrices.
- A smart implementation of these distributions would cache the Cholesky factorizations, log determinants, etc of matrices which are only a function of data.  Stan has no capacity to do this, making some models *very* inefficient because the same large matrix must be refactored at every log_prob evaluation.

I've actually been thinking about how we could solve the second issue if we were so inclined by adding an optional "cache" structure where the *_log functions could store and reuse information about data parameters.  I don't really have time to do it, but it could significantly speed up GP prediction models as well as these kings of spatial distributions.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Thank you all.  Technically such functions model actual chemical processes.  In reality the step is not so sharp.  One way is to add some artificial parameter to underlying model to "soften" the step so it becomes "acceptable" by algorithm.  Another way is to implement step function as a "soft" step - not a mathematical step.  Because all measurements have error perhaps it doesn't matter which way to approach the discontinuity in the derivative.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] step function in Stan
messages.body_plain:
I added warning sections in the manual for if_else(), step()
and the rounding functions round(), floor() and ceil(), indicating
that they'll break derivatives and hence might slow down the
efficiency of HMC sampling.

I don't have very concrete expectations of speed for HMC sampling,
and I suspect most of our users are in the same boat.
In Stan, efficiency's tied up with HMC in terms of the geometry of the
unconstrained parameter space induced by the model (including the
effect of the size and shape of data), and the time to evaluate the
log probability function depends on the size of the expression tree
implied by the model and data and the efficiency of auto-diff on
the particular formulation of the model.

- Bob

On 12/19/13, 5:21 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Yeah, but then we have a false expectation for HMC-like performance and I don't want
> anyone thinking ill of Stan because of that.  Such models can also significantly stress
> adaptation (namely the step size), upping the potential for poor results.

>
>> Michael:
>>

And I think the quick answer to the question is that the model _can_ be written in Stan easily enough; we do actually have the ability to implement a step function.
>

messages.body_plain:
On 12/19/13, 7:54 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> ...

> Now, maybe your posterior is *mostly* continuous but has a few discontinuities.  (E.G., a mixture model of a Gaussian
> and a uniform over a small region.)

Given that we don't have discrete parameters, usershave
to marginalize out the mixture indicator.

So rather than

   z[n] ~ bernoulli(theta);
   if (z[n])
     y ~ uniform(L,U);
   else
     y ~ normal(mu,sigma);

we're suggesting writing a new distribution

   p(y) =def= theta * uniform(y|L,U) + (1 - theta) * normal(y|mu,sigma)

implemented on the log scale as

   increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(theta) + uniform_log(y[n],L,U),
                      log1m(theta) + normal_log(y[n],mu,sigma));

I'm pretty sure the result's continuous.

(And relevant to your message in the other thread on CAR, you'd want
to cache the log(theta) and log1m(theta) values into a local variable
and reuse in the loop over n.)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] help with model
messages.body_plain:
The variables you define locally in the model need to be
defined as parameters:

 >      vector<lower=0, upper=100>[M] sigma_b_s;
 >      vector[M] eta_b_s;

Unlike in BUGS, Stan variables must be defined before
they are used.  Data and transformed data is defined as
data is read in.  Parameters are defined externally and
transformed parameters must be defined in their block.
Local variables must be defined with "<-" before they are
used in a block.

Your problem is with local variables, which must be defined
before they are used.  The sampling statement "~" doesn't
literally do sampling --- it just increments the log
probability function.

- Bob

messages.subject: what is refactoring?
messages.body_plain:
On 12/19/13, 8:39 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
> thanks for providing more insight into how stan works.  i'd appreciate your defining 'refactoring'?

We talk about this a lot, so it's worth mentioning with its
own subject.  You could do worse than reading this:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_refactoring

The first paragraph is:

   Code refactoring is a "disciplined technique for restructuring
   an existing body of code, altering its internal
   structure without changing its external behavior",[1] undertaken
   in order to improve some of the nonfunctional
   attributes of the software. Advantages include improved code
   readability and reduced complexity to improve the
   maintainability of the source code, as well as a more expressive
   internal architecture or object model to improve
   extensibility.

It's a grey line as to when something moves from being "refactoring"
into more general code development.

Fowler's book is great, by the way, even if it is in Java.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: WAIC in the context of spatial models, data imputation/censoring, and/or measurement error
messages.body_plain:
I've read this chapter (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf <http://www.stat.columbia.edu/%7Egelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf>) and still have some questions how to compute WAIC for a hierarchical model. Let me describe what I think is a correct way to compute WAIC...

Let's say I have data from N subjects (i=1,2,3,..., N) and each subject has T trials. I build a model that has P individual parameters and each individual parameter has its hyper parameters. Assume each parameter is coming from a normal distribution, so group parameters will be the mean and SD of each individual parameter.

1. First compute each subject's lppd_i (Eq 5, the chapter). I used the notation lppd_i to indicate that this is lppd of subject i. First calculate p(y_i | theta^s). I would do it by programming the model again in Python (or R) and using posterior samples. Use each subject's posterior samples (s=1,2,3,..., S) of individual parameters (not group parameters) to compute the probability over S samples and T trials. Calculate lppd_i using Eq 5 for each subject.
2. Compute pWAIC, either pWAIC1 or pWAIC2 (Eq 11). Again use each subject's posterior samples of individual parameters.
3. Compute each subject's WAIC_i ( WAIC_i = 2*lppd_i - 2* pWAIC_i)
4. Sum up all subjects' WAIC_i to compute a single value WAIC (WAIC = sum_{i=1}^N WAIC_i

If someone could check if this is a correct way to compute WAIC for a hiearchical model, it would be great. Thanks.

CS

On Thursday, December 12, 2013 10:06:12 AM UTC-5, Aki Vehtari wrote:
> Cody> "First, I am wondering how WAIC (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_understand_final.pdf) deals with data imputation and measurement error. Can the llpd and effective number parameters be calculated when the dependent variable is a random node itself?"
>
> I assume that you have multivariate dependent variable y_ij, where i=1,...,n and j=1,...p.  I think it is easiest first to think how CV would work as WAIC is approximation of CV. There's two options.
>
> The first options is the pure M-open approach (see http://dx.doi.org/10.1214/12-SS102 for discussion of M-open etc.) where you compute the llpd only for the observed outputs. For example, if p=2 the collection of lppd_i's contain mix of terms p_post(-i)(y_i1), p_post(-i)(y_i2), p_post(-i)(y_i1,y_i2) depending which observations y_ij are missing. As same observations are missing for all models, obtained lppd_CV is ok for model comparison.
>
> The second option is to use mix of M-open and M-completed/closed approaches. For example, if p=2 the collection of lppd_i's contain the terms p_post(-i)(y_i1,y_i2), where in case of missing data we integrate over the missing data distribution using the imputation model (which may be problematic if the imputation algorithm is not consistent as Mike warned).
>
> In the case of measurement error, I assume that you have all observations and it's just that your model is slightly more complicated.
>
> WAIC can be used in these cases, too. The first option is simpler to implement.
>
> Cody> "Secondly, WAIC, like other metrics, seems to be derived under assumptions of independent errors. Some people have found that measures like AIC and BIC perform reasonably in model comparison in spite of violating these assumptions (using simulated data). Would it be insane to include a WAIC comparison in a paper comparing spatial models?"
>
> If WAIC is derived from cross-validation it does not need the assumption of independent errors. The prediction task consists of a collection of independent marginal predictions (1a). It depends on your decision problem, whether this the correct prediction task or should you care more about the joint predictions (1b). Although WAIC and CV are asymptotically equal, they assume slightly different prediction tasks: WAIC) interested in the predictions only at the observed covariate values (2a), CV) interested in the predictions also at the not yet observed covariate values (2b). If your answer is 1a+2a, then WAIC is sane choice although it seems that it can break sometimes when using very flexible models (like Gaussian process or Markov random field spatial models). See the slides http://www.lce.hut.fi/~ave/slides_trondheim.pdf (we are writing a paper about this and further developments).
>
> Mike> "Actually AIC is an approximation to WAIC, which is an approximation to the KL divergence between the predictive posterior predictive distribution and the true data distribution (assuming one exists).  It's really not as assumption of independent errors for WAIC, but rather an assumption that each datum is really two independent data (as in cross validation)."
>
> cross-validation assumes exhangeability, not independence
>
> To summarise: if your choice is between WAIC or some other *IC, use WAIC. If you can use CV, it is a more robust choice.
>

> > In the case of measurement error, I assume that you have all observations and it's just that your model is slightly more complicated.
> >
> > WAIC can be used in these cases, too. The first option is simpler to implement.
> >
> > Cody> "Secondly, WAIC, like other metrics, seems to be derived under assumptions of independent errors. Some people have found that measures like AIC and BIC perform reasonably in model comparison in spite of violating these assumptions (using simulated data). Would it be insane to include a WAIC comparison in a paper comparing spatial models?"
> >
> > If WAIC is derived from cross-validation it does not need the assumption of independent errors. The prediction task consists of a collection of independent marginal predictions (1a). It depends on your decision problem, whether this the correct prediction task or should you care more about the joint predictions (1b). Although WAIC and CV are asymptotically equal, they assume slightly different prediction tasks: WAIC) interested in the predictions only at the observed covariate values (2a), CV) interested in the predictions also at the not yet observed covariate values (2b). If your answer is 1a+2a, then WAIC is sane choice although it seems that it can break sometimes when using very flexible models (like Gaussian process or Markov random field spatial models). See the slides http://www.lce.hut.fi/~ave/slides_trondheim.pdf (we are writing a paper about this and further developments).
> >
> > Mike> "Actually AIC is an approximation to WAIC, which is an approximation to the KL divergence between the predictive posterior predictive distribution and the true data distribution (assuming one exists).  It's really not as assumption of independent errors for WAIC, but rather an assumption that each datum is really two independent data (as in cross validation)."
> >
> > cross-validation assumes exhangeability, not independence
> >
> > To summarise: if your choice is between WAIC or some other *IC, use WAIC. If you can use CV, it is a more robust choice.
> >
>

messages.body_plain:
Terrance,

You can find the version of matrix_normal_prec in this branch: https://github.com/mbrubake/stan/tree/improper_matrix_normal_prec in my personal repo.  Note that it's based on an ancient (by Stan standards) version of Stan so it's likely to have issues and uses the old command line interface.  Also, note that the only thing it really does is skip the positive-definiteness check of matrices which are data.  This avoids some unnecessary computation and lets you use a semi-definite matrix, however you need to make sure the result isn't an improper posterior so use at your own risk.

Cheers,
Marcus

>
> On 12/19/13, 7:54 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> > ...
> >
> > Now, maybe your posterior is *mostly* continuous but has a few discontinuities.  (E.G., a mixture model of a Gaussian
> > and a uniform over a small region.)
>
> Given that we don't have discrete parameters, usershave
> to marginalize out the mixture indicator.
>
> So rather than
>
>   z[n] ~ bernoulli(theta);
>   if (z[n])
>     y ~ uniform(L,U);
>   else
>     y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>
> we're suggesting writing a new distribution

>

The resulting posterior is not continuous because the uniform distribution has finite support, but I would expect NUTS/Stan to work ok on it.

> (And relevant to your message in the other thread on CAR, you'd want
> to cache the log(theta) and log1m(theta) values into a local variable
> and reuse in the loop over n.)

Yup, caching like that is always worth it in Stan.

Marcus

a) if zero is a constant, then it should be declared and assigned to in
a transformed data block;
b) if you define an Omega correlation matrix you don't need to compute
correlations, they are in Omega;

messages.body_plain:
The number of data points

   int<lower=1> N;

should probably be lower=0.  With that, you just
sample from the prior (assuming it's proper).

You should define L in the transformed parameters block and
only Sigma in the generated quantities block.  Transformed parameters
are there to let you calculate and then print out (save)
values that are functions of parameters (+ optionally data).
Functions of just data should go in transformed data.

The reason is that local variables like the L in the model
are not saved.  So you have to redefine the variable in
generated quantities to save it.

Rather than passing in a vector of zeroes, you can do this:

transformed data {
   vector[4] mu_prior;                 // vector of zeros
   mu_prior <- rep_vector(0.0,4);
}

You can really speed up the following significantly:

for (n in 1:N) {
   mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*c1[n] + beta[3]*c2[n] + beta[4]*c3[n]
            +  u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n] + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];
}

Because u and id and c1..c3 are data, you can compute a single
vector u_id_c[n] in transformed data:

   for (n in 1:N)
     u_id_c[n] <- u[id[n], 1] + u[id[n], 2]*c1[n] + u[id[n], 3]*c2[n] + u[id[n], 4]*c3[n];

and then calculate mu in a fully vectorized way:

   mu <- u_id_c beta[1] + beta[2] * c1 + beta[3] * c2 + beta[4] * c3

But I wouldn't try these kinds of optimizations until you're happy
with the model.  They all make it a bit less readable in my opinion.

- Bob

Thanks.  I hadn't seen Tabular before (another name that's
going to be hard to search for), nor had I heard of "probabilistic

The description of what they are on the Wikipedia page:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_relational_programming_language

just pointed to:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probabilistic_relational_model

Neither Stan nor BUGS seem to fit the model of relational model, which
seems derived from relational databases.  But then neither do Dyna or
Factorie, both of which I know form natural language processing.  And for
that matter, neither do Church or Infer.NET, both of which are much more
general.

- Bob

I think "schema" is synonymous to a certain degree to "model" in addition to "relational schema". In stan's case, the model has attributes organized as columns (rather than the rows of a traditional SQL database), and specifies their type, value constraints, and relationships (either "strong" in the case of transformed data or "weak" in case of modeling statements).

This seems like "schema" to me? What do you think?
Emil

messages.body_plain:
I just read the Tabular paper's examples and descriptions.

I believe by "schema" they just mean a relational schema
of the kind used to define the tables in a database.

Tabular's overall approach reminds me very much of a company called
Prior Knowledge's product, which filled in missing database tables using
some kind of non-parametric Bayesian models.  PK was acquired and apparently
dismantled or rebranded by Salesforce --- I can't find anything with
the query ["prior knowledge" site:salesforce.com <http://salesforce.com>].

I think I'd need to know Tabular's underlying languages Fun and
Infer.NET in order to actually understand how sampling works.
I don't understand how Church samples, either.

I don't see any evidence in the paper supporting the claim that Tabular
makes it easier for non-statistics-savvy users to build useful models.
By the time the paper gets to IRT models (figure 2), the annotations look
pretty complex.  But then we're interested in a different angle ---
building semi-automated tools for statistics-savvy users.

Andrew Gelman kicked off the Stan project by getting us to think about
specifying hierarchical models in a database-like way (he didn't know that's
what he was talking about, but Matt and I did).  And we've
talked about it off and on in our meetings ever since --- I think Michael
even has some sketches of how to make it all work in practice.
Linking databases and Stan would be a great project.  At least some subset
of these Tabular models could be directly translated to Stan.   Especially if
there were some hierarchical examples.  It would even be possible to wrap
the I/O to databases in the same way that RStan and PyStan wrap
I/O in the R and Python.  Discrete variables would be a challenge, but we
wouldn't have to start there.

- Bob

P.S.  As an aside, papers like this stress how isolated machine learning
is from the applied statistics --- the paper cites a machine learning
paper in 2012 as introducing IRT models!

On 12/24/13, 1:26 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, Bob, is the stuff you're discussing at all related to this:
> http://probcomp.csail.mit.edu/bayesdb/

Not quite.  BayesDB skips the specification/annotation step, so
should be even more amenable to non-statistically-trained users:

   BayesDB assumes that each row of your table is a sample from some fixed population or generative process, and
   estimates the joint distribution over the columns. BQL then allows you to draw Bayesian inferences about individuals
   and about the overall population or process. The estimates are currently provided by CrossCat, a new nonparametric
   Bayesian method for analyzing high-dimensional data tables.

They do say you can override the defaults.

As to CrossCat, they say:

   CrossCat is a domain-general, Bayesian method for analyzing high-dimensional data tables. CrossCat estimates the full
   joint distribution over the variables in the table from the data, via approximate inference in a hierarchical,
   nonparametric Bayesian model, and provides efficient samplers for every conditional distribution. CrossCat combines
   strengths of nonparametric mixture modeling and Bayesian network structure learning: it can model any joint
   distribution given enough data by positing latent variables, but also discovers independencies between the observable
   variables.

That really reminds me of what Prior Knowledge were doing.

And it's related to Yajuan's thesis.

I'd rather these authors tried to make what they were doing sound
less brand new and relate it to other things.

Digging into Appendix A, they're using a factor model that's composed
of a mixture of mixtures, both mixing levels controlled by a Dirichlet
process.  So it'd be able to non-parametrically fit something like
a generalized multidimensional ideal-point model (I use that example because
you and Jennifer discuss a 2D example in your regression book).  They
seem to be overly optimistic about convergence of Gibbs samplers in
practice given the extreme multimodality of these factor models (there's
been some neat work lately in the machine learning literature on
spectral separability conditions for identifying general forms of factor
models, which might be relevant).

> Also see attached paper that describes what they're doing.  It reminds me a lot of the "virtual database query" idea

> that I've been yapping about for the past few yearsï¿½  This one could actually be fun to do as a side project, perhaps

> with that NYT programmer guy we've heard about.

Exactly what I was saying, minus the descriptive term "yapping" :-)

- Bob
