messages.subject: Constraints for hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I'm having trouble figuring out the best way to code models where there is a hierarchical structure on parameters that need to be constrained. The simplest example I could come up with is here:
https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/8119696

In that model, data are generated from a gaussian with mean of zero and standard deviation ("sigma") that is influenced by two variables, "participant" and "condition". There are 100 levels of participant and 2 levels of condition. Sigma values vary across participants according to a gaussian, and the effect of condition on sigma values also varies across participants according to a gaussian.

Ideally the model should be set up so that it only explores areas of the parameter space that yield positive values for sigma, but despite my efforts thus far, I can't seem to figure out how to achieve this constraint. The result is initialization failure with error messages indicating that some sampled sigma values were negative (ex. "Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter[0]  is -2.6257961330947777:0, but must be > 0!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.")

Any suggestions?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.body_plain:
You could always write it as a log-linear model instead of
a linear model --- just exp() transform the linear
predictor.

Your code:

   for (i in 1:trialNumTotal)
     thisSigma[i] <- personSigma[personNum[i]] + conditionContrast[i] * personSigmaEffect[personNum[i]];

   y ~ normal(0, thisSigma);

would change on the second line to this:

   y ~ normal(0, exp(thisSigma));

You don't need a Jacobian adjustment for parameter transforms on the
right-hand side of sampling statements.

You can then get rid of all the constraints on the slope
and intercept in the regression for thisSigma.

Alternatively, you could tranform the predictor conditionContrast[i]
if you really want personSigma and personSigmaEffect to be positive.

- Bob

On 12/26/13, 1:26 PM, Mike Lawrence wrote:
> Thanks Bob!
>
> Question on the idea of switching to a log-linear model: if the data are truly generated by a linear-linear process,
> would the inferences from the log-linear analysis remain valid? For example, since the sigma for a given participant in
> a given condition is
>

>      thisSigma[i] = personSigma[personNum[i]] + conditionContrast[i] * personSigmaEffect[personNum[i]__]

>
> , if I make the model log-linear by doing "y ~ normal(0, exp(thisSigma));", the previously additive relationship between
> "personSigma" and "personSigmaEffect" becomes multiplicative, does it not? Doesn't this constitute an inferentially
> important change in the model?

It's definitely different.  Whether it's inferentially important
or not is an empirical question.   The linear relationship obviously
doesn't make sense except for values that produce positive scales.

Andrew may jump in here with other advice.

> And a question on the idea of simply recoding the contrasts to avoid negative values: I had them coded as -1/+1 so that
> it was orthogonal with the intercept; if I recode to +1/+2, is it simply a matter of transforming the samples after
> sampling to get the original -1/+1 coding back?

You could translate so the predictor's range is in (0,2), and
then requiring the slope and intercept to be positive will
guarantee the scale is positive.  You can translate back, but
that may no longer guarantee positive scales.  You need to
invert the linear rescaling, which can be done on the samples.

- Bob

messages.subject: prediction/simulation/causal analysis
messages.body_plain:
This is a question about interpreting stan models, not estimating them.
I don't think it's really stan-specific, but I thought I'd see if anyone
has suggestions.  I am trying to compute effects, defined as the average
change in outcomes.  The problem is that for each set of coefficients I
have to draw repeated simulations, and it's taking forever.  Is there a
better way?

I want to find the average causal effect of some variable for my sample:
define the effect, delta, to be mean(B | low) - mean(B | high).
B is an outcome; the mean is across members of the sample; low and high
are versions of the data with some variable A manipulated to take on low
or high values (e.g., observed - 1/2 and observed + 1/2).
The distribution of B depends on covariates X through a model with
parameters b.  A is one of the covariates.

I want the  posterior distribution of delta, or at least the mean and
standard deviation of that distribution.

Given the posterior distribution of b, estimated with stan, one can draw
b(i), the i'th simulated set of coefficients, and compute delta(i) if
the model is straightforward.

If not, one can simulate outcomes B for each set of coefficients, giving
delta(i, j) where i is the i'th set of coefficients and j indexes
simulated outcomes for those coefficients.  One can estimate delta(i)
with the mean over j of the delta(i, j).

There are 2 reasons the direct computation of delta(i) does not seem
feasible for me.  The main one is that I am working in a multi-stage
model, in which A->B->C->D, A causes B, B causes C, and so on.  There
are also control variables, and earlier variables can have direct as
well as indirect effects on later ones.  This means that one set of
coefficients for the A->B model create a distribution of B's, and each
distribution of B's implies a different set of downstream estimates.
This seems to leave me with numerical integration as the only reasonable
strategy.

The minor problem is that computing the expected outcome for each
individual, given all the covariates and a set of parameter values, is
not always straightforward because the models may have truncation,
censoring, or mixtures.

At the moment B is a count; C is multinomial; and D is binary.

I'm thinking of capturing the predicted means directly when feasible.
This should increase precision, but does not eliminate the need to draw
repeatedly for each parameter set.

Ross Boylan

On Fri, 2013-12-27 at 17:18 +0100, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Ross:
> I think you can just draw one simulation of the outcome for each parameter value, so you can do that in the "predictive quantities" block or whatever it is called, right?  But maybe there is something I'm missing here.

If all I wanted was an estimate of the mean effect, I think doing one
simulation per parameter set would suffice, but I don't think that gives
me the uncertainty I need.

Concretely, I can simulate draws from a count distribution, and compare
the average counts between the high and low scenarios.  But the
variability in the outcome arises partly from variability in the
parameters and partly from the variability induced by the random process
for a given set of parameters (mechanically, the last part corresponds
to the simulation given parameter values).  I only want the former.
Since I'm taking means for my sample of individuals (or subsets of them)
I thought the simulation induced variability would be trivial (since I'm
taking the mean of many simulated values), but some testing showed it is
not.

A more mechanical problem is that I'm estimating each model separately
(e.g., A->B, A+B->C, ...) but I need to combine them all at the end.  So
I can't do predictions within a single model estimation.

In a perfect world I would estimate all the models jointly, and thus
avoid assuming the coefficients between models were independent, but
estimating them singly was hard enough.

A final mechanical issue is that the prediction is not based on the data
used to fit the model, but a modified version of that data.

> Also, I assume you've seen this paper:
> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf
> A

I hadn't.  Thank you for the reference.

I looked around in the 3rd edition of BDA but didn't find much; my
impression is the 2nd edition had a bit more, though I haven't checked
it.

Ross

P.S. Fortunately I've been able to speed up the R code, though the
post-analysis is still much slower than the model estimation, which
seems off.  It took about 900 CPU hours to evaluate 2000 sets of
coefficients with 400 simulations for each.  In contrast, I think
fitting all the models took only a handful of CPU hours.

messages.subject: Instrumental variable estimation
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am trying to figure out how to estimate an instrumental variable model using Stan. The attached file is a very simple simulated example in which three variables are involved: y is dependent variable, x is the treatment variable, and z is the treatment assignment (i.e., instrument) variable. The stan code was borrowed from example 23.4 of the ARM code repo (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/feature/ARM/src/models/ARM/Ch.23/sesame_street1.stan) but is much simpler because I am not doing any multilevel stuff. The model seems to work but I got a lot of warnings saying that:

"Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Invalid value of Sigma_yt: Error in function validate transformed params N4stan5agrad3varE: Sigma_ytSigma_yt is not positive definite. Sigma_yt(0,0) is 1.3618914389258178e-17:0.
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."

Should I be worried? Are there ways to improve the code?

Thanks and happy new years!

Best,
Shige

> the treatment assignment (i.e., instrument) variable. The stan code was borrowed from example 23.4 of the ARM code repo

> positive definite. Sigma_yt(0,0) is 1.3618914389258178e-17:0.
> If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the
> sampler is fine,
> but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified."
>
> Should I be worried? Are there ways to improve the code?

No, you shouldn't be worried.  We don't know how to convince users
that the message means what it says!

Part of the issue is on our end --- we need to relax the
tolerance on our tests for positive definiteness.

What you do want to check is that your estimates are not
jammed up against parameer boundaries.  That is, if you
get rho_yt near -1 or 1, or sigma_t or sigma_y near 0 or 100,
that probably indicates a mismatch of your model to your data.

- Bob

On Dec 27, 2013, at 9:22 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:

> On Fri, 2013-12-27 at 17:18 +0100, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> Ross:
>> I think you can just draw one simulation of the outcome for each parameter value, so you can do that in the "predictive quantities" block or whatever it is called, right?  But maybe there is something I'm missing here.
> If all I wanted was an estimate of the mean effect, I think doing one
> simulation per parameter set would suffice, but I don't think that gives
> me the uncertainty I need.

Ahh, I see what you are saying.  In this case, I suspect that two random draws of new data per simulation of the parameters would suffice.

>
> Concretely, I can simulate draws from a count distribution, and compare
> the average counts between the high and low scenarios.  But the
> variability in the outcome arises partly from variability in the
> parameters and partly from the variability induced by the random process
> for a given set of parameters (mechanically, the last part corresponds
> to the simulation given parameter values).  I only want the former.
> Since I'm taking means for my sample of individuals (or subsets of them)
> I thought the simulation induced variability would be trivial (since I'm
> taking the mean of many simulated values), but some testing showed it is
> not.
>
> A more mechanical problem is that I'm estimating each model separately
> (e.g., A->B, A+B->C, ...) but I need to combine them all at the end.  So
> I can't do predictions within a single model estimation.
>
> In a perfect world I would estimate all the models jointly, and thus
> avoid assuming the coefficients between models were independent, but
> estimating them singly was hard enough.
>
> A final mechanical issue is that the prediction is not based on the data
> used to fit the model, but a modified version of that data.
>
>> Also, I assume you've seen this paper:
>> http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/ape17.pdf
>> A
> I hadn't.  Thank you for the reference.
>
> I looked around in the 3rd edition of BDA but didn't find much; my
> impression is the 2nd edition had a bit more, though I haven't checked
> it.

No, the place we discuss this is in my book with Jennifer Hill.  But the treatment in the paper with Pardoe is more comprehensive.

>
> Ross
>
> P.S. Fortunately I've been able to speed up the R code, though the
> post-analysis is still much slower than the model estimation, which
> seems off.  It took about 900 CPU hours to evaluate 2000 sets of
> coefficients with 400 simulations for each.

With only 2 each it should be faster!

>  In contrast, I think
> fitting all the models took only a handful of CPU hours.
>
>>
>> On Dec 27, 2013, at 12:07 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
>>
>>> This is a question about interpreting stan models, not estimating them.
>>> I don't think it's really stan-specific, but I thought I'd see if anyone
>>> has suggestions.  I am trying to compute effects, defined as the average
>>> change in outcomes.  The problem is that for each set of coefficients I
>>> have to draw repeated simulations, and it's taking forever.  Is there a
>>> better way?
>>>
>>> I want to find the average causal effect of some variable for my sample:
>>> define the effect, delta, to be mean(B | low) - mean(B | high).
>>> B is an outcome; the mean is across members of the sample; low and high
>>> are versions of the data with some variable A manipulated to take on low
>>> or high values (e.g., observed - 1/2 and observed + 1/2).
>>> The distribution of B depends on covariates X through a model with
>>> parameters b.  A is one of the covariates.
>>>
>>> I want the  posterior distribution of delta, or at least the mean and
>>> standard deviation of that distribution.
>>>
>>> Given the posterior distribution of b, estimated with stan, one can draw
>>> b(i), the i'th simulated set of coefficients, and compute delta(i) if
>>> the model is straightforward.
>>>
>>> If not, one can simulate outcomes B for each set of coefficients, giving
>>> delta(i, j) where i is the i'th set of coefficients and j indexes
>>> simulated outcomes for those coefficients.  One can estimate delta(i)
>>> with the mean over j of the delta(i, j).
>>>
>>> There are 2 reasons the direct computation of delta(i) does not seem
>>> feasible for me.  The main one is that I am working in a multi-stage
>>> model, in which A->B->C->D, A causes B, B causes C, and so on.  There
>>> are also control variables, and earlier variables can have direct as
>>> well as indirect effects on later ones.  This means that one set of
>>> coefficients for the A->B model create a distribution of B's, and each
>>> distribution of B's implies a different set of downstream estimates.
>>> This seems to leave me with numerical integration as the only reasonable
>>> strategy.
>>>
>>> The minor problem is that computing the expected outcome for each
>>> individual, given all the covariates and a set of parameter values, is
>>> not always straightforward because the models may have truncation,
>>> censoring, or mixtures.
>>>
>>> At the moment B is a count; C is multinomial; and D is binary.
>>>
>>> I'm thinking of capturing the predicted means directly when feasible.
>>> This should increase precision, but does not eliminate the need to draw
>>> repeatedly for each parameter set.
>>>

messages.subject: (R/Py/Cmd)Stan 2.1.0
messages.body_plain:
We're happy to announce the release of Stan C++, CmdStan,
RStan, and PyStan 2.1.0.  This is a minor feature release,
but it is also an important bug fix release.  As always, the
place to start is the (all new) Stan web pages:

  http://mc-stan.org/

Major Bug in 2.0.0, 2.0.1
------------------------------
Stan 2.0.0 and Stan 2.0.1 introduced a bug in the implementation
of the NUTS criterion that led to poor tail exploration and
thus biased the posterior uncertainty downward.  There was no
bug in NUTS in Stan 1.3 or earlier, and 2.1 has been extensively tested
and tests put in place so this problem will not recur.

If you are using Stan 2.0.0 or 2.0.1, you should switch to 2.1.0 as
soon as possible and rerun any models you care about.

New Target Acceptance Rate Default for Stan 2.1.0
------------------------------
Another big change aimed at reducing posterior estimation bias
was an increase in the target acceptance rate during adaptation
from 0.65 to 0.80.  The bad news is that iterations will take
around 50% longer because of the reduced step size required to
achieve the higher acceptance rate.  The good news is that chains
should be less variable and tails of hierarchical models should
be explored more efficiently (in particular, fewer "stuck" chains).

There are also new configuration parameters that let you control how
long the various phases of adaptation last, with explanations in the
command section of the manual.

The change was motivated by:

    M. J. Betancourt, Mark Girolami.  2013.
    Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Models.
    http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906

New Features and Minor Bug Fixes
------------------------------
The full list can be found in the release notes at:

    https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/tag/v2.1.0

The highlights in addition to adaptation are a switch to BFGS
as the default optimizer (about an order of magnitude faster and
also more stable), fixes to bugs in bin/print for CmdStan for
matrices, bug fixes to multi_normal_prec(), bernoulli(), bernoulli_logit(),
and Phi(), sd(), var(), all of which are now more stable for vectorization and
arithmetic (former bugs caused crashes, not wrong answers).  Windows
now builds in 64-bit mode, and g++ 4.4 now works.  There were also many
updates to clarify the manual.

As always, we'd love to hear from you on our mailing lists if
you have suggestions, bug reports, problems installing, etc.

- Stan Development Team

messages.subject: a Waic example!
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I've programmed a simple example of WAIC for the example on p.165 and p.177 of BDA3.  Attached are three files:
waic_example.R
lm_waic.stan
hibbs.dat

I have some thoughts on how we could alter Stan to do this automatically.  The simplest approach would be to just put a function waic() in rstan that looks in the output for the variable "log_lik" and, if such a variable exists, calculates Waic.  A more comprehensive approach would allow tagging of the Stan model so that certain lines of code would be identified with the loglikelihood so that "log_lik" would get calculated automatically.

By the way:  in calculating Waic, we do want to use the full loglik (including the normalizing factor); this gets done automatically when we use increment_log_prob in Stan. If we did it using tagging, we'd just have to be sure to remember to include those factors.

---

messages.subject: implementing waic
messages.body_plain:
We could do Waic in rstan as is (just using the function I already wrote!), conditional on the user creating the log_lik vector correctly in the Stan program.  But maybe it makes sense to get it working in regular Stan using tagging.  That sort of user intervention (tagging lines in the model as components in the loglik vector) would be necessary in any case.  There's no way that it could be done automatically given only the log posterior function with no labeling.

I do think, however, that we should be able to do it without setting up intermediate log probability variables.  I think it should be possible (at least for many many common examples) to just have the user tag the appropriate lines in the model as being log-likleihood terms.

A

messages.subject: Another question about fitting linear mixed models
messages.subject_clean: Another question about fitting linear mixed models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to understand the difference between these two lmer models in the context of Stan:

m2<-lmer(rrt~so+(1+so|subj)+(1|item),headnoun)
m3<-lmer(rrt~so+(1|subj)+(so-1|subj)+(1|item),headnoun)

Thanks to Sergio, Bob, and Andrew, I understand now how the prior for the correlation matrix is defined for m2 such that we can get a posterior distribution for the variance covariance matrix of the random effects.

In model m3, we have one variance component for varying intercepts by subject, say:

sigma_u[1] ~ normal(0,5)

and another variance component for slopes, also by subject, say

sigma_u[2] ~ normal(0,5)

Importantly, the correlation parameter is not estimated in m3, i.e., lmer does not print out any correlation value.

For pedagogical reasons, I was wondering whether I can dispense with the variance-covariance matrix completely (and therefore any prior for the correlation matrix). I could simply define two priors for the two components shown above.

When I do this in Stan, I get pretty comparable results with respect to lmer (fully worked example below---my apologies to Bob for not indenting my comments properly). My question is: is this a correct way to fit the model m3, i.e., without specifying a prior for the correlation matrix? Or is it technically incorrect to do this, i.e., is it always necessary to specify such multiple variance components in terms of the variance-covariance matrix?

Here are the estimates from Stan vs lmer for the variance components in m2 vs m3. The items std deviation is much larger in Stan, but this is not an important detail, the Stan estimate is realistic.

## m2:
##                    Stan  lmer
#subjintercept   0.6  0.610
#subjslope        0.1  0.229
#item                 6.3  0.331 <= don't match
#error                1.0  0.946
## m3
##                     Stan                              lmer
#subjintercept   0.6                               0.610
#subjslope        0.2 (was 0.1 in m2)     0.229
#item                4.2 (was 6.3 in m2)     0.331 <= don't match
#error               1.0                               0.946

##Code:

## varying intercepts and varying slopes, without correlation (m3):
data<-read.table("gibsonwu2012data.txt",header=T)
## convert to reciprocal rt:
data$rrt<- -1000/data$rt
## contrast coding:
data$so <- ifelse(
  data$type%in%c("subj-ext"),-0.5,0.5)

headnoun.dat <- list(subj=
                       sort(as.integer(
                         factor(headnoun$subj) )),
                     item=sort(as.integer(
                       factor(headnoun$item) )),
                     rrt = headnoun$rrt,
                     so = headnoun$so,
                     N = nrow(headnoun),
                     I =
                       length( unique(headnoun$subj) ),
                     K =
                       length( unique(headnoun$item) )
)

varyingintslopes_codev2 <- 'data {
int<lower=1> N;
real rrt[N];   //outcome
real so[N];   //predictor
int<lower=1> I;   //number of subjects
int<lower=1> K;   //number of items
int<lower=1, upper=I> subj[N];  //subject id
int<lower=1, upper=K> item[N];  //item id
}
parameters {
vector[2] beta;      // intercept and slope
vector[2] u[I];   // random intercept and slope
real w[K];   // random intercept item
real<lower=0> sigma_e;  // residual sd
vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_u;   // subj sd
real<lower=0> sigma_w;   // item sd
}
model {
real mu[N];   // mu for likelihood
for (i in 1:I) u[i,1] ~ normal(0, sigma_u[1]);
for (i in 1:I) u[i,2] ~ normal(0, sigma_u[2]);
for (k in 1:K) w[k] ~ normal(0,sigma_w);
for (n in 1:N) {
mu[n] <- beta[1] + beta[2]*so[n] + u[subj[n], 1] + u[subj[n], 2]*so[n];
}
rrt ~ normal(mu,sigma_e);    // likelihood
beta ~ normal(0,5);
sigma_e ~ normal(0,5);
sigma_u ~ normal(0,5);
sigma_w ~ normal(0,5);
}
'

library(rstan)
set_cppo("fast")

fitv2 <- stan(model_code = varyingintslopes_codev2,
            data = headnoun.dat,
            iter = 1000, chains = 2)

print(fitv2)

--
Shravan Vasishth
Professor for Psycholinguistics und Neurolinguistics
Department of Linguistics
University of Potsdam, Germany
http://www.ling.uni-potsdam.de/~vasishth

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Another question about fitting linear mixed models
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Shravan. I think that your m3 is a way to have varying intercepts and varying slopes while forcing their correlation to be 0. I'd guess that is a bad idea, it should be better to allow that covariance to be estimated.  But . . . in regular lmer, the cov is estimated by maximum likelihood so it can be unstable.  I think blmer would work better; see here:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/ms.pdf
In Stan it should be fine because you're averaging over the posterior distribution of the cov matrix rather than using a noisy point estimate.
A

messages.subject: Understanding Model-Specific Speed Decrease between Stan 1.3 and Stan 2.x
messages.subject_clean: Understanding Model-Specific Speed Decrease between Stan 1.3 and Stan 2.x
messages.body_plain:
Dear wonderful Stan list,

I've spent the past several months using Stan in the context of causal inference models. Overall, Stan has been a life-saver, allowing me to fit vastly more complicated models than I would be able to quickly code by hand. So thanks again for making such a great product.

I'm writing because the upgrade from Stan 1.3 to Stan 2.x (both 2.0 and 2.1) proved to be a mixed blessing for the kinds of models I've been focusing on. On the one hand, effective sample sizes for the same models are marginally higher overall under Stan 2.1 than Stan 1.3. On the other, total computation time for the same number of iterations increased dramatically between v.1.3 and v.2.x, often by a factor of 3 or 4 in some of the more complicated models. While I haven't done a particularly scientific side-by-side (it's a pain to uninstall and re-install different versions), I'm confident that there's been a sizable decrease in ESS/sec when using Stan 2.x for these kinds of models.

I have two related questions.

First, is there a way to re-create the old Stan 1.3 default sampler behavior using the current version? I realize that this is not a sustainable question for future versions, but if someone's already thought about this, it would make it much easier for me to isolate the source of the slow-down and better understand the trade-offs in this case. (I've indeed tinkered with the sampler options but have yet to find a consistent speed-up)

Second, I've attached some much-simplified example Stan code, which is based on Hirano, Imbens, Rubin, and Zhou (2000; Biostatistics). Unfortunately, I can't post the original data set, but am happy to email it directly to folks if that's useful. My actual data set of interest involves many more bells-and-whistles, but the overall speed change seems to hold for this simpler model. I very much welcome suggestions on how to speed up this base model (note that I've been hard-coding the 'softmax' transform given the persistent memory leak issues there).

Thanks, as always, for the help. Session info below.

Best,
Avi

messages.body_plain:
A,

Thanks for the response. I've messed around with a few vectorization approaches for the big 'for' loop. But these tend to be clunky due to the need to add (i.e., 'log_sum_exp') mixture terms. More importantly, doing so doesn't seem to increase the speed all that much, since 'for' loops are pretty damn fast on their own!

Of course, the 'softmax' part is still an extra loop (though N_type is typically very small; e.g., 2 or 3):

    for(k in 1:N_type){
      pi[k] <- exp(gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n]);
    }
    pi <- pi/sum(pi);

Unfortunately, when I've tried to directly use 'softmax' here, I didn't see any speed-up. It's possible that this could change with the latest hot fix, but I'm not too hopeful.

Of course, I'll do whatever works. If there's an elegant vectorization that I've missed, I'd love to hear about it.

Thanks,
Avi

messages.body_plain:
Avi,

One suggestion on your model -- using softmax to compute pi will be more efficient.  Or it should be if we didn't have a memory leak in the softmax code right now.  Once its fixed you should definitely make the change.

The biggest difference in 2.1 that would effect performance is the increasing of the target acceptance probability to improve the robustness of our sampler, particularly for hierarchical models.  You can recreate the 1.3 behavior by setting adapt delta=0.65, but be careful that you're not biasing the samples!  1.3 might be faster but also might be biased in the tails.  For more information about the possible issues and some relevant diagnostics, see http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906.

> More importantly, doing so doesn't seem to increase the speed all that much, since 'for' loops are pretty damn fast on their own!

Vectorization isn't trying to avoid the for loop, it has to do with our autodiff implementation.  Needless to say, for the current version
of Stan creating a temporary array to hold each type of data and then using the vectorized calls will be MUCH faster.  In your case
you can do even better since the groups are partitioned by data that can be done in preprocessing, either external to Stan or in
the transformed data block.

What you'll want to do here is compute the sums over each group first (using the vectorized bernoulli_logit_log and separate
arrays for each group/alpha_type) then sum over the mixture components in increment_log_prob.

(Actually, looking at the model again you may be boned.  If the mixture is over each datum individually then there's nothing you can do).

>
> Of course, the 'softmax' part is still an extra loop (though N_type is typically very small; e.g., 2 or 3):
>
>     for(k in 1:N_type){
>       pi[k] <- exp(gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n]);
>     }
>     pi <- pi/sum(pi);
>
> Unfortunately, when I've tried to directly use 'softmax' here, I didn't see any speed-up. It's possible that this could change with the latest hot fix, but I'm not too hopeful.

Hypothetically, softmax will make the code easier to read so there's really no reason not to use it.  Of course you shouldn't use it
yet because of the bug.  The sampling issue here is that the gamma_type and delta are non-identified because of the constraint
and the way you've written your model there's not way to place the more-appropriate simplex data type in here.

messages.subject: speeding up softmax-based models
messages.body_plain:
[changed subject for a slight digression]

There's also a basic problem with non-identifiability of
softmax-based parameterizations which requires one of
two solutions to identify well:  (1) keep one of the
values fixed, as is typically done in a K-1-ary logistic
regression in the statistics world, or (2) provide strong
priors for whatever goes into determining the components.

In the loop under discussion:

 >>      for(k in 1:N_type){
 >>        pi[k] <- exp(gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n]);
 >>      }
 >>      pi <- pi/sum(pi);

This means either setting one of the pi[k] = 0, or
putting strong priors on gamma_type[k] in particular to
avoid the translation non-identifiability (add z to all
of the pi and you get the same answer.

For solution 2, you can also simplify the whole thing and
write:

   pi <- softmax(gamma_type + delta * x[n]);

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Understanding Model-Specific Speed Decrease between Stan 1.3 and Stan 2.x
messages.body_plain:
I.  There's nothing to be gained speedwise from doing this:

   for (n in 1:N)
     ... set log_p_vec[n] <- ...val comp for n ...
   }

   increment_log_prob( sum(log_p_vec) );

instead of:

   for (n in 1:N)
     ... increment_log_prob(...val comp for n...); ...

The increment_log_prob builds up its own internal
vector and applies a big sum at the end that includes all
of the contributions of Jacobians and sampling statements and
other increment_log_prob calls.    In fact, it'll be faster
than writing out into an array because (a) no array or
allocation or copies, and (b) flatter auto-diff expression
tree because the val will be flattened into every other
component of the log_prob (such as the priors here).

II.  What would speed things up is only computing
pi[k] / sum(pi) for the k that you need.  You only use
one per loop and then you take the log, so that'd be:

     for(k in 1:N_type)
       pi[k] <- exp(gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n]);

as is, and then instead of using

     pi <- pi/sum(pi);

and then pulling out one of the pi and logging it, as in
log(pi[k]), use:

     log(pi[k] / sum(pi))

which is the same as:

    log(pi[k]) - log(sum(pi)).

You could keep going and instead of taking the
log of an exp for log(pi[k]), just use

     for(k in 1:N_type)
       pi[k] <- gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n];

(FWIW, I don't like setting variables and the renormalizing;  I
know we do it in our examples, but here, two variables pi and exp_pi
would be preferable --- I should update our doc.)

Then, for whichever component j you use, just do:

the log_sum_exp operation.

> I.  There's nothing to be gained speedwise from doing this:

>   for (n in 1:N)

>   }
>
>   increment_log_prob( sum(log_p_vec) );

> instead of:
>

>     ... increment_log_prob(...val comp for n...); ...
>
> The increment_log_prob builds up its own internal
> vector and applies a big sum at the end that includes all
> of the contributions of Jacobians and sampling statements and
> other increment_log_prob calls.    In fact, it'll be faster
> than writing out into an array because (a) no array or
> allocation or copies, and (b) flatter auto-diff expression
> tree because the val will be flattened into every other
> component of the log_prob (such as the priors here).

> II.  What would speed things up is only computing

> the log_sum_exp operation.

Speaking of which, thanks for that helpful summary of the two softmax approaches. I've been going back and forth between them for some time now and haven't noticed a difference in speed or stability either way. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speeding up softmax-based models
messages.body_plain:
Really the probabilities need to be parameterized in the (n-1)-dimensional
latent space, but that's non-trivial for the model as defined here.  Really
you'd need to define some product of simplices that yields another simplex.

On Dec 30, 2013, at 6:14 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> [changed subject for a slight digression]
>
> There's also a basic problem with non-identifiability of
> softmax-based parameterizations which requires one of
> two solutions to identify well:  (1) keep one of the
> values fixed, as is typically done in a K-1-ary logistic
> regression in the statistics world, or (2) provide strong
> priors for whatever goes into determining the components.
>
> In the loop under discussion:
>
> >>      for(k in 1:N_type){
> >>        pi[k] <- exp(gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n]);
> >>      }
> >>      pi <- pi/sum(pi);

> This means either setting one of the pi[k] = 0, or
> putting strong priors on gamma_type[k] in particular to
> avoid the translation non-identifiability (add z to all
> of the pi and you get the same answer.
>
> For solution 2, you can also simplify the whole thing and
> write:
>
>  pi <- softmax(gamma_type + delta * x[n]);
>
> - Bob

messages.body_plain:
Why is that a problem?  Just make gamma_type and delta
of dimension (N_type - 1) and use:

   for(k in 1:(N_type - 1))

     pi[k] <- exp(gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n]);

   pi[N_type] <- 0;

At least that's the usual multi-logit used in the GLM
world in stats.  If you read the machine learning literature,
they usually use N dimensions instead of (N - 1) and don't
bother with identifiability.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Vectorization only makes things faster in Stan if it
reduces the size of the expression tree.  It's a bit
subtle to tell where that is, but it's basically when
you reuse the same input for multiple outputs (as in
scalar * vector) or reuse multiple inputs for the same
output (as in the vectorized probability functions).
In contrast, exp(vector) is no faster than the loop, just
easier to write.

- Bob

messages.subject: Numeric overflow
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone.

I've been wrestling with this issue for a couple days now and I'm pretty much out of ideas. I'm using Pystan to fit a model (model string and dat attached). Python version is 3.3.3. 64bit Linux, Kernel 3.12.3-1-ARCH, 8GB memory. gcc is version 4.8.2 and I believe that's what Stan is using (I've seen gcc errors before).

I'm getting a numeric overflow exception when trying to fit a model with 3 chains and 10000 saved steps. The model is fairly simple and the data seems valid, so I'm not really sure what's going on. The model is being fit in a big loop - I'm fitting on the order of 100 models in a long batch job. The exception occurs non-deterministically in this loop, no doubt due to the Monte Carlo nature of the sampler.

Is it reasonable to call a model valid if I continually re-fit until the exception doesn't occur, or should I be changing the model so that it does not numerically overflow 100% of the time. Is there a clear reason why I'm seeing this behaviour?

Thanks for any help.

messages.body_plain:
Are you just seeing a warning or is exception causing the code to die?  Numerical overflow
should lead to rejected samples, which is fine statistically if inefficient.

For best performance, however, try to make your model more well-posed.  Try tighter priors
or reparameterizing so that the bulk of the posterior mass is within a reasonable range.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Numeric overflow
messages.body_plain:
I'm surprised you're getting overflow given the fairly dispersed
data you have.   Even some mild priors on alpha and beta should
solve the problem, though --- you're using an improper prior that's
uniform on (0,inf).  Gelman et al. discuss priors for beta distributions
in chapter 5 and reparameterize in terms of mean alpha/(alpha + beta)
and total count (alpha + beta) --- we use that as an example in the
reparameterization chapter of the manul.

Unfortunately for this model choice, your data don't look like they come from
a beta distribution --- the data looks multimodal concentrated around .99
and .36 (with all the values around 0.36 apparently identical).
So a simple beta distribution won't be very good for this
data, even when you get the model to fit.  So I'm guessing the model runs
off to fit one of the modes really well.

I'd also suggest a constraint on the data variables N and y, because your
model requires N >= 0 and 0 < y[n] < 1.  It won't change behavior,
only help with error checking.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speeding up softmax-based models
messages.body_plain:
On 12/31/13, 8:34 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> Why is that a problem?  Just make gamma_type and delta
>> of dimension (N_type - 1) and use:
>>
>> for(k in 1:(N_type - 1))
>>    pi[k] <- exp(gamma_type[k] + delta[k] * x[n]);
>> pi[N_type] <- 0;
>>
>> At least that's the usual multi-logit used in the GLM
>> world in stats.
>
> But then pi[N_type] is always zero -- isn't that an odd modeling choice?

It's standard to identify the model.  They even discuss it in
the Wikipedia entry under identifiability:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_logistic_regression

saying:

   Because only differences of vectors of regression coefficients are used,
   adding an arbitrary constant to all coefficient vectors has no effect on the
   model. This means that, just as in the log-linear model, only K-1 of the
   coefficient vectors are identifiable, and the last one can be set to an arbitrary
   value (e.g. 0).

The downside is that then the priors don't make a lot of sense
due to the asymmetry of the parameterization.

>> If you read the machine learning literature,
>> they usually use N dimensions instead of (N - 1) and don't
>> bother with identifiability.
>
> Sure, but when you only care about point prediction identifiability isn't so important!

Because only differences of vectors of regression coefficients are used, adding an arbitrary constant to all coefficient
vectors has no effect on the model. This means that, just as in the log-linear model, only K-1 of the coefficient
vectors are identifiable, and the last one can be set to an arbitrary value (e.g. 0).

I assume that's why they don't care about it.  It
does make error checking problematic as well as convergence monitoring
if you look at parameters and have some randomization.  Hastie et al.'s
machine learning book uses the (K-1)-parameterization, whereas Bishop's
uses the K-parameterization.  This confused me so much a few years ago that
I had to work through all the math myself:

We should really be providing a (K-1)-parameterized softmax along with
a complete multi-logit model.  The gradients are really simple and it
would be much much faster than using softmax the way we do now.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 12/31/13, 6:51 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I'd prefer to parameterize in K dimensions, that just seems cleaner.

I agree that it's cleaner.  But you have to have stronger priors
to avoid all the problems of (additively) non-identifiable models (or singular
models in Watanabe's terminology), such as effective sample size
and R-hat measurements.  For example, your general Cauchy-prior recommendation
is a disaster in terms of sampling efficiency.

You can mitigate the convergence monitoring problem by creating generated quantities
by subtracting the K-th coefficient from all coefficients, but that's not so
easy in a GLM.  And it doesn't help with adaptation.

I've played around with this a bit and the K-dimensional parameterization
requires MANY more samples to converge or much stronger priors.

- Bob
